T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the AVR in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Automatically maintains constant output voltage by controlling excitation current
T01_Alternator.exp: AVR = Automatic Voltage Regulator. It senses terminal voltage and adjusts field current to keep voltage constant under varying loads.

T01_Alternator.q: In a brushless alternator, the rotating rectifiers are mounted on:
T01_Alternator.a: The rotor shaft
T01_Alternator.exp: Rotating rectifiers (diodes) are on the rotor shaft, converting AC from exciter to DC for the main field winding — no brushes needed.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is a brushless alternator preferred in marine applications?
T01_Alternator.a: No brush/slip ring maintenance, no sparking, suitable for humid environments
opts: No brush/slip ring maintenance, no sparking, suitable for humid environments
T01_Alternator.exp: No carbon brush dust, no sparking in hazardous areas, suitable for UMS (unattended machinery spaces).

T01_Alternator.q: What does 'droop' refer to in parallel generator operation?
T01_Alternator.a: Deliberate slight speed reduction with increasing load for stable load sharing
opts: Deliberate slight speed reduction with increasing load for stable load sharing
T01_Alternator.exp: Droop characteristic allows governors to share load automatically. Without droop, two generators on bus would 'hunt' — fighting each other for load.

T01_Alternator.q: Before synchronising a generator, which conditions must be met?
T01_Alternator.a: Voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle must match
opts: Voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle must match
T01_Alternator.exp: All four conditions: same voltage magnitude, same frequency, same phase sequence, and same phase angle (confirmed by synchroscope at 12 o'clock position moving slowly clockwise).

T01_Alternator.q: What happens if a generator is closed onto busbar with wrong phase sequence?
T01_Alternator.a: Violent mechanical shock, possible winding damage, catastrophic failure
opts: Violent mechanical shock, possible winding damage, catastrophic failure
Automatic protection trips instantly with no damage
T01_Alternator.exp: Phase sequence reversal causes the machine to act as a brake against itself — enormous current surge and mechanical stress.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the function of a synchroscope?
T01_Alternator.a: Indicates phase difference and relative speed between incoming and running generator
opts: Indicates phase difference and relative speed between incoming and running generator
T01_Alternator.exp: Pointer rotating clockwise = incoming is fast (slightly). Pointer at 12 o'clock = in phase. Close breaker just before 12 o'clock while rotating slowly clockwise.

T01_Alternator.q: Air gap in a marine alternator is typically:
T01_Alternator.a: 2–4 mm
T01_Alternator.exp: Typical air gap is 2–4 mm. Uneven air gap causes vibration, noise, unbalanced magnetic pull and affects output waveform.

T01_Alternator.q: How is the air gap of an alternator measured?
T01_Alternator.a: Using feeler gauges at multiple points around the circumference
opts: Using feeler gauges at multiple points around the circumference
T01_Alternator.exp: Feeler gauges inserted between rotor and stator at 4–8 positions. Values should be within ±10% of each other.

T01_Alternator.q: An open-circuited rotating diode in a brushless alternator causes:
T01_Alternator.a: Reduced output voltage and increased ripple/vibration
opts: Reduced output voltage and increased ripple/vibration
T01_Alternator.exp: One diode failing open means only part of the AC cycle is rectified — unbalanced DC to field, causing voltage reduction and vibration.

T01_Alternator.q: A short-circuited rotating diode causes:
T01_Alternator.a: Heavy field current, high voltage output, possible AVR instability
opts: Heavy field current, high voltage output, possible AVR instability
T01_Alternator.exp: Shorted diode short-circuits part of field circuit — current circulates, causing overheating, high excitation, and hunting.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the reverse power relay?
T01_Alternator.a: Trips the generator breaker if the machine starts motoring (taking power from busbar)
opts: Trips the generator breaker if the machine starts motoring (taking power from busbar)
T01_Alternator.exp: If prime mover fails with breaker closed, alternator would run as synchronous motor — consuming power. Reverse power relay detects this and opens breaker.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'preferential trip' / 'dead ship protection'?
T01_Alternator.a: Sequential shedding of non-essential loads when generator is overloaded, to maintain essential services
opts: Sequential shedding of non-essential loads when generator is overloaded, to maintain essential services
T01_Alternator.exp: Loads shed in pre-set sequence (non-essential first) to prevent generator overload trip. Essential services (steering, fire pump, navigation) preserved.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the typical insulation class of marine alternator windings?
T01_Alternator.a: Class F (155°C)
T01_Alternator.exp: Class F is standard for marine alternators — allows operation at higher temperatures common in engine rooms.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'flashing the field' of an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Applying a momentary DC voltage to restore residual magnetism in the field core
opts: Applying a momentary DC voltage to restore residual magnetism in the field core
T01_Alternator.exp: If residual magnetism is lost, voltage won't build up. Momentary DC (usually from battery) restores residual flux and allows voltage to build.

T01_Alternator.q: What safeties are typically fitted to a ship's alternator/generator?
T01_Alternator.a: Reverse power, overspeed, overcurrent, earth fault, low oil pressure, high temperature
opts: Reverse power, overspeed, overcurrent, earth fault, low oil pressure, high temperature
T01_Alternator.exp: Both electrical (reverse power, overcurrent, earth fault, undervoltage) and mechanical (overspeed, low lube oil, high coolant temp) protections.

T01_Alternator.q: Two alternators in parallel — one has higher KW, other has lower KW. Likely cause?
T01_Alternator.a: Governor settings differ — one governor allows more fuel than the other
opts: Governor settings differ — one governor allows more fuel than the other
T01_Alternator.exp: KW (active power) is shared by governor/speed control. Unequal KW = unequal governor droop settings. Adjust governor of the heavily loaded machine.

T01_Alternator.q: Two alternators in parallel — one has higher KVAR, other lower. Likely cause?
T01_Alternator.a: AVR settings differ — one has higher excitation voltage
opts: AVR settings differ — one has higher excitation voltage
T01_Alternator.exp: KVAR (reactive power) is shared by excitation/AVR. Unequal KVAR = unequal excitation. Adjust AVR of the over-excited machine.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the significance of the KVA rating of a generator?
T01_Alternator.a: Maximum apparent power it can deliver continuously without overheating
opts: Maximum apparent power it can deliver continuously without overheating
T01_Alternator.exp: KVA = KW/PF. At unity PF, KVA = KW. At low PF, same KVA delivers less KW. Stator current (hence heating) depends on KVA, not KW.

T01_Alternator.q: Emergency generator SOLAS requirement — automatic starting must occur within:
T01_Alternator.a: 45 seconds for cargo ships, 30 seconds for passenger ships
opts: 45 seconds for cargo ships, 30 seconds for passenger ships
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1/43: cargo ships 45 seconds, passenger ships 30 seconds after main power failure.

T01_Alternator.q: Emergency generator fuel flash point must be:
T01_Alternator.a: Above 43°C (SOLAS requirement)
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1/43.3.2: fuel for emergency generator must have flash point not less than 43°C. That's why diesel not gasoline — safety in ER.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the damper winding (amortisseur) in a synchronous machine?
T01_Alternator.a: Dampen oscillations during load changes and assist starting
opts: Dampen oscillations during load changes and assist starting
T01_Alternator.exp: Short-circuited bars in rotor face — induced currents oppose oscillations (hunting). Also allows synchronous motor to start as induction motor.

T01_Alternator.q: What reading would you expect from an IR test on a healthy alternator winding?
T01_Alternator.a: Greater than 1 MΩ (and ideally much higher, >100 MΩ for new winding)
opts: Greater than 1 MΩ (and ideally much higher, >100 MΩ for new winding)
T01_Alternator.exp: Polarization Index (PI) test: IR at 10 min / IR at 1 min ≥ 2 indicates healthy insulation. Minimum 1 MΩ required before starting.

T01_Alternator.q: What voltage and frequency is standard for ship's main power supply?
T01_Alternator.a: 440V, 60Hz (common) or 440V/380V, 50Hz/60Hz depending on flag
T01_Alternator.exp: Most merchant ships: 440V, 60Hz. Some European vessels: 380V, 50Hz. Emergency lighting: often 220V single phase. High power ships: 6.6kV or 11kV.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of a load-dependent start (LDS) in an automatic power management system?
T01_Alternator.a: Automatically starts standby generator when connected load exceeds a set percentage of running capacity
opts: Starts generator at fixed time intervals
Automatically starts standby generator when connected load exceeds a set percentage of running capacity
T01_Alternator.exp: LDS prevents overload by bringing on second generator before first becomes overloaded. Typical setting: 70–80% of rated KW.

T01_Alternator.q: What is a synchronous motor?
T01_Alternator.a: AC motor that runs exactly at synchronous speed (NS = 120f/P), with no slip
opts: AC motor that runs exactly at synchronous speed (NS = 120f/P), with no slip
T01_Alternator.exp: NS = 120f/P. No slip. Used for constant speed drives and as synchronous capacitor for PF correction.

T01_Alternator.q: What checks must be done before closing an ACB for synchronisation?
T01_Alternator.a: Voltage match, frequency match, synchroscope at 12 slowly clockwise, phase sequence verified
opts: Voltage match, frequency match, synchroscope at 12 slowly clockwise, phase sequence verified
T01_Alternator.exp: All four synchronising conditions must be met. Phase sequence checked once at installation — not every time. Voltage, freq and phase angle checked every sync.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you test the overspeed trip of a diesel generator?
T01_Alternator.a: Gradually increase speed by adjusting governor until overspeed trip activates (typically 115% of rated speed)
opts: Disconnect governor and let engine run freely
Gradually increase speed by adjusting governor until overspeed trip activates (typically 115% of rated speed)
T01_Alternator.exp: Mechanical overspeed trip typically set at 110–115% of rated speed. Test with generator off-load, gradually increasing speed via governor control. Record test in logbook.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the Ward Leonard system used for?
T01_Alternator.a: Variable speed DC drive for applications like cranes, winches, and steering gear
opts: Variable speed DC drive for applications like cranes, winches, and steering gear
T01_Alternator.exp: Generator-motor set: AC motor drives DC generator, DC generator output feeds DC motor. Smooth, wide-range speed control by varying field excitation.

T01_Alternator.q: Why must alternator AVR be disconnected before megger testing?
T01_Alternator.a: High megger voltage would damage AVR electronic components
opts: High megger voltage would damage AVR electronic components
T01_Alternator.exp: AVR contains sensitive electronics (transistors, ICs) that cannot withstand the 500V–1000V applied during insulation resistance testing.

T01_Alternator.q: Nominal speed of a 4-pole alternator on a 60 Hz system is:
T01_Alternator.a: 1800 RPM
T01_Alternator.exp: NS = 120f/P = 120×60/4 = 1800 RPM. For 50 Hz with 4 poles: NS = 1500 RPM.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the exciter in a brushless alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Provides AC supply that is rectified to give DC field current for main alternator
opts: Provides AC supply that is rectified to give DC field current for main alternator
T01_Alternator.exp: Small AC exciter (stator fixed, rotor rotates) → rotating diodes rectify → DC fed to main rotor field → main alternator produces 3-phase output.

T01_Alternator.q: Hunting in parallel generators refers to:
T01_Alternator.a: Oscillation of load between generators due to poor governor response
opts: Oscillation of load between generators due to poor governor response
T01_Alternator.exp: Hunting occurs when governor droop is insufficient or governors have different characteristics. Load swings back and forth between machines.

T01_Alternator.q: What action if voltage not building up after starting alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Check residual magnetism, test AVR, check diodes, check exciter winding, check field connections
opts: Check residual magnetism, test AVR, check diodes, check exciter winding, check field connections
T01_Alternator.exp: Systematic approach: check battery exciter supply → flash field if needed → test AVR output → check rotating diodes → check exciter winding IR → check main field connections.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the PI (Polarisation Index) test?
T01_Alternator.a: Ratio of 10-minute to 1-minute megger reading; PI ≥ 2 indicates good insulation
opts: Ratio of 10-minute to 1-minute megger reading; PI ≥ 2 indicates good insulation
T01_Alternator.exp: PI = R10min/R1min. Values: <1 = bad, 1–2 = questionable, ≥2 = good, ≥4 = excellent. Indicates moisture/contamination in winding insulation.

T01_Alternator.q: What is meant by 'cold ironing' or 'shore power connection'?
T01_Alternator.a: Supplying ship's electrical power from shore supply while in port to reduce emissions
opts: Supplying ship's electrical power from shore supply while in port to reduce emissions
T01_Alternator.exp: Shore power (cold ironing) allows engines to be shut down in port. Requires careful synchronisation or transfer switching. May need frequency/voltage conversion if shore ≠ ship standard.

T01_Alternator.q: An alternator is rated 500 kVA at 0.8 PF. What is its kW rating?
T01_Alternator.a: 400 kW

T01_Alternator.q: What is the effect of increasing excitation on an alternator running in parallel?
T01_Alternator.a: Increases reactive power (kVAR) output and raises PF of that machine
opts: Increases reactive power (kVAR) output and raises PF of that machine
T01_Alternator.exp: In parallel operation, excitation controls reactive power sharing. More excitation = more kVAR output = more lagging current supplied to load.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the significance of the number of poles in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Determines synchronous speed: NS = 120f/P
T01_Alternator.exp: More poles = lower synchronous speed. A slow diesel engine (typically 750 RPM) needs 8 poles for 50 Hz output.

T01_Alternator.q: Which type of excitation system eliminates all rotating electrical connections?
T01_Alternator.a: Brushless (static exciter with rotating rectifiers)
T01_Alternator.exp: Brushless system: AC exciter stator (fixed) → AC exciter rotor (rotates) → rotating rectifiers → main field (rotates). Zero rotating electrical contacts.

T01_Alternator.q: What is meant by 'voltage regulation' of an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Percentage change in terminal voltage from no-load to full load: (VNL−VFL)/VFL × 100
opts: Percentage change in terminal voltage from no-load to full load: (VNL−VFL)/VFL × 100
T01_Alternator.exp: Good regulation = small percentage. Marine alternators: typically 3–5% regulation with AVR active, could be 20–40% without AVR.

T01_Alternator.q: What does 'blackout' mean in ship's electrical context?
T01_Alternator.a: Complete loss of electrical power to the main switchboard
opts: Complete loss of electrical power to the main switchboard
T01_Alternator.exp: Total blackout: all generators trip. Emergency generator should start automatically within 45 seconds. ETO priorities: restore power, start emergency gen, restore main gen.

T01_Alternator.q: After a blackout, what is the correct sequence for power restoration?
T01_Alternator.a: Emergency gen starts → main engine cooling → start main gen → synchronise → restore loads in sequence
opts: Emergency gen starts → main engine cooling → start main gen → synchronise → restore loads in sequence
T01_Alternator.exp: Systematic restoration prevents overload. Emergency gen provides essential services first. Main gen started, synchronised, then loads restored in priority order.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the function of the droop resistor in an AVR?
T01_Alternator.a: Causes terminal voltage to droop with increasing reactive current for stable parallel operation
opts: Causes terminal voltage to droop with increasing reactive current for stable parallel operation
T01_Alternator.exp: Without reactive droop, two paralleled generators with identical AVRs would have unstable reactive power sharing — one machine would take all kVAR.

T01_Alternator.q: What is shaft generator (shaft driven generator)?
T01_Alternator.a: Generator driven by main propulsion shaft, providing power at variable frequency corrected by frequency converter
opts: Generator driven by main propulsion shaft, providing power at variable frequency corrected by frequency converter
Emergency generator mounted on propeller shaft
T01_Alternator.exp: Power take-off (PTO) from main engine shaft. Uses frequency converter (cycloconverter or rectifier-inverter) to maintain constant 50/60 Hz output despite varying shaft speed.

T01_Alternator.q: What maintenance is typically done on a brushless alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Check diodes, IR test windings, clean, check connections, check air gap, check bearings, test safeties
opts: Check diodes, IR test windings, clean, check connections, check air gap, check bearings, test safeties
T01_Alternator.exp: Comprehensive PM: IR test all windings, check/test rotating diodes, check bearing condition (vibration, temperature, noise), clean air passages, verify AVR operation, test all protections.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the typical test voltage for a megger test on a 440V alternator winding?
T01_Alternator.a: 500V DC
T01_Alternator.exp: 500V megger for 440V equipment is standard. For 11kV equipment: 2500V–5000V megger. Rule of thumb: megger voltage ≈ twice rated voltage + 1000V (min 500V).

T01_Alternator.q: What is Automatic Mains Failure (AMF)?
T01_Alternator.a: System that automatically starts and connects standby generator when main supply fails
opts: System that automatically starts and connects standby generator when main supply fails
T01_Alternator.exp: AMF panel monitors bus voltage/frequency. On failure, starts standby gen, waits for it to reach stable output, closes breaker. Typical time: <10 seconds for start + stabilise.

T01_Alternator.q: Two generators in parallel — what happens if one governor fails and engine races?
T01_Alternator.a: Overcurrent, reverse power, frequency relay may trip it; mechanical overspeed trip as last resort
opts: Overcurrent, reverse power, frequency relay may trip it; mechanical overspeed trip as last resort
Nothing — the load sharing is stable
T01_Alternator.exp: Racing engine causes that generator to take all load → overcurrent. If it overspeeds, overspeed trip fires. The 'healthy' generator may have breaker open by reverse current from the racing machine.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of current transformers (CTs) on the alternator outputs?
T01_Alternator.a: Step down high currents to safe levels for metering and protection relays
opts: Step down high currents to safe levels for metering and protection relays
T01_Alternator.exp: CTs: typically 5A secondary for standard meters and relays. Never open-circuit a CT secondary when primary is energised — dangerous overvoltage develops.

T01_Alternator.q: What does the AVR sense to regulate voltage?
T01_Alternator.a: Terminal voltage of the alternator (and sometimes reactive current for droop)
opts: Terminal voltage of the alternator (and sometimes reactive current for droop)
T01_Alternator.exp: AVR compares sensed terminal voltage against setpoint. Error signal adjusts field current. Some AVRs also use reactive current droop feedback for parallel operation stability.

T01_Alternator.q: Which protection trips immediately on large overcurrent (instantaneous)?
T01_Alternator.a: Short circuit/overcurrent instantaneous element of ACB
opts: Short circuit/overcurrent instantaneous element of ACB
T01_Alternator.exp: Instantaneous overcurrent (typically 8–10× rated current) operates the ACB trip without intentional time delay — for bus bar faults. IDMT overcurrent has time delay for grading.

T01_Alternator.q: What is meant by 'reactive droop compensation' in AVR?
T01_Alternator.a: AVR reduces excitation slightly as reactive current increases, enabling stable sharing of kVAR between parallel generators
opts: AVR reduces excitation slightly as reactive current increases, enabling stable sharing of kVAR between parallel generators
T01_Alternator.exp: Without reactive droop, parallel generators fight over reactive load. Droop compensation gives a slightly drooping V vs Q characteristic to ensure stable sharing.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the main advantage of static excitation over rotating exciter?
T01_Alternator.a: Faster response time for AVR control and no rotating exciter maintenance
opts: Faster response time for AVR control and no rotating exciter maintenance
T01_Alternator.exp: Static exciter (thyristor-controlled) has millisecond response vs seconds for rotating exciter — better for rapid load changes and transient voltage control.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you calculate synchronous speed?
T01_Alternator.a: NS = 120 × f / P (RPM), where f=frequency in Hz, P=number of poles
opts: NS = 120 × f / P (RPM), where f=frequency in Hz, P=number of poles
T01_Alternator.exp: For 4-pole, 50Hz: NS = 120×50/4 = 1500 RPM. For 6-pole, 60Hz: NS = 120×60/6 = 1200 RPM.

T01_Alternator.q: What type of protection prevents circulating currents between two paralleled generators with slight voltage difference?
T01_Alternator.a: Reactive droop setting in AVR limits circulating reactive current
opts: Reactive droop setting in AVR limits circulating reactive current
T01_Alternator.exp: Small voltage difference causes reactive circulating current. AVR droop compensation limits this. Differential protection (not common on marine generators) would detect internal faults.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you safely remove a generator from parallel operation?
T01_Alternator.a: Transfer load to other generator(s), reduce kW to minimum, open breaker, shut down prime mover
opts: Transfer load to other generator(s), reduce kW to minimum, open breaker, shut down prime mover
T01_Alternator.exp: Never open breaker under heavy load — causes voltage spike and potential damage to loads. Always transfer load first, reduce kW to near zero (reverse power protection will trip if you go negative).

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'cold spare' vs 'hot spare' for standby generator?
T01_Alternator.a: Cold: off and cold; Hot: running and warm, ready to take load faster
opts: Cold: off and cold; Hot: running and warm, ready to take load faster
Cold: on bus at low power; Hot: on bus at full power
Only cold spare used in marine practice
T01_Alternator.exp: Hot standby: engine running, generator on bus at very low load or just spinning in sync — instant load pickup. Cold standby: stopped, needs start time. AMF bridges the gap for cold standby.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the power management system (PMS)?
T01_Alternator.a: Automatically manages generator start/stop, load sharing, fault response and load shedding
opts: Automatically manages generator start/stop, load sharing, fault response and load shedding
T01_Alternator.exp: PMS monitors total load, starts generators before overload, sheds non-essential loads on fault, manages parallel operation — reduces need for manual intervention in UMS operations.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'earth fault' on a generator?
T01_Alternator.a: One or more phases of stator winding making electrical contact with the earthed frame
opts: One or more phases of stator winding making electrical contact with the earthed frame
T01_Alternator.exp: Earth fault: phase conductor contacts machine frame (which is earthed). Detected by earth fault relay (usually 64 relay). On high-resistance earthed systems, fault current is limited.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the construction difference between salient pole and cylindrical rotor alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Salient: protruding poles (low speed, multi-pole), Cylindrical: smooth rotor (high speed, 2-4 poles)
opts: Salient: protruding poles (low speed, multi-pole), Cylindrical: smooth rotor (high speed, 2-4 poles)
Salient is for AC, cylindrical for DC
Salient used for HV, cylindrical for LV
T01_Alternator.exp: Marine diesel-driven: salient pole (slow speed, 6-12 poles). Steam turbine driven: cylindrical (high speed, 2-4 poles). Both are synchronous machines.

T01_Alternator.q: What is a 'dead bus' synchronisation?
T01_Alternator.a: Closing generator onto a dead (de-energised) busbar — no synchronisation needed
opts: Closing generator onto a dead (de-energised) busbar — no synchronisation needed
T01_Alternator.exp: Dead bus: just check that busbar is truly dead, confirm polarity and phase sequence, then close breaker. No synchroscope needed since there's nothing to synchronise to.

T01_Alternator.q: Alternator maintenance schedule — what is checked at 250 running hours?
T01_Alternator.a: Check connections, clean air filters, check bearing temperatures, record insulation values
opts: Check connections, clean air filters, check bearing temperatures, record insulation values
T01_Alternator.exp: Typical 250-hour PM: visual inspection, clean air passages, check and tighten connections, take IR reading, check bearing temperature/vibration trend, check cooler condition.

T01_Alternator.q: What safety precautions before working on an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Isolate main breaker, lock out and tag, prove dead, discharge capacitors, permit to work
opts: Isolate main breaker, lock out and tag, prove dead, discharge capacitors, permit to work
T01_Alternator.exp: Full LOTO procedure. For large generators: wait for rotor to stop completely. Discharge any capacitors in AVR circuit. Earth the stator terminals before working.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the function of a 'trimmer' potentiometer in the AVR?
T01_Alternator.a: Allows fine adjustment of output voltage setpoint
opts: Allows fine adjustment of output voltage setpoint
T01_Alternator.exp: Trimmer on AVR panel allows ±5% voltage adjustment. Used to equalise voltage between two generators before synchronising and for reactive power sharing adjustment.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of a capacitor in the AVR sensing circuit?
T01_Alternator.a: Filters out harmonics and smooths the sensed voltage signal
opts: Filters out harmonics and smooths the sensed voltage signal
T01_Alternator.exp: Harmonics in terminal voltage (from non-linear loads like VFDs) can cause AVR instability. Input filter capacitors smooth the sensing signal.

T01_Alternator.q: How does the load sharing panel enable load sharing between generators?
T01_Alternator.a: Provides cross-current compensation — generators with higher load feed signal to others to increase their load
opts: Provides cross-current compensation — generators with higher load feed signal to others to increase their load
Controls both kW and kVAR automatically without droop
T01_Alternator.exp: Cross-current compensation (circulating current method) allows reactive load sharing without droop — preferred for generators in permanent parallel operation.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of an overvoltage relay on an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Trips generator if output voltage exceeds safe limit (typically 110% of rated)
opts: Trips generator if output voltage exceeds safe limit (typically 110% of rated)
T01_Alternator.exp: Overvoltage could damage loads, especially sensitive electronics. OV relay (typically set at 110%) trips generator breaker. AVR failure causing field forcing is common cause.

T01_Alternator.q: What does a power factor meter on the switchboard indicate?
T01_Alternator.a: Ratio of active power (kW) to apparent power (kVA) — cos φ
opts: Ratio of active power (kW) to apparent power (kVA) — cos φ
T01_Alternator.exp: PF meter: typically reads 0–1 lagging/leading. Most ship loads are inductive (lagging PF 0.8–0.9). Running generators at very low PF is inefficient and stresses the machine.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the difference between KW and KVA?
T01_Alternator.a: KW = actual useful power; KVA = apparent power including reactive component; KW = KVA × PF
opts: KW = actual useful power; KVA = apparent power including reactive component; KW = KVA × PF
KVA is larger only at 50 Hz
KW is always greater than KVA
T01_Alternator.exp: KVA² = KW² + KVAR². At PF = 1.0, KVA = KW. At PF = 0.8, 1000 kVA delivers only 800 kW. Generator is rated in kVA because stator current (heating) depends on total current, not just active component.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the temperature detector (PT100) in the alternator stator?
T01_Alternator.a: Monitors winding temperature to prevent insulation overheating; triggers alarm and trip
opts: Monitors winding temperature to prevent insulation overheating; triggers alarm and trip
T01_Alternator.exp: PT100s embedded in stator slots sense winding temperature. Typical alarm: 120°C, trip: 155°C for Class F insulation. Trend monitoring is important for early fault detection.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'magnetic flux' in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: The total magnetic field produced by the field winding, measured in Webers
opts: The total magnetic field produced by the field winding, measured in Webers
T01_Alternator.exp: Flux density (Tesla) × Area = flux (Weber). Faraday's law: EMF = N × dΦ/dt. Stronger field = higher voltage output (basis of AVR control).

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of harmonic filters on modern ship generators?
T01_Alternator.a: Reduce voltage distortion caused by non-linear loads like VFDs, UPS, and rectifiers
opts: Reduce voltage distortion caused by non-linear loads like VFDs, UPS, and rectifiers
T01_Alternator.exp: Non-linear loads draw non-sinusoidal currents, causing harmonic voltages. Harmonics cause overheating, AVR instability, and interference with electronics. Filters (passive L-C or active) reduce THD.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the SOLAS requirement for emergency source of power on cargo ships?
T01_Alternator.a: SOLAS II-1/43: must supply for minimum 18 hours with specified services
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1/43.2.1: cargo ships — emergency source must supply essential services for minimum 18 hours (passenger ships: 36 hours).

T01_Alternator.q: How is the air gap of an alternator adjusted?
T01_Alternator.a: By shimming or adjusting bearing pedestals/end shields — requires major dismantling
opts: By shimming or adjusting bearing pedestals/end shields — requires major dismantling
T01_Alternator.exp: Air gap adjustment requires opening up the machine, removing rotor, shimming bearing housings. This is class/manufacturer-supervised work, typically done in drydock.

T01_Alternator.q: What are symptoms of an overloaded alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: High stator current, winding temperature rise, voltage drop despite AVR, possible tripping on overcurrent
opts: High stator current, winding temperature rise, voltage drop despite AVR, possible tripping on overcurrent
T01_Alternator.exp: Overload → excessive stator current → I²R heating → insulation damage if prolonged. AVR tries to maintain voltage but may reach field current limit. Action: shed load or start another generator.

T01_Alternator.q: What are the SOLAS requirements for main source of electrical power?
T01_Alternator.a: SOLAS II-1/41: maintain all services needed for normal operation and safety, survive any single failure
opts: SOLAS II-1/41: maintain all services needed for normal operation and safety, survive any single failure
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1/41: main electrical installation must supply all services under normal and emergency conditions. n+1 redundancy concept — losing any single generator must not affect essential services.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the 'dead man alarm' / UMS watchkeeping system?
T01_Alternator.a: Alerts bridge if no manual acknowledgement from ECR within set period — prevents unattended machinery failure going unnoticed
opts: Alerts bridge if no manual acknowledgement from ECR within set period — prevents unattended machinery failure going unnoticed
T01_Alternator.exp: UMS (Unattended Machinery Space) regulations require dead man alarm — officer must acknowledge alarm every 30 minutes (varies by system) or bridge/general alarm sounds.

T01_Alternator.q: What is an 'earth leakage alarm' on the main switchboard?
T01_Alternator.a: Detects insulation leakage to earth in the IT (isolated) distribution system
opts: Detects insulation leakage to earth in the IT (isolated) distribution system
T01_Alternator.exp: Ship's distribution is typically IT (isolated from earth) allowing one fault without current flow. Earth leakage relay detects the first fault and alarms — no trip on first fault. Second fault = short circuit.

T01_Alternator.q: For what reason is the ship's electrical system typically isolated (not solidly earthed)?
T01_Alternator.a: Single earth fault does not cause shock hazard or trip supply — gives time to trace and rectify fault
opts: Single earth fault does not cause shock hazard or trip supply — gives time to trace and rectify fault
T01_Alternator.exp: IT (isolated) system: one fault = no current flows. Allows continued operation while fault is traced. Two simultaneous faults on different phases = direct short circuit — hence earth fault alarm is critical.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the typical no-load voltage droop percentage allowed in AVR specification?
T01_Alternator.a: ±1% of nominal voltage
T01_Alternator.exp: Good AVR specification: voltage regulation ≤1% at no-load to full-load. Response time: <1 second for 10% load change. Modern digital AVRs achieve ±0.5% regulation.

T01_Alternator.q: What are rotating diodes tested with?
T01_Alternator.a: Multimeter on diode test function, or ohmmeter — check forward voltage drop and no reverse conduction
opts: Multimeter on diode test function, or ohmmeter — check forward voltage drop and no reverse conduction
T01_Alternator.exp: Rotating diodes: check with multimeter in diode mode. Forward: ~0.6V drop (silicon). Reverse: open circuit (OL). Short: 0 both ways. Open: OL both ways. Test with rotor stationary and diodes accessible.

T01_Alternator.q: What protection is provided by the 'negative sequence' relay?
T01_Alternator.a: Detects unbalanced phase currents (often due to open circuit or single-phase loading)
opts: Detects unbalanced phase currents (often due to open circuit or single-phase loading)
T01_Alternator.exp: Negative sequence components arise from asymmetrical faults or loads. Cause dangerous rotor overheating in synchronous machines. Negative sequence relay (46) protects large generators.

T01_Alternator.q: How many main generators does a typical merchant ship have?
T01_Alternator.a: Usually 3 generators (2 running for sea passage, 1 standby; 3 running in port for heavy loads)
opts: Usually 3 generators (2 running for sea passage, 1 standby; 3 running in port for heavy loads)
T01_Alternator.exp: Configuration varies: 3 is most common — provides N+1 redundancy. Large ships may have 4 or more. Some modern ships have shaft generator as primary with 2 auxiliaries.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'excitation current' in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: DC current fed to field winding to create magnetic flux for voltage generation
opts: DC current fed to field winding to create magnetic flux for voltage generation
T01_Alternator.exp: Field (excitation) current: typically 5–20A DC for small generators, up to 100A+ for large machines. Controls magnetic flux → controls output voltage → controlled by AVR.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens when a generator's AVR fails in the 'full field' position?
T01_Alternator.a: Generator output voltage rises rapidly, overvoltage trips, equipment potentially damaged
opts: Generator output voltage rises rapidly, overvoltage trips, equipment potentially damaged
No change — another AVR takes over
T01_Alternator.exp: AVR fail to full field = field forcing → voltage shoots up → overvoltage relay should trip generator breaker → if OV relay fails, loads and insulation are at risk.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you determine which of two paralleled generators has the higher load?
T01_Alternator.a: Read kW meters on switchboard for each generator
opts: Read kW meters on switchboard for each generator
T01_Alternator.exp: kW meters directly indicate active power sharing. For reactive sharing, check kVAR meters or power factor meters. Adjust governors for kW, AVR trimmers for kVAR.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'voltage build-up' in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Process by which residual magnetism induces initial voltage, which excites field further, bootstrapping to rated voltage
opts: Process by which residual magnetism induces initial voltage, which excites field further, bootstrapping to rated voltage
T01_Alternator.exp: Residual flux → small induced EMF → AVR senses → increases field current → more flux → more EMF → builds up to rated voltage. If residual magnetism lost, no build-up — flash the field.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'reactive power' and how is it produced in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Non-working power stored/released by reactive elements (inductors/capacitors); produced by increasing excitation
opts: Non-working power stored/released by reactive elements (inductors/capacitors); produced by increasing excitation
T01_Alternator.exp: Reactive power (kVAR) circulates between source and reactive loads without doing work. Inductive loads absorb reactive power; alternator supplies it by being 'over-excited' (field current above normal).

T01_Alternator.q: How is an alternator cooled in marine applications?
T01_Alternator.a: Self-ventilation (fan on rotor), forced air cooling, or closed circuit water cooler (TEWAC)
opts: Self-ventilation (fan on rotor), forced air cooling, or closed circuit water cooler (TEWAC)
T01_Alternator.exp: TEWAC (Totally Enclosed Water-Air Cooled): internal air circulates through water-cooled heat exchanger — no engine room air enters winding. Good protection against salt-laden, humid marine air.

T01_Alternator.q: What records must be kept for generator maintenance?
T01_Alternator.a: Running hours, IR readings, bearing temperatures, maintenance done, faults, test results — in PMS and logbook
opts: Running hours, IR readings, bearing temperatures, maintenance done, faults, test results — in PMS and logbook
T01_Alternator.exp: Good records enable trend analysis (deteriorating IR = impending insulation failure), demonstrate compliance to class surveyor, support planned maintenance intervals.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'field current limit' in AVR?
T01_Alternator.a: Maximum excitation current allowed — prevents overheating of field winding
opts: Maximum excitation current allowed — prevents overheating of field winding
T01_Alternator.exp: If load demands more reactive power than field can supply, AVR hits field current limit. Terminal voltage then drops. Underexcitation limit (UEL) prevents loss of synchronism.

T01_Alternator.q: What action if two paralleled generators have different frequencies (slightly)?
T01_Alternator.a: Adjust governor of the off-speed machine — they must run at same synchronous frequency
opts: Adjust governor of the off-speed machine — they must run at same synchronous frequency
T01_Alternator.exp: In parallel, both machines are locked at same bus frequency. Speed difference shows as circulating currents. Adjust governor on faster/slower machine to achieve equal governor settings and stable operation.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the standard voltage for ship's emergency lighting?
T01_Alternator.a: Typically 220V single phase AC or 24V DC (battery backed)
opts: Typically 220V single phase AC or 24V DC (battery backed)
T01_Alternator.exp: Emergency lighting fed from emergency switchboard (220V from emergency gen) and additionally from independent battery-backed sources for specific areas per SOLAS.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'generator earthing' and why is it done?
T01_Alternator.a: Connecting generator neutral/frame to earth to control touch voltage and assist fault detection
opts: Connecting output to earth for safety
Connecting generator neutral/frame to earth to control touch voltage and assist fault detection
T01_Alternator.exp: Marine generators typically isolated (IT system) — frame earthed for safety, but neutral not solidly earthed. HV generators use high-resistance neutral earthing (NER) to limit earth fault current.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the fundamental principle on which an alternator works?
T01_Alternator.a: Electromagnetic induction (Faraday's Law)
T01_Alternator.exp: Faraday's Law: EMF is induced in a conductor when there is a relative change in magnetic flux. In an alternator, the rotating DC-excited rotor field cuts the stator conductors, inducing AC EMF.

T01_Alternator.q: In a marine alternator, which part rotates and which is stationary?
T01_Alternator.a: Rotor carries DC field winding (rotates); stator carries AC output winding (stationary)
opts: Stator carries field winding; rotor carries output winding
Rotor carries DC field winding (rotates); stator carries AC output winding (stationary)
Both are stationary and EMF is induced by flux changes
T01_Alternator.exp: The rotor field (DC-excited) rotates driven by the prime mover. The stator winding is fixed and has AC induced in it. Output is taken from the stationary stator — no brushes on output side.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is an alternator rated in kVA and not kW?
T01_Alternator.a: Winding heating depends on current (kVA), which is independent of load power factor
opts: kVA is a larger number making the rating look impressive
Because alternators cannot supply real power
Winding heating depends on current (kVA), which is independent of load power factor
kW rating only applies to DC machines
T01_Alternator.exp: Winding copper losses (I²R heating) depend only on current magnitude, regardless of whether the load is resistive or reactive. Since kVA = V × I, and heating is determined by I, the alternator is rated in kVA — it doesn't know the power factor of the load.

T01_Alternator.q: What determines the output frequency of a marine alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: f = (N × P) / 120, where N = RPM and P = number of poles
opts: Only the load connected to it
f = (N × P) / 120, where N = RPM and P = number of poles
T01_Alternator.exp: Frequency is set by mechanical speed and pole pairs. For 60 Hz at 4 poles: N = 1800 RPM. For 50 Hz at 4 poles: N = 1500 RPM. This is why governor control maintains constant frequency.

T01_Alternator.q: In a separately excited alternator, where does the field excitation come from?
T01_Alternator.a: External DC source supplied via slip rings
opts: The alternator supplies its own field via rectifier
External DC source supplied via slip rings
The permanent magnets on the rotor
T01_Alternator.exp: Separately excited means DC field current is supplied from an external source (battery, rectifier) through slip rings. Problem: requires slip rings and brushes, causing maintenance issues in marine environments.

T01_Alternator.q: In a self-excited shunt alternator, what provides the initial excitation?
T01_Alternator.a: Residual magnetism in the rotor core
opts: Residual magnetism in the rotor core
T01_Alternator.exp: Residual magnetism induces a small initial voltage → this feeds back to field winding → field builds up → voltage builds up. This 'bootstrap' process builds voltage from zero. If residual magnetism is lost, flashing is needed.

T01_Alternator.q: What are the THREE machines mounted on the same shaft in a brushless alternator system?
T01_Alternator.a: PMG (Permanent Magnet Generator), Main Exciter, Main Alternator
opts: PMG (Permanent Magnet Generator), Main Exciter, Main Alternator
T01_Alternator.exp: All three rotate together on one shaft: (1) PMG — provides stable AC to feed AVR. (2) Main Exciter — stator is fed by AVR, rotor generates 3-phase AC. (3) Main Alternator — rotor field carries DC (from rotating rectifiers), stator gives 3-phase output.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the function of the PMG (Permanent Magnet Generator) in a brushless system?
T01_Alternator.a: Provides independent, stable AC power supply to the AVR
opts: Directly excites the main alternator field
Provides independent, stable AC power supply to the AVR
Acts as backup generator during blackout
Controls the speed of the prime mover
T01_Alternator.exp: PMG uses permanent magnets, so its output is unaffected by main alternator voltage changes. It provides a clean, stable supply to the AVR. This means the AVR functions correctly even when the main alternator is in fault condition.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is the brushless alternator called 'brushless'?
T01_Alternator.a: No brushes or slip rings are needed to transfer current from stationary to rotating parts
opts: It uses fewer windings than conventional alternators
No brushes or slip rings are needed to transfer current from stationary to rotating parts
The stator does not use carbon brush contacts
It eliminates the need for a commutator
T01_Alternator.exp: In a brushless design, the exciter field is on the stator (stationary), exciter armature is on the rotor. Rotating rectifiers on the shaft convert AC to DC without needing physical contact (no brushes/slip rings). DC goes directly to main field winding on the shaft.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the path of excitation current in a brushless alternator (correct sequence)?
T01_Alternator.a: PMG → AVR → Exciter field stator → Exciter rotor AC → Rotating diodes → Main field rotor → Main stator output
opts: AVR → PMG → Rotating diodes → Main field
Battery → Slip rings → Field winding → Output
PMG → AVR → Exciter field stator → Exciter rotor AC → Rotating diodes → Main field rotor → Main stator output
T01_Alternator.exp: This is the complete brushless excitation chain. PMG generates AC → AVR rectifies and controls → DC fed to exciter stator field → exciter rotor generates 3-phase AC → rotating rectifier diodes convert to DC → DC field on main rotor → main stator cuts field → 3-phase output.

T01_Alternator.q: Where are the rotating rectifier diodes physically located in a brushless alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Mounted on the rotor shaft between the exciter armature and main field winding
opts: On the stator frame near ventilation openings
Mounted on the rotor shaft between the exciter armature and main field winding
In a separate rectifier cabinet next to the alternator
T01_Alternator.exp: Rotating rectifiers are a diode wheel mounted directly on the rotating shaft. They spin with the shaft, converting the exciter's 3-phase AC output to DC. Being on the shaft eliminates the need for slip rings — the DC stays within the rotating assembly.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens if ONE rotating rectifier diode goes OPEN CIRCUIT while the alternator is running?
T01_Alternator.a: Output voltage drops 15–20% with fluctuation; unbalanced excitation causes ripple
opts: Complete loss of voltage — machine trips immediately
Output voltage drops 15–20% with fluctuation; unbalanced excitation causes ripple
No effect — remaining diodes compensate fully
Frequency drops proportionally to voltage drop
T01_Alternator.exp: With one open diode, one phase of the 3-phase exciter output is not rectified. The remaining diodes handle only partial DC. Result: DC ripple in field current → pulsating output voltage. Stroboscope check can detect discoloured/pitted diodes while running.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens if ONE rotating rectifier diode goes SHORT CIRCUIT while running?
T01_Alternator.a: AC component appears in field current causing severe voltage fluctuation and field overheating
opts: Minor voltage fluctuation, self-corrects within minutes
Generator shuts down automatically via thermal protection
AC component appears in field current causing severe voltage fluctuation and field overheating
Output becomes DC instead of AC
T01_Alternator.exp: A shorted diode creates a reverse current path — AC flows through the short, superimposing on the DC field. This causes both severe output voltage fluctuation and dangerous heating in the field winding. Immediate action needed: shut down and inspect.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you detect a faulty rotating diode while the alternator is running?
T01_Alternator.a: Using a stroboscope — check for discoloured, pitted or cracked diodes; also check for unbalanced output voltage
opts: Remove the diode cover and inspect with a torch
Using a multimeter on the AC output terminals
Using a stroboscope — check for discoloured, pitted or cracked diodes; also check for unbalanced output voltage
Inject test voltage through the slip rings
T01_Alternator.exp: A stroboscope freezes the apparent rotation of the diode wheel, allowing visual inspection while running. Faulty diodes show discolouration or pitting. Electrical symptoms: ripple on output voltage, unbalanced 3-phase voltage. Confirm by shutdown and diode test.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the primary function of the AVR (Automatic Voltage Regulator)?
T01_Alternator.a: Automatically maintains alternator terminal voltage at set value by adjusting excitation current
opts: Controls the speed of the prime mover
Automatically maintains alternator terminal voltage at set value by adjusting excitation current
Protects the alternator from short circuit
Monitors and logs alternator performance data
T01_Alternator.exp: AVR continuously senses output voltage, compares it to the setpoint, and adjusts field current via thyristors/transistors to keep voltage constant. If voltage drops (more load added), AVR increases field current. If voltage rises (load removed), it reduces field current.

T01_Alternator.q: According to SOLAS, what is the steady-state voltage regulation requirement for marine alternators?
T01_Alternator.a: Within ±2.5% of rated voltage from no-load to full-load
opts: Within ±2.5% of rated voltage from no-load to full-load
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS Ch. II-1/Reg 40.3: Steady-state voltage must be maintained within ±2.5% of rated voltage under any load condition from no-load to full-load. Transient deviation must not exceed ±10% before recovering to ±2.5%.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the maximum transient voltage excursion allowed by SOLAS during sudden load changes?
T01_Alternator.a: ±10% of rated voltage, recovering within required time
opts: ±10% of rated voltage, recovering within required time
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS allows up to ±10% transient excursion on sudden load pickup or shedding — this accounts for the AVR response time. The voltage must then recover to within ±2.5% steady-state band. This is tested during load acceptance trials.

T01_Alternator.q: Why must the AVR be DISCONNECTED before performing a megger (IR) test on the alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Megger voltage (500–1000V DC) can permanently damage AVR semiconductors (thyristors, transistors, capacitors)
opts: To prevent the AVR from showing false readings on the display
Megger voltage (500–1000V DC) can permanently damage AVR semiconductors (thyristors, transistors, capacitors)
To allow manual field control during testing
AVR will reverse the polarity of megger readings
T01_Alternator.exp: The megger applies 500–1000V DC to the winding. AVR contains sensitive solid-state components rated for much lower voltages. Also, the AVR may back-feed current into the winding, giving a false (higher) IR reading. Always disconnect and short AVR terminals before meggering.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the 'Voltage Adjust' trimmer in an AVR used for?
T01_Alternator.a: Sets the output voltage setpoint (e.g., 440V) of the alternator
opts: Sets the output voltage setpoint (e.g., 440V) of the alternator
Adjusts the reactive load sharing between parallel generators
T01_Alternator.exp: The voltage adjust trimmer sets the reference setpoint that AVR tries to maintain. Turning it up → field current increases → terminal voltage rises. This is adjusted during commissioning to set exactly 440V (or 6600V on HV ships).

T01_Alternator.q: What is the 'Droop' trimmer in the AVR used for?
T01_Alternator.a: Sets the reactive power (kVAR) sharing between generators running in parallel
opts: Reduces output voltage gradually under heavy load for safety
Sets the reactive power (kVAR) sharing between generators running in parallel
Controls frequency droop for kW sharing
T01_Alternator.exp: AVR droop causes the terminal voltage to slightly decrease as reactive (kVAR) load increases. When two machines are in parallel, this ensures equal kVAR sharing. Without droop, one AVR 'wins' and supplies all reactive current — other machine runs at near unity PF or capacitive.

T01_Alternator.q: What is residual magnetism in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Small amount of magnetic flux retained in rotor core material even when field current is zero
opts: The permanent magnetic field used in synchronous operation
Small amount of magnetic flux retained in rotor core material even when field current is zero
Static charge on stator windings after shutdown
The minimum field current required to start voltage buildup
T01_Alternator.exp: Rotor core material retains some magnetism after the field current is removed. This residual flux induces a small initial voltage during run-up. The self-excited alternator uses this to bootstrap its own voltage. If lost (e.g., by a large external discharge), flashing is needed.

T01_Alternator.q: An alternator runs at rated RPM but shows zero voltage on the voltmeter. What are the possible causes?
T01_Alternator.a: Residual magnetism lost, AVR fault, rotating diode failure, PMG fault, open circuit field winding, or voltmeter fault
opts: Residual magnetism lost, AVR fault, rotating diode failure, PMG fault, open circuit field winding, or voltmeter fault
Always means the stator winding is burnt
Caused by wrong phase rotation only
T01_Alternator.exp: Systematic check: (1) Is voltmeter accurate? (2) Residual magnetism — try flashing. (3) Check AVR supply and function. (4) Check PMG output. (5) Check rotating diodes. (6) Measure field winding resistance. Multiple causes — systematic elimination is key.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the procedure for FLASHING an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Bring to rated speed; connect 12–24V battery briefly (2–3 sec) to exciter field with correct polarity; check voltage builds
opts: Apply 415V AC from shore supply to the stator terminals
Bring to rated speed; connect 12–24V battery briefly (2–3 sec) to exciter field with correct polarity; check voltage builds
Use megger at 500V to restore magnetism in rotor core
Short circuit the AVR output terminals for 5 seconds
T01_Alternator.exp: Flashing uses a DC battery to restore the residual magnetism in the rotor. CRITICAL: correct polarity must be maintained. Reverse polarity will destroy the residual magnetism further. Connect only 2–3 seconds — longer connection risks winding damage. Check voltage builds up as soon as battery is disconnected.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the main risk during a flashing operation?
T01_Alternator.a: Wrong polarity destroys residual magnetism; battery sparking can ignite flammable gases
opts: Wrong polarity destroys residual magnetism; battery sparking can ignite flammable gases
AVR permanent damage from battery voltage
Voltmeter burning out from sudden voltage surge
T01_Alternator.exp: Risk 1: Reversed polarity → residual magnetism is demagnetised further → harder to restore. Risk 2: Battery spark at connection/disconnection. A fire extinguisher must be nearby. Also ensure all personnel are clear of rotating parts before starting.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you ensure an alternator is electrically safe (dead) when residual magnetism may still be present?
T01_Alternator.a: Measure terminal voltage with an approved voltmeter before working — do not assume dead just because ACB is open
opts: If ACB is open, machine is always dead — no further check needed
Only use it if it's been switched off for over 30 minutes
Measure terminal voltage with an approved voltmeter before working — do not assume dead just because ACB is open
Remove all three phases from the busbar simultaneously
T01_Alternator.exp: Residual magnetism means a small voltage IS present at stator terminals even with ACB open and no field current. This can cause shock. Always verify with a voltmeter before working on stator terminals. Earth the machine if necessary for complete safety.

T01_Alternator.q: What does a synchroscope indicate?
T01_Alternator.a: Speed difference and phase angle difference between incoming generator and the running busbar
opts: Only the voltage difference between two generators
The total load on the busbar
Speed difference and phase angle difference between incoming generator and the running busbar
The power factor of the incoming generator
T01_Alternator.exp: Synchroscope is a phase-difference measuring instrument. It shows: (1) CW rotation = incoming machine too fast. (2) CCW rotation = too slow. (3) Pointer position = phase angle between incoming and busbar. Close ACB when pointer at 12 o'clock approaching slowly CW.

T01_Alternator.q: Describe the construction of a synchroscope.
T01_Alternator.a: Small induction motor: stator connected to busbar, rotor connected to incoming generator, pointer mounted on rotor shaft
opts: Small induction motor: stator connected to busbar, rotor connected to incoming generator, pointer mounted on rotor shaft
A current transformer connected across two generators
T01_Alternator.exp: Synchroscope stator creates rotating magnetic field from busbar supply. Incoming generator supply feeds the rotor. Relative speed/phase difference makes rotor (and pointer) spin. At synchronism, rotor field and stator field lock → pointer stops at 12 o'clock.

T01_Alternator.q: When should the ACB be closed during synchronisation using a synchroscope?
T01_Alternator.a: When pointer is at 12 o'clock (in phase) and approaching from slightly before 12 (CW — just fast)
opts: When pointer is at 6 o'clock for safety margin
When pointer is at 12 o'clock (in phase) and approaching from slightly before 12 (CW — just fast)
When pointer is at 3 o'clock position
T01_Alternator.exp: Close ACB just BEFORE the pointer reaches 12, while it moves slowly CW. This ensures the incoming generator takes load immediately (rather than motoring). If closed exactly at 12 but slightly slow (CCW), the machine will briefly motor before taking load.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens if the ACB is closed when the synchroscope pointer is at 6 o'clock (180° out of phase)?
T01_Alternator.a: CATASTROPHIC — massive circulating current, severe mechanical shock to coupling, possible alternator winding burnout
opts: The generator safely comes up to speed on the busbar
CATASTROPHIC — massive circulating current, severe mechanical shock to coupling, possible alternator winding burnout
The reverse power relay trips the circuit safely
T01_Alternator.exp: 180° out of phase means two generators are directly opposing each other. The effective voltage causing circulating current = 2 × Vline ≈ 880V across internal impedances. Current is extremely high — enough to instantly burn windings and cause severe mechanical shock to shafts and couplings.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens if the incoming generator is running FASTER than the busbar (synchroscope rotating CW)?
T01_Alternator.a: On closing ACB, incoming generator takes a heavy sudden load — high current surge, may trip on overcurrent
opts: On closing ACB, incoming generator takes a heavy sudden load — high current surge, may trip on overcurrent
Reverse power relay trips the incoming machine
Frequency of the busbar increases to match
T01_Alternator.exp: Too fast = incoming is ahead in phase. When ACB closes, the incoming generator tries to 'push' current into the busbar. It immediately takes a heavy load surge. If too fast, the surge current may trip OCR. This is why speed should be just slightly fast — not excessively so.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens if the incoming generator is running SLOWER than the busbar (synchroscope rotating CCW)?
T01_Alternator.a: On closing ACB, the busbar motors the incoming generator — reverse power relay trips it
opts: Nothing — generator continues at lower speed
On closing ACB, the busbar motors the incoming generator — reverse power relay trips it
The busbar frequency drops to match
T01_Alternator.exp: Too slow = incoming is behind in phase. When ACB closes, the running generator (busbar side) back-feeds power into the incoming generator, which runs as a motor. Reverse power relay detects this backward power flow and trips the ACB.

T01_Alternator.q: The synchroscope is faulty. How will you parallel the alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Dark lamp method: connect 3 lamps between corresponding phases; close ACB when ALL THREE lamps are simultaneously dark
opts: Estimate by ear — match engine speed to busbar frequency
Use voltmeter across ACB contacts; close when voltage difference is minimum
Dark lamp method: connect 3 lamps between corresponding phases; close ACB when ALL THREE lamps are simultaneously dark
Wait for superintendent to arrive with portable synchroscope
T01_Alternator.exp: Dark lamp: lamps glow when phases are out of sync, dim to darkness when in phase. Close when ALL three dark simultaneously. Alternative: Bright lamp (lamps connected in sequence) — close when all three equally bright. Dark lamp is more common in practice.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the phase sequence check done BEFORE paralleling two generators?
T01_Alternator.a: Verify both generators have the same phase rotation sequence (R-Y-B) using a phase sequence meter
opts: Check frequency only — phase sequence doesn't matter for paralleling
Verify both generators have the same phase rotation sequence (R-Y-B) using a phase sequence meter
Measure the voltage at all three phases
Check the insulation resistance of both machines
T01_Alternator.exp: Phase sequence MUST be identical. If wrong phase sequence is used, even when synchroscope shows 12 o'clock, there's actually a 120° voltage difference between phases — causes large circulating current when ACB is closed. Always verify phase sequence on new or rewound generators.

T01_Alternator.q: In parallel generators, what controls ACTIVE POWER (kW) sharing?
T01_Alternator.a: Governor droop settings — governor controls prime mover speed and thus kW output
opts: Governor droop settings — governor controls prime mover speed and thus kW output
T01_Alternator.exp: kW (active power) sharing is purely a function of speed/frequency. The governor controls diesel engine fuel injection — more fuel = more torque = more kW. Droop setting ensures when one machine takes more kW, its speed slightly drops, prompting the governor to back off.

T01_Alternator.q: In parallel generators, what controls REACTIVE POWER (kVAR) and power factor sharing?
T01_Alternator.a: AVR droop settings — AVR controls excitation and thus reactive current sharing
opts: AVR droop settings — AVR controls excitation and thus reactive current sharing
T01_Alternator.exp: kVAR (reactive power) is controlled by excitation (field current). More excitation → higher terminal voltage → machine pushes out more reactive current (inductive kVAR). AVR droop ensures equal kVAR sharing: as one machine takes more kVAR, its voltage slightly drops, signalling AVR to reduce excitation.

T01_Alternator.q: Two generators running in parallel: G1 shows 600 kW, G2 shows 200 kW. What is the problem?
T01_Alternator.a: Unequal active (kW) load sharing — governor droop settings differ or governor trimmer needs adjusting
opts: Unequal active (kW) load sharing — governor droop settings differ or governor trimmer needs adjusting
T01_Alternator.exp: Unequal kW means governors are not equally sharing the load. Check: (1) Governor droop settings equal on both. (2) If electronic governor — check speed trimmer. (3) If mechanical — check speeder spring. Adjust trimmer on the overloaded machine to reduce its kW.

T01_Alternator.q: Two generators running in parallel: kW output is equal but current differs. What is the cause?
T01_Alternator.a: Unequal reactive (kVAR) load sharing — AVR droop settings differ between the machines
opts: Governor is faulty on one machine
Unequal reactive (kVAR) load sharing — AVR droop settings differ between the machines
Both generators have different rated voltages
T01_Alternator.exp: Equal kW but different current means the machine with higher current is supplying more reactive power (kVAR) — it's more heavily excited. Adjust AVR droop trimmer on the over-excited machine to reduce reactive contribution until currents are equal.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'droop' in the context of governor control?
T01_Alternator.a: Intentional slight reduction in speed/frequency as load (kW) increases — ensures stable kW sharing between parallel machines
opts: The physical drooping of the governor spring
Intentional slight reduction in speed/frequency as load (kW) increases — ensures stable kW sharing between parallel machines
A fault condition where governor fails to respond
T01_Alternator.exp: Without droop, two governors would fight each other (hunt). Droop: if machine A takes more load, its speed drops slightly → governor reduces fuel slightly → load redistributes. Typical droop: 3–5%. Droop = (no-load speed – full-load speed) / rated speed × 100%.

T01_Alternator.q: One generator LOSES EXCITATION while running in parallel with another. What happens?
T01_Alternator.a: Machine runs as induction generator — absorbs reactive power from busbar, voltage drops, AVR tries to compensate, may lead to instability
opts: Machine immediately trips on reverse power relay
It safely continues running on reduced output
Machine runs as induction generator — absorbs reactive power from busbar, voltage drops, AVR tries to compensate, may lead to instability
T01_Alternator.exp: With lost excitation, the machine loses synchronism and operates as an induction generator. It now ABSORBS reactive power (instead of supplying). This pulls busbar voltage down. Loss-of-excitation relay (or under-voltage relay) should detect and trip. Risk: if not tripped, can cause voltage collapse.

T01_Alternator.q: What does the DIFFERENTIAL PROTECTION RELAY do on an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Compares current entering and leaving the winding — any difference indicates an internal fault
opts: Compares voltage of two generators before paralleling
Compares current entering and leaving the winding — any difference indicates an internal fault
T01_Alternator.exp: Differential protection: current transformers at both ends of stator winding compare ingoing vs outgoing current. Normally identical. Internal fault (turn-to-turn, phase-to-earth within winding) causes an imbalance → relay trips instantaneously. Highly sensitive — fastest protection for internal faults.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the setting for the REVERSE POWER RELAY on a marine alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Trips at 5–10% of rated kW in reverse direction
opts: Trips at any detectable reverse current
Trips at 5–10% of rated kW in reverse direction
Trips at 100% reverse power — only for severe motoring
T01_Alternator.exp: Reverse power relay is set at 5–10% of rated kW. This is sensitive enough to detect motoring (prime mover failure) but insensitive enough to avoid nuisance trips during normal load fluctuations. Very large generators may have settings as low as 2–3%.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the function of the PREFERENTIAL TRIP relay?
T01_Alternator.a: Automatically sheds non-essential loads in stages when generator is persistently overloaded — before tripping the generator
opts: Instantly disconnects the most important loads
Automatically sheds non-essential loads in stages when generator is persistently overloaded — before tripping the generator
Trips the generator if voltage is too high
Prevents any additional loads from connecting
T01_Alternator.exp: Preferential trip protects the generator from overload without blacking out the ship. It sheds non-essential services (galley, HVAC, etc.) in timed stages while keeping essential loads (navigation, steering, safety systems) running. Much better than total blackout.

T01_Alternator.q: What is a DASHPOT and why is it used with the preferential trip relay?
T01_Alternator.a: A pneumatic/hydraulic time-delay device — introduces time delay before shedding, allowing transient overloads to pass without unnecessary tripping
opts: An oil reservoir for generator bearing lubrication
A pneumatic/hydraulic time-delay device — introduces time delay before shedding, allowing transient overloads to pass without unnecessary tripping
A capacitor that stores energy for instantaneous relay operation
A mechanical brake on the generator shaft
T01_Alternator.exp: The dashpot provides a settable time delay (typically 5–30 seconds). Without it, starting a large motor would trigger immediate load shedding. The dashpot allows the transient overload to pass. If overload persists beyond the delay → load is shed.

T01_Alternator.q: What bearing temperature values trigger ALARM and TRIP on a marine alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Alarm at approximately 80°C, Trip at approximately 95°C
opts: Alarm at approximately 80°C, Trip at approximately 95°C
T01_Alternator.exp: PT100 resistance temperature detectors in bearings: ~80°C alarm gives warning to investigate (inadequate lubrication, overload). ~95°C trip prevents bearing seizure/damage. Different ships may have slightly different values — always check ship's documentation.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of the THERMISTOR protection in an alternator stator?
T01_Alternator.a: Embedded in stator winding — trips if winding temperature exceeds Class F insulation limit (155°C)
opts: Monitors ambient temperature in the engine room
Embedded in stator winding — trips if winding temperature exceeds Class F insulation limit (155°C)
Controls AVR output based on temperature
Measures coolant temperature of the prime mover
T01_Alternator.exp: Thermistors (PTC type) are embedded directly in stator winding slots during manufacturing. Class F insulation is rated to 155°C. Trip prevents insulation degradation and winding burnout. The thermistor resistance increases sharply at the trip temperature, triggering the relay circuit.

T01_Alternator.q: What is EARTH FAULT PROTECTION on an alternator, and what percentage of stator is protected?
T01_Alternator.a: Detects stator winding earth faults — typically 95% stator earth fault protection (5% nearest neutral is unprotected)
opts: 100% of stator is protected in all modern ships
Only the terminal box connections are protected
Detects stator winding earth faults — typically 95% stator earth fault protection (5% nearest neutral is unprotected)
Earth fault protection is optional on marine alternators
T01_Alternator.exp: 95% protection is standard — the 5% nearest the star-point (neutral) has insufficient voltage to drive the detection relay. For 100% protection, a low-frequency injection method is used. Earth fault protection prevents single earth fault from developing into a phase-to-phase fault.

T01_Alternator.q: What does OVER-VOLTAGE RELAY protect against, and at what setting does it trip?
T01_Alternator.a: Protects insulation from damage — trips at approximately 110% of rated voltage
opts: Protects against reverse power — trips at 50% over
Protects insulation from damage — trips at approximately 110% of rated voltage
Only operates during synchronisation — no trip setting
T01_Alternator.exp: Over-voltage damages insulation and connected equipment. AVR should prevent this, but if AVR fails (thyristor short circuit), voltage can shoot up. Over-voltage relay trips at ~110% rated voltage. Response time is typically definite-time (short delay to avoid nuisance trips on transients).

T01_Alternator.q: What is the minimum acceptable IR (Insulation Resistance) value for a marine alternator winding?
T01_Alternator.a: Minimum 1 MΩ; Polarisation Index (PI) > 2 indicates good insulation
opts: Minimum 10 kΩ is acceptable for marine service
Minimum 1 MΩ; Polarisation Index (PI) > 2 indicates good insulation
Any reading above zero is acceptable
T01_Alternator.exp: 1 MΩ is the absolute minimum. In practice, a good dry winding reads hundreds of MΩ. PI (10-min reading / 1-min reading) > 2 = good insulation condition. PI 1–2 = fair. PI <1 = dangerous — do not run. Always discharge winding after meggering.

T01_Alternator.q: What voltage megger is used for a 440V alternator IR test?
T01_Alternator.a: 500V DC megger
opts: 250V DC — to avoid damaging the insulation
T01_Alternator.exp: Rule of thumb: megger voltage should be approximately equal to rated voltage + 250V, or use standard values: 500V for low voltage equipment (<1000V), 1000V for medium voltage, 5000V for high voltage (>11kV). 500V for 440V alternator is standard.

T01_Alternator.q: What must be done to the winding AFTER performing an IR test?
T01_Alternator.a: Discharge the winding by connecting it to earth via a resistor — capacitive charge can cause electric shock
opts: Re-connect to AVR immediately to restore normal operation
Discharge the winding by connecting it to earth via a resistor — capacitive charge can cause electric shock
Measure AC voltage at terminals to confirm discharge
No action needed — megger automatically discharges
T01_Alternator.exp: Megger charges the winding capacitance to DC test voltage (500V or more). This charge is retained after removing the megger. Short-circuiting directly causes arc — use a high resistance first, then earth. Time constant depends on winding capacitance. Always discharge before touching.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you maintain alternator insulation during cold region drydock?
T01_Alternator.a: Use anti-condensation heaters to maintain winding temperature above dewpoint; megger frequently to monitor IR
opts: Keep the machine running at full load throughout drydock
Wrap the machine in plastic sheeting to exclude moisture
Use anti-condensation heaters to maintain winding temperature above dewpoint; megger frequently to monitor IR
Apply oil to windings to repel moisture
T01_Alternator.exp: Cold air holds less moisture, but when it warms up near the winding, condensation forms. Winding heaters keep the winding slightly above ambient — prevents dew point from being reached. If IR is already low, use gentle heating to dry out before switching on. Never megger a wet winding.

T01_Alternator.q: After receiving a rewound alternator from shore — what checks must you do before commissioning?
T01_Alternator.a: Visual check, IR test, phase rotation check, no-load voltage check, then gradual load test
opts: Just run at full load for 30 minutes
Visual check, IR test, phase rotation check, no-load voltage check, then gradual load test
Send it back for further testing — never trust shore rewind
T01_Alternator.exp: Systematic commissioning: (1) Visual — winding quality, varnish, connections. (2) IR test — all phases to earth. (3) Phase rotation — must match ship's system. (4) No-load run — check voltage, frequency, noise, vibration. (5) Parallel with running generator — check load sharing. (6) Gradually apply load.

T01_Alternator.q: What checks are included in DAILY running checks on an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Check voltage, current, frequency, power factor, bearing temperatures, vibration, abnormal noise
opts: Check voltage, current, frequency, power factor, bearing temperatures, vibration, abnormal noise
Perform IR test and AVR calibration daily
T01_Alternator.exp: Daily checks are visual/instrument — no shutdown needed. Look at: switchboard meters (V, A, Hz, PF, kW). Listen for: abnormal noise, vibration. Touch (briefly): check bearing housing temperature. Log all readings. Any trend change warrants investigation.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the 'air gap' in an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: The clearance between the rotor pole face and the inner surface of the stator bore
opts: The space between stator teeth for ventilation
The clearance between the rotor pole face and the inner surface of the stator bore
The gap in the rectifier circuit for voltage regulation
The distance between two phase windings in the stator
T01_Alternator.exp: The air gap is critical: too small → rotor rubs on stator (mechanical damage). Too large → increased reluctance → less efficient, lower output for same excitation. Uneven air gap → unbalanced magnetic pull → vibration and bearing wear.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens if the air gap is UNEVEN around the circumference?
T01_Alternator.a: Unbalanced magnetic pull causes rotor vibration, bearing wear, and in severe cases rotor-stator contact
opts: Nothing — air gap unevenness is normal and acceptable
Voltage output becomes unbalanced between phases
Unbalanced magnetic pull causes rotor vibration, bearing wear, and in severe cases rotor-stator contact
Only affects power factor, no mechanical effects
T01_Alternator.exp: Uneven air gap means the magnetic field is stronger where the gap is smaller. This creates a net radial force pulling the rotor towards the smaller gap side (UMP — Unbalanced Magnetic Pull). This is self-aggravating — as rotor moves closer, force increases. Can lead to bearing failure or rotor/stator contact.

T01_Alternator.q: At what speed does the overspeed trip activate on a marine auxiliary diesel-alternator set?
T01_Alternator.a: 110–115% of rated speed
T01_Alternator.exp: Overspeed trip is set to activate at 110–115% of rated speed (not 100% — that would interfere with normal speed variations). For a 1500 RPM generator, trip activates at 1650–1725 RPM. It's a mechanical or electronic trip that cuts fuel supply.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you test the overspeed trip of a marine auxiliary engine?
T01_Alternator.a: Run off-load with ACB open, gradually increase governor speed until trip activates; note trip RPM and compare to specification
opts: Only check by monitoring the trip in emergency — never test deliberately
Apply full rated load then suddenly remove it
Run off-load with ACB open, gradually increase governor speed until trip activates; note trip RPM and compare to specification
Simulate by injecting a signal into the electronic governor
T01_Alternator.exp: Method 1 (actual): ACB open, increase fuel slowly until trip fires. Verify RPM at trip. Method 2 (simulated): Electronic engines — simulate via test function. Record: date, trip speed, result in engine log. Frequency: annually or at drydock as per class/SOLAS requirement.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of a blackout test?
T01_Alternator.a: Verify emergency generator auto-starts and supplies essential loads within 45 seconds
opts: Test the fire detection system under power failure
Verify emergency generator auto-starts and supplies essential loads within 45 seconds
Check battery capacity for emergency lighting only
Test the preferential trip relay sequence
