T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS requires emergency generator to start automatically and supply essential services within 45 seconds of main power failure. The blackout test verifies this. Essential loads: emergency lighting, navigation lights, steering gear, fire pump, communications.

T01_Alternator.q: During a blackout test, what is the correct sequence of actions for the ETO?
T01_Alternator.a: Brief staff, inform bridge, verify emergency DG ready, trip main ACBs, time DG start, verify essential loads, restore main power, reconnect in sequence
opts: Simply trip the main breaker and observe
Brief staff, inform bridge, verify emergency DG ready, trip main ACBs, time DG start, verify essential loads, restore main power, reconnect in sequence
Only the chief engineer performs blackout test — ETO observes
Run emergency generator for 10 minutes without tripping main power
T01_Alternator.exp: Safety first: always inform bridge (safe navigational situation), brief all staff (machinery spaces and bridge watchkeepers). Verify emergency DG has fuel, lube oil, coolant. Trip ACBs. Start stopwatch — DG must start and supply within 45 sec. Record results in log.

T01_Alternator.q: After a blackout, in what ORDER should loads be restored when bringing main generator back on line?
T01_Alternator.a: Navigation/steering first, then essential safety services, then machinery systems, lastly non-essential services
opts: Restore all loads simultaneously to speed up recovery
Largest loads first to test generator capacity
Navigation/steering first, then essential safety services, then machinery systems, lastly non-essential services
Non-essential loads first — leave critical loads on emergency generator longer
T01_Alternator.exp: Sequence matters to avoid overloading the generator during recovery. Priority: (1) Navigation, bridge equipment, steering. (2) Fire detection, bilge pumps, safety systems. (3) Essential machinery (fuel pumps, cooling pumps). (4) Accommodation, galley, HVAC last. Introduce loads with time delays between groups.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is the main generator NOT placed at the bottom of the engine room (tank top level)?
T01_Alternator.a: Flooding risk, excessive vibration, poor maintenance access, inadequate cooling — all prevented by elevated placement
opts: It would be too cold at tank top level
SOLAS specifically prohibits bottom placement for weight distribution
Flooding risk, excessive vibration, poor maintenance access, inadequate cooling — all prevented by elevated placement
The prime mover would overheat if placed at tank top
T01_Alternator.exp: (1) Tank top floods first — submerged generator = complete power loss. (2) Tank top vibration from ME + shaft is highest. (3) Overhead crane access needed for major maintenance. (4) Better forced ventilation at upper levels. SOLAS II-1/Reg 40 mandates flood protection for main power sources.

T01_Alternator.q: Where MUST the emergency generator be located according to SOLAS?
T01_Alternator.a: Above the bulkhead deck, OUTSIDE the main machinery space, in a separate compartment
opts: In a waterproof enclosure at tank top level
Adjacent to the main switchboard in the ECR
Above the bulkhead deck, OUTSIDE the main machinery space, in a separate compartment
Any location that can be remotely started from bridge
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS Ch. II-1 Reg 42/43: Emergency generator must be (1) Above the bulkhead deck (so flooding of machinery space doesn't affect it). (2) Entirely outside the machinery space (so fire or flooding in ER doesn't disable it). Purpose: independent survival in any casualty.

T01_Alternator.q: A 440V motor receives only 280V. What happens to its torque?
T01_Alternator.a: Torque reduces proportional to voltage squared: (280/440)² ≈ 0.40 — only ~40% of rated torque
opts: Torque increases as motor tries harder
Torque reduces proportional to voltage squared: (280/440)² ≈ 0.40 — only ~40% of rated torque
No change in torque — only speed changes
T01_Alternator.exp: Torque ∝ V². This is because torque depends on both the field strength and armature current — both reduced at lower voltage. With only 40% torque, an under loaded motor may run slowly; a normal-load motor will stall. This is a critical design consideration for motor starting.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens to the current drawn by a motor running on under-voltage?
T01_Alternator.a: Current rises 2–3× rated value to compensate for reduced torque — causes severe overheating
opts: Current reduces in proportion to voltage
Current stays constant — it's load-dependent only
Current rises 2–3× rated value to compensate for reduced torque — causes severe overheating
Current fluctuates randomly with voltage changes
T01_Alternator.exp: Under voltage → reduced air-gap flux → reduced back-EMF → motor draws more current to maintain torque. If motor is carrying load and voltage drops significantly, it may fail to maintain speed, slip increases dramatically, current rockets up, and thermal protection (overload relay) should trip it.

T01_Alternator.q: What causes pitting marks on alternator slip rings?
T01_Alternator.a: High current sparking from worn, misaligned or incorrect grade brushes; contamination on ring surface
opts: High current sparking from worn, misaligned or incorrect grade brushes; contamination on ring surface
Normal wear — pitting is expected and acceptable
T01_Alternator.exp: Causes: (1) Brush pressure incorrect — too low allows bouncing (sparking), too high causes excessive wear. (2) Wrong brush grade — not matched to ring material. (3) Contamination — oil, water, carbon dust. (4) Mechanical misalignment — eccentric running. All cause arcing → pitting.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the correct brush pressure range for slip ring brushes?
T01_Alternator.a: Typically 150–200 g/cm²
opts: As tight as possible to ensure good contact
T01_Alternator.exp: Too low pressure: brush bounces → arcing → pitting → more resistance → more heat → brush burns. Too high pressure: excessive friction → overheating → rapid brush wear → brush dust contamination. 150–200 g/cm² is the standard — check with a spring balance gauge.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you correct slip ring pitting while the machine is running?
T01_Alternator.a: Use fine emery cloth held in an insulated holder to lightly dress the surface — reduce load to minimum first
opts: Machine must always be stopped before any slip ring work
Remove slip ring cover and polish by hand
Use fine emery cloth held in an insulated holder to lightly dress the surface — reduce load to minimum first
Apply conductive paste to fill in the pits
T01_Alternator.exp: Minor pitting can be dressed in-service: reduce load, use fine emery cloth on an insulated stick/holder (NEVER bare hands near live slip rings). This smooths the surface, improving contact. Check afterward: smooth bright contact surface, sparking subsided. Severe pitting: machine lathe in drydock.

T01_Alternator.q: What actually happens when an ACB is closed on a generator that is NOT running?
T01_Alternator.a: Running generator back-feeds through ACB — idle machine runs as induction motor (motoring), reverse power relay trips ACB
opts: Nothing happens — no circuit without running generator
Running generator back-feeds through ACB — idle machine runs as induction motor (motoring), reverse power relay trips ACB
Both generators trip on overcurrent simultaneously
T01_Alternator.exp: This is a classic exam trick question. Non-running generator has no voltage. When ACB closes, it's just connecting a dead winding to the live busbar. The live busbar now drives current through the idle stator winding, causing it to rotate (induction motor effect). Reverse power relay detects reverse power flow and trips the ACB — if it works correctly.

T01_Alternator.q: Which protection relay prevents an alternator from 'motoring' when connected to the busbar?
T01_Alternator.a: Reverse power relay
T01_Alternator.exp: Reverse power relay monitors the direction of real power (kW) flow. Normal operation: power flows FROM generator TO busbar. Motoring: power flows FROM busbar TO generator. When reverse power exceeds setpoint (5–10% rated) for the set time, relay trips ACB.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the Polarisation Index (PI) and what does PI > 2 indicate?
T01_Alternator.a: PI = IR at 10 minutes ÷ IR at 1 minute; PI > 2 = good dry insulation in good condition
opts: PI measures the alternator's power factor improvement
PI = maximum current ÷ rated current; PI > 2 means overload capacity
PI = IR at 10 minutes ÷ IR at 1 minute; PI > 2 = good dry insulation in good condition
PI is the ratio of bearing temperature to winding temperature
T01_Alternator.exp: Polarisation Index distinguishes good dry insulation (resistance keeps rising over time) from contaminated/wet insulation (resistance stays constant or drops). PI > 2 = excellent. PI 1–2 = fair (investigate). PI < 1 = dangerous — do not energise. Wet windings show very low PI.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is an alternator rated with Class F insulation significant for temperature monitoring?
T01_Alternator.a: Class F insulation is rated to 155°C — thermostat/thermistor trip settings are calibrated to this limit
opts: Class F means the alternator can only run in F-rated (flammable) zones
Class F insulation is rated to 155°C — thermostat/thermistor trip settings are calibrated to this limit
All marine alternators use Class B — Class F is only for shore installations
Class F certification is required by MARPOL
T01_Alternator.exp: Insulation class defines maximum continuous temperature: Class B=130°C, Class F=155°C, Class H=180°C. Marine alternators use Class F. Thermistor trip is set just below 155°C (typically 145–150°C to give margin). Running above this degrades insulation life exponentially.

T01_Alternator.q: During a survey, the surveyor asks you to test the overcurrent relay. How do you perform this?
T01_Alternator.a: Secondary injection test: rack ACB to TEST position, inject calculated current into CT secondary terminals, verify relay trips at set value
opts: Overload the generator to 110% and observe relay
Short the generator terminals briefly and measure response time
Secondary injection test: rack ACB to TEST position, inject calculated current into CT secondary terminals, verify relay trips at set value
Simulate fault using an insulation tester connected to phase terminals
T01_Alternator.exp: Secondary injection: don't need to actually overload the machine. Disconnect CT secondary. Inject a measured AC current (using test set) that corresponds to the relay's trip setting when scaled by CT ratio. Time the relay trip. Record: set value, actual trip current, trip time. Compare to manufacturer spec.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the minimum time for the emergency generator to start and supply essential loads per SOLAS?
T01_Alternator.a: 45 seconds
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS Ch. II-1 Reg 43: Emergency generator must start automatically and supply at least the emergency loads within 45 seconds of main power failure. This is why emergency generators are kept warm (pre-heaters) and tested regularly to ensure reliable starting.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the advantage of a brushless alternator over a conventionally excited alternator for UMS ships?
T01_Alternator.a: No brushes means no carbon dust, no brush inspection needed, no sparking — suitable for unattended operation
opts: No brushes means no carbon dust, no brush inspection needed, no sparking — suitable for unattended operation
Brushless alternators always have higher efficiency
They can operate on lower frequency for UMS operation
T01_Alternator.exp: UMS (Unattended Machinery Space) ships need equipment that can run reliably without continuous monitoring. Brushless: no brush replacement, no slip ring pitting, no carbon tracking, no brush gear sparking (safer in gas-risk areas). Much lower maintenance requirement — ideal for UMS.

T01_Alternator.q: What checks should be done when receiving a 'no voltage' complaint on a running alternator — in order?
T01_Alternator.a: 1. Check voltmeter accuracy, 2. Check frequency/speed, 3. Try AVR trimmer, 4. Check PMG output, 5. Flash if needed
opts: 1. Check voltmeter accuracy, 2. Check frequency/speed, 3. Try AVR trimmer, 4. Check PMG output, 5. Flash if needed
Run at half load and restart from scratch
T01_Alternator.exp: Systematic: (1) Is voltmeter working? (check with handheld). (2) Is generator at speed? (check tacho). (3) Is AVR supplying field? (check AVR output). (4) Is PMG generating? (check PMG output). (5) Residual magnetism — try flashing. (6) Field winding open circuit — resistance check. (7) Rotating diodes — stroboscope.

T01_Alternator.q: State Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction as it applies to an alternator.
T01_Alternator.a: EMF is induced in a conductor proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage
opts: EMF is constant when flux is constant
EMF is induced in a conductor proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage
EMF depends only on conductor resistance
EMF is produced by the static field alone
T01_Alternator.exp: Faraday's Law: e = -N(dΦ/dt). In an alternator, the rotating rotor field cuts stator conductors — rate of flux change induces the EMF. The negative sign (Lenz's Law) means induced EMF opposes the change.

T01_Alternator.q: A 4-pole alternator runs at 1500 RPM. What is its output frequency?
T01_Alternator.a: 50 Hz
T01_Alternator.exp: f = (N × P) / 120 = (1500 × 4) / 120 = 50 Hz. Standard shore frequency in most countries (Europe, Asia). US/Americas use 60 Hz → requires 1800 RPM for 4 poles.

T01_Alternator.q: A 4-pole alternator must produce 60 Hz. What RPM is required?
T01_Alternator.a: 1800 RPM
T01_Alternator.exp: N = (f × 120) / P = (60 × 120) / 4 = 1800 RPM. This is the standard speed for diesel-alternator sets on ships serving US/Canadian ports or built to USCG standards.

T01_Alternator.q: A 6-pole alternator runs at 1000 RPM. What frequency does it produce?
T01_Alternator.a: 50 Hz
T01_Alternator.exp: f = (1000 × 6) / 120 = 50 Hz. More poles allow lower shaft speed for the same frequency — useful for low-speed prime movers. Larger diameter rotor needed.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is a marine alternator rated in kVA rather than kW?
T01_Alternator.a: Heating depends on current (which determines kVA), not on power factor — so kVA is the true capacity rating
opts: kVA is always a larger number than kW
kW rating is only for DC machines
Heating depends on current (which determines kVA), not on power factor — so kVA is the true capacity rating
SOLAS mandates kVA rating for all AC machines
T01_Alternator.exp: Copper losses I²R cause winding heating — depend only on current magnitude. A 100 kVA machine at 0.5 PF delivers 50 kW but carries full rated current → full rated heating. At 1.0 PF it delivers 100 kW with same current → same heating. The machine doesn't 'know' the PF of its load.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the relationship between frequency, number of pole pairs, and speed?
T01_Alternator.a: f = n × P/2 (where n = rev/sec, P = total poles) or f = N × P / 120 (N in RPM)
opts: f = n × P/2 (where n = rev/sec, P = total poles) or f = N × P / 120 (N in RPM)
T01_Alternator.exp: The formula f = NP/120 uses RPM. Equivalently f = nP/2 where n is rev/second and P is total pole count. Each rotation of a P-pole rotor completes P/2 full cycles. Governor maintains constant N → constant f.

T01_Alternator.q: In a marine alternator, why is AC output taken from the stator and not the rotor?
T01_Alternator.a: Stator is stationary — no slip rings needed to take output; rotor only carries DC field (low current)
opts: Rotor windings cannot carry AC current
Stator is stationary — no slip rings needed to take output; rotor only carries DC field (low current)
Rotor output would have incorrect frequency
T01_Alternator.exp: Taking AC output from a rotating part would require slip rings rated for full output current (hundreds of amps). The stationary stator allows direct cable connection. The DC field current on the rotor is much smaller — manageable via slip rings (in conventional machines) or eliminated entirely (brushless).

T01_Alternator.q: What is the synchronous speed of a 2-pole alternator for 50 Hz output?
T01_Alternator.a: 3000 RPM
T01_Alternator.exp: N = (f × 120) / P = (50 × 120) / 2 = 3000 RPM. Two-pole machines run very fast — typically turbo-alternators on steam/gas turbine ships. Cylindrical (non-salient) rotor construction used for structural integrity at high speed.

T01_Alternator.q: Name the THREE types of excitation systems used on marine alternators.
T01_Alternator.a: Separately excited, Self-excited (shunt), Brushless (PMG + exciter + rotating rectifiers)
opts: AC excited, DC excited, Static excited
Separately excited, Self-excited (shunt), Brushless (PMG + exciter + rotating rectifiers)
Permanent magnet, Thyristor controlled, Transformer excited
T01_Alternator.exp: (1) Separately excited: external DC source via slip rings. (2) Self-excited shunt: output feeds back via rectifier to field. (3) Brushless: PMG → AVR → exciter stator → exciter rotor → rotating diodes → main field. Modern marine = brushless.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the main disadvantage of a separately excited alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Requires slip rings and brushes for field supply — maintenance-intensive, prone to sparking
opts: Requires slip rings and brushes for field supply — maintenance-intensive, prone to sparking
Cannot be used on ships above 5000 GRT
T01_Alternator.exp: Slip rings and brushes need regular maintenance: brush replacement, slip ring cleaning/polishing, pressure checking. In marine environment — humidity, vibration, salt air — brushes wear faster and can cause tracking/arcing. Brushless eliminates this entirely.

T01_Alternator.q: In a self-excited shunt alternator, what happens if you briefly disconnect the field?
T01_Alternator.a: Voltage collapses completely — no external source to restore it without residual magnetism or flashing
opts: Voltage collapses completely — no external source to restore it without residual magnetism or flashing
T01_Alternator.exp: Self-excitation relies on the bootstrap cycle: residual magnetism → small voltage → field current → more voltage. Interrupt this cycle (field disconnect) and voltage collapses. PMG-based brushless machines are immune — PMG provides stable power to AVR regardless of main output voltage.

T01_Alternator.q: What voltage does the PMG typically output, and what is it used for?
T01_Alternator.a: 100–200V AC, used solely to power the AVR — completely independent of main alternator output
opts: 100–200V AC, used solely to power the AVR — completely independent of main alternator output
12V DC — directly feeds the field winding
48V DC — powers the AVR and ship's DC systems
T01_Alternator.exp: PMG output voltage and frequency vary with speed, but since it's used to power the AVR (which can handle varying input), this is acceptable. Critical feature: PMG output is unaffected by main alternator faults, AVR faults, or load disturbances — providing a truly independent supply.

T01_Alternator.q: Can a brushless alternator self-excite if the PMG magnets demagnetise completely?
T01_Alternator.a: No — if PMG loses all magnetism, AVR has no supply and cannot excite the main field; machine won't build voltage
opts: Yes — residual magnetism in main rotor will still build voltage
No — if PMG loses all magnetism, AVR has no supply and cannot excite the main field; machine won't build voltage
Yes — the self-excited bypass mode activates automatically
No — but the battery charger provides backup excitation
T01_Alternator.exp: In a brushless machine, the PMG is the sole supply to the AVR. If PMG permanent magnets lose their field (rare, but possible from severe shock or temperature), the AVR starves → no excitation → no output. Unlike a self-excited machine, there's no residual magnetism path to bootstrap. Machine must be workshop-repaired.

T01_Alternator.q: List the THREE machines on the shaft of a brushless alternator system in correct order from drive end.
T01_Alternator.a: PMG → Main Exciter → Main Alternator (all on same shaft, driven by prime mover)
opts: PMG → Main Exciter → Main Alternator (all on same shaft, driven by prime mover)
T01_Alternator.exp: Drive end (prime mover) → PMG (permanent magnet generator, small) → Main Exciter (stator is fed by AVR; rotor generates 3-phase AC) → Main Alternator (rotor carries DC field from rotating rectifiers; stator gives 3-phase output). All on one shaft.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the role of the exciter stator winding in a brushless alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Carries DC field current from AVR — creates the magnetic field that the rotating exciter armature cuts
opts: Carries the 3-phase AC output to the main switchboard
Connects to the PMG to boost its output
Carries DC field current from AVR — creates the magnetic field that the rotating exciter armature cuts
Acts as the regulating winding for frequency control
T01_Alternator.exp: The exciter is essentially a small DC-excited generator. Its stator (stationary) receives DC from the AVR. This creates a stationary magnetic field. The exciter rotor (rotating with shaft) cuts this field → generates 3-phase AC on the exciter rotor. This AC goes to rotating rectifiers on the shaft.

T01_Alternator.q: Why are rotating rectifier diodes used instead of slip rings in a brushless alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Rotating diodes eliminate physical sliding contact — no brushes, no sparking, no maintenance, suitable for UMS
opts: Diodes produce higher voltage than slip rings
Rotating diodes eliminate physical sliding contact — no brushes, no sparking, no maintenance, suitable for UMS
Slip rings cannot handle AC current
Diodes regulate the field current automatically
T01_Alternator.exp: The exciter rotor generates 3-phase AC. To get DC into the main field winding (also on the rotor), you need rectification. Mounting diodes on the shaft means they rotate with the rotor — converting AC to DC right there on the shaft, without any need for electrical contact between stationary and rotating parts.

T01_Alternator.q: What protection component is fitted across the rotating rectifier diode bank?
T01_Alternator.a: Zener diode suppressor — clamps transient overvoltages that could destroy the rectifier diodes
opts: A fuse bank rated at 3× diode current
Zener diode suppressor — clamps transient overvoltages that could destroy the rectifier diodes
A thermistor to limit current during starting
T01_Alternator.exp: Transient voltages occur in the field circuit during load changes or faults. Zener diodes across the diode bank clamp these spikes — they conduct when voltage exceeds their breakdown voltage, dissipating the energy. Without this protection, transients could instantly destroy the rectifier diodes.

T01_Alternator.q: During a stroboscope inspection of rotating diodes, what specifically indicates a failed (open circuit) diode?
T01_Alternator.a: Discolouration (burn marks), pitting on the diode body, or cracks on the diode casing
opts: The diode appears to spin faster than the others
Discolouration (burn marks), pitting on the diode body, or cracks on the diode casing
All diodes glow red under the stroboscope
The diode appears to be at a different angle than neighbours
T01_Alternator.exp: A failed diode that has burnt shows heat discolouration — typically brown/black marks. Pitting indicates arcing. Cracks mean mechanical failure. The stroboscope freezes apparent rotation so these visual defects are visible. An open circuit diode also shows up as: unbalanced 3-phase output voltage + ripple on output.

T01_Alternator.q: A brushless alternator has 6 rotating diodes (3 positive, 3 negative). One negative diode goes open. What is the electrical effect?
T01_Alternator.a: One phase of exciter AC is not rectified → ripple in field current → pulsating terminal voltage
opts: Complete loss of excitation — machine de-excites immediately
Machine runs normally — remaining 5 diodes compensate
One phase of exciter AC is not rectified → ripple in field current → pulsating terminal voltage
T01_Alternator.exp: The 3-phase bridge rectifier loses one leg. The remaining 5 diodes still rectify 2 of the 3 phases (partially). The unrectified phase component creates an AC ripple superimposed on the DC field. Result: 'hunting' or pulsating terminal voltage — typically 15-20% drop with visible fluctuation.

T01_Alternator.q: How would you confirm a suspected rotating diode failure WITHOUT stopping the alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Use stroboscope to freeze rotor visually (inspect diodes); measure output voltage imbalance; check for AC ripple on field supply
opts: Disconnect the PMG and see if voltage changes
Use stroboscope to freeze rotor visually (inspect diodes); measure output voltage imbalance; check for AC ripple on field supply
Open the terminal box and probe with voltmeter
Increase load to 100% and measure current balance
T01_Alternator.exp: Three diagnostic approaches without stopping: (1) Stroboscope — freeze rotor, visual diode inspection. (2) Voltmeter — check for unbalanced phase voltages or reduced output. (3) If accessible, measure AC ripple on AVR output (field supply side). Full confirmation requires stopping, dismantling the rotating assembly, and testing each diode with a multimeter.

T01_Alternator.q: Describe the control loop of an AVR in one sentence.
T01_Alternator.a: AVR senses output voltage, compares to setpoint, and adjusts field current via thyristors to maintain constant voltage
opts: AVR measures current and adjusts frequency
AVR senses output voltage, compares to setpoint, and adjusts field current via thyristors to maintain constant voltage
AVR controls governor speed to regulate voltage
AVR switches loads on/off to maintain stable voltage
T01_Alternator.exp: It's a closed-loop feedback control: Sense (voltage transformer samples output) → Compare (error amplifier: actual vs. setpoint) → Actuate (thyristor/transistor varies excitation current) → Effect (field current changes → flux changes → EMF changes). Response time: typically 20-200ms.

T01_Alternator.q: The SOLAS steady-state voltage regulation requirement is ±2.5%. What does this mean practically?
T01_Alternator.a: From zero load to full rated load, the terminal voltage must not deviate more than ±2.5% from the rated value
opts: Voltage can vary by 2.5% per second during operation
From zero load to full rated load, the terminal voltage must not deviate more than ±2.5% from the rated value
2.5% variation is acceptable during paralleling only
The AVR must respond within 2.5 seconds
T01_Alternator.exp: For a 440V system: ±2.5% means voltage must stay within 429V–451V under any load from 0 to 100%. This is tested during sea trials: connect full rated load, then disconnect — voltage must not go outside 429-451V at steady state. The transient (instant response) allowance is ±10%.

T01_Alternator.q: What does the 'stability' trimmer on an AVR control?
T01_Alternator.a: Controls the damping of the AVR response — prevents hunting/oscillation of terminal voltage
opts: Controls the damping of the AVR response — prevents hunting/oscillation of terminal voltage
Adjusts the frequency trim via governor link
T01_Alternator.exp: If stability trimmer is set too low → AVR is sluggish, slow response to load changes → voltage dips. Too high → AVR over-corrects → voltage oscillates (hunts). Correct setting: smooth response that reaches steady state without overshoot. Adjusted during commissioning while monitoring a scope or voltmeter.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens to terminal voltage when two generators run in parallel and one AVR is set significantly higher than the other?
T01_Alternator.a: Higher-set AVR supplies all the reactive current (kVAR) — the other machine operates near unity PF or goes capacitive
opts: Both machines maintain equal voltage and share kVAR equally
Higher-set AVR supplies all the reactive current (kVAR) — the other machine operates near unity PF or goes capacitive
Frequency difference causes one machine to trip on reverse power
Both machines trip on overcurrent simultaneously
T01_Alternator.exp: In parallel, both machines must have the same terminal voltage (they're connected to the same busbar). The machine with higher AVR setpoint 'pushes' more reactive current into the bus. The other machine absorbs it — effectively operating at leading PF. This causes circulating reactive current and overheating of the over-excited machine. AVR droop prevents this.

T01_Alternator.q: Define 'AVR droop' and explain its purpose in parallel operation.
T01_Alternator.a: Droop = intentional voltage reduction as kVAR load increases; ensures stable reactive load sharing between parallel machines
opts: Droop = voltage reduction on no-load for safety
Droop = intentional voltage reduction as kVAR load increases; ensures stable reactive load sharing between parallel machines
Droop = frequency compensation during load shedding
T01_Alternator.exp: Without droop: two AVRs both trying to hold exact voltage → one machine 'wins' and takes all reactive current → unstable. With droop: as machine A takes more kVAR, its terminal voltage droops slightly → AVR backs off → load redistributes. Droop = (no-load V - full-load V) / rated V × 100%. Typical: 2-5%.

T01_Alternator.q: Before performing an IR (megger) test, the ETO forgets to disconnect the AVR. What are the TWO consequences?
T01_Alternator.a: (1) Megger voltage damages AVR semiconductors; (2) AVR back-feeds current into winding giving false (high) IR reading
opts: No consequences — modern AVRs are rated for megger voltage
(1) Megger voltage damages AVR semiconductors; (2) AVR back-feeds current into winding giving false (high) IR reading
(1) AVR blows its fuse; (2) Megger shows zero reading
(1) Field winding burns out; (2) Stator winding gets double voltage
T01_Alternator.exp: Consequence 1: 500-1000V DC from megger is far above AVR component ratings (thyristors, capacitors, transistors typically rated 400-600V with margins). Irreversible damage likely. Consequence 2: AVR senses an 'undervoltage' (machine not running) and tries to boost excitation — feeds current back through field winding into megger circuit → falsely elevated IR reading.

T01_Alternator.q: What component in the AVR directly controls the field current magnitude?
T01_Alternator.a: Thyristors (SCRs) or power transistors — phase-angle fired or PWM controlled to vary DC output to exciter field
opts: Thyristors (SCRs) or power transistors — phase-angle fired or PWM controlled to vary DC output to exciter field
A relay that switches fixed resistors
T01_Alternator.exp: Modern AVRs use thyristors (SCRs) in a phase-controlled rectifier — by varying the firing angle, the average DC output to the exciter field is varied. Some use IGBT transistors with PWM control. Older AVRs used carbon pile regulators (mechanical). The firing angle/duty cycle is controlled by the error amplifier signal.

T01_Alternator.q: The terminal voltage is set at 445V but the surveyor says it should be 440V. Which trimmer do you adjust and which way?
T01_Alternator.a: Reduce the 'Voltage Adjust' trimmer — this lowers the AVR's reference setpoint, reducing field current and output voltage
opts: Reduce the 'Voltage Adjust' trimmer — this lowers the AVR's reference setpoint, reducing field current and output voltage
Adjust the governor speed trimmer downward
T01_Alternator.exp: Voltage Adjust trimmer sets the target voltage. Current output 445V > desired 440V → reduce voltage setpoint. Turn the trimmer down (usually counterclockwise) in small increments, monitor voltmeter. Adjust under representative load (typically 50-75% rated load) for best accuracy. Log the before/after reading.

T01_Alternator.q: Why might an alternator lose its residual magnetism?
T01_Alternator.a: Large external discharge (short circuit, capacitor discharge), prolonged storage, degaussing nearby, or reverse-polarity field connection
opts: Large external discharge (short circuit, capacitor discharge), prolonged storage, degaussing nearby, or reverse-polarity field connection
Running at low speed for long periods
T01_Alternator.exp: Residual magnetism can be erased by: (1) External magnetic field opposing the existing one — nearby degaussing operations. (2) Capacitor discharge or short circuit creating a demagnetising pulse. (3) Very long storage without running. (4) Incorrectly polarity-flashing. Any of these can leave the rotor with insufficient residual flux to bootstrap voltage buildup.

T01_Alternator.q: An alternator at rated speed shows 5V on voltmeter instead of 440V. What is the most likely cause?
T01_Alternator.a: Very low residual magnetism — insufficient to bootstrap voltage buildup; flashing required
opts: Governor has failed — speed is too low
Very low residual magnetism — insufficient to bootstrap voltage buildup; flashing required
All three phases are open circuit
T01_Alternator.exp: 5V at rated speed suggests some magnetism exists but insufficient for full voltage buildup. This points to degraded (not completely lost) residual magnetism. Check: Is voltmeter accurate? Is speed actually at rated? If both confirmed → attempt flashing with 12-24V battery to boost residual magnetism → voltage should build to rated.

T01_Alternator.q: During flashing: the battery is connected but voltage does NOT build up after disconnection. Next step?
T01_Alternator.a: Check polarity was correct; if polarity was wrong, re-flash with OPPOSITE polarity; if polarity correct, investigate AVR and field circuit
opts: Check polarity was correct; if polarity was wrong, re-flash with OPPOSITE polarity; if polarity correct, investigate AVR and field circuit
Repeat flashing 10 times — residual builds gradually
Call superintendent — machine is beyond repair
T01_Alternator.exp: If polarity was wrong: the flash destroyed existing residual magnetism instead of restoring it. Re-flash with correct polarity. If polarity was correct but no buildup: (1) Is machine at rated speed? (2) Is AVR functioning? (3) Check field winding continuity (resistance test). (4) Check rotating diodes (brushless). Don't keep flashing blindly.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the correct battery voltage for flashing an alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: 12V or 24V DC battery — brief connection of 2-3 seconds only
opts: 12V or 24V DC battery — brief connection of 2-3 seconds only
T01_Alternator.exp: 12V or 24V (typical ship's battery) is sufficient to restore residual magnetism. Higher voltage risks overheating the field winding. Duration must be short (2-3 seconds) — sustained current could damage the winding. The goal is just to magnetise the rotor core, not to supply steady field current.

T01_Alternator.q: After successfully flashing, what should you observe at the voltmeter?
T01_Alternator.a: Voltage builds progressively from low value to near-rated value as the bootstrap cycle takes effect
opts: Voltage jumps instantly to exactly rated value
Voltage builds progressively from low value to near-rated value as the bootstrap cycle takes effect
Voltage remains at battery voltage level
T01_Alternator.exp: The bootstrap cycle: residual → small voltage → field current → more flux → more voltage → field current → ... This is progressive, not instant. You should see the voltmeter needle rise steadily over a few seconds until the AVR takes control and stabilises at rated voltage. If voltage doesn't build → residual still insufficient → investigate further.

T01_Alternator.q: State the FOUR conditions that must be met before closing the ACB to parallel two generators.
T01_Alternator.a: (1) Same voltage, (2) Same frequency, (3) Same phase sequence, (4) Phase angle difference = 0° (in phase)
opts: (1) Same kVA rating, (2) Same voltage, (3) Same brand, (4) Same fuel type
(1) Same voltage, (2) Same frequency, (3) Same phase sequence, (4) Phase angle difference = 0° (in phase)
(1) Same voltage, (2) Same frequency, (3) Different phase to cancel
(1) Same current, (2) Same voltage, (3) Same fuel consumption
T01_Alternator.exp: All four must be satisfied simultaneously: (1) Voltage: equal magnitudes, typically within ±2%. (2) Frequency: equal Hz — synchroscope pointer stopped. (3) Phase sequence: R-Y-B must match (checked once at commissioning). (4) Phase angle: 0° — synchroscope pointer at 12 o'clock. Miss any one → current surge on ACB closing.

T01_Alternator.q: The synchroscope pointer rotates ANTICLOCKWISE (CCW). What does this mean and what action do you take?
T01_Alternator.a: Incoming generator is SLOWER than busbar — increase governor setting to speed it up
opts: Incoming generator is faster — reduce governor speed
Incoming generator is SLOWER than busbar — increase governor setting to speed it up
Phase sequence is wrong — swap two phases
Voltage is too low — increase AVR setting
T01_Alternator.exp: CCW rotation = incoming lags busbar = incoming machine is slow. Action: increase governor (fuel) on incoming machine to raise speed → pointer slows then stops → accelerate to just barely CW → close ACB when pointer at 12 o'clock moving slowly CW. Never close while pointer is moving CCW — machine will motor.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is the ACB closed when the synchroscope pointer is 'just past 11 o'clock moving slowly CW' rather than exactly at 12?
T01_Alternator.a: ACB closing takes ~80-100ms — closing just before 12 o'clock accounts for this delay so actual closing occurs at or near 12
opts: It doesn't matter — close at any position
ACB closing takes ~80-100ms — closing just before 12 o'clock accounts for this delay so actual closing occurs at or near 12
The 11 o'clock position is in-phase for 50 Hz systems
The synchroscope is 30 seconds behind actual phase
T01_Alternator.exp: Mechanical ACBs have a closing time of 80-150ms. If you wait until exactly 12 o'clock and then press close, the breaker physically closes 80-150ms later — by which time the phase angle has advanced slightly. Anticipating this by closing at ~11 o'clock (for slow-moving pointer) means the breaker contacts meet very close to true in-phase.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the 'dark lamp' method of synchronisation?
T01_Alternator.a: Three lamps connected between corresponding phases of incoming and busbar — lamps are dark when in phase, close ACB when ALL three are simultaneously dark
opts: Connect one lamp across the ACB — close when it dims
Three lamps connected between corresponding phases of incoming and busbar — lamps are dark when in phase, close ACB when ALL three are simultaneously dark
Use flashlight to illuminate the pointer — close at 12 o'clock
Three lamps connected in star — close when all equally bright
T01_Alternator.exp: Each lamp sees the voltage difference between corresponding phases. When in phase: V_diff = 0 → lamps dark. When out of phase: V_diff = 2V → lamps bright. They cycle bright-dim-dark at the difference frequency. Close when ALL THREE dark simultaneously — this confirms phase angle AND frequency match. One dark lamp alone is not sufficient.

T01_Alternator.q: What happens to the 'bright lamp' synchronisation method — when should the ACB be closed?
T01_Alternator.a: Close when all three lamps are EQUALLY BRIGHT
opts: Close when all three lamps are dark
Close when all three lamps are EQUALLY BRIGHT
Close when two are bright and one is dark
T01_Alternator.exp: Bright lamp: lamps connected in cross-phase sequence (not corresponding phases). At synchronism, each lamp sees 1/3 of line voltage difference — all equal brightness. Out of sync: one bright, one dim, one dark — rotating pattern. Close at equal brightness. Dark lamp is more common — brighter/clearer signal to operator.

T01_Alternator.q: The synchroscope is showing 12 o'clock but rotating VERY FAST CW. What should you do?
T01_Alternator.a: DO NOT close ACB — reduce governor speed until pointer barely moves CW before closing
opts: Close ACB immediately — it's at 12 o'clock position
DO NOT close ACB — reduce governor speed until pointer barely moves CW before closing
Increase AVR voltage to match busbar
Close ACB and let reverse power relay trip it if wrong
T01_Alternator.exp: Fast rotation means large speed/frequency difference — even at 12 o'clock, the phase angle is changing rapidly. By the time ACB closes (80-100ms), phase angle has already shifted significantly. Result: large current surge, possible overcurrent trip. Speed should be adjusted so pointer rotates at <1 RPM — approaching 12 very slowly — before closing.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you determine the correct PHASE SEQUENCE of a new alternator before paralleling?
T01_Alternator.a: Use a phase sequence meter (Ferraris disc type or electronic) — verify R-Y-B rotation matches existing busbar
opts: Check the nameplate — phase sequence is always R-Y-B
Use a phase sequence meter (Ferraris disc type or electronic) — verify R-Y-B rotation matches existing busbar
Measure voltage between phases — if equal, sequence is correct
Connect the synchroscope — it will indicate wrong sequence
T01_Alternator.exp: Phase sequence must be physically checked for any new or rewound machine. A Ferraris disc (small induction motor with disc) rotates CW for R-Y-B and CCW for R-B-Y. Electronic meters have LED indicators. Synchroscope will NOT indicate wrong phase sequence — it just shows phase angle. Wrong sequence gives large currents on ACB closing even if synchroscope shows 12 o'clock.

T01_Alternator.q: Generator G1 shows high kW output, G2 shows low kW. Both governors are set equally. What is the cause?
T01_Alternator.a: Governor droop settings differ between the two machines — one governor is more responsive than the other
opts: Generator rotor bearing friction is different
Governor droop settings differ between the two machines — one governor is more responsive than the other
Prime mover fuel viscosity is different
T01_Alternator.exp: Equal governor settings should give equal kW in theory. But if droop settings differ (one at 3%, one at 5%), the lower-droop machine tends to take more load. Check and equalise droop first. If still unequal: adjust speed trimmer on the overloaded machine to reduce its speed slightly → load shifts to G2.

T01_Alternator.q: Generators G1 and G2 have equal kW output but G1 has much higher current than G2. What needs adjustment?
T01_Alternator.a: AVR droop on G1 needs to be increased — G1 is supplying too much reactive (kVAR) current
opts: Governor droop on G1 needs adjustment
AVR droop on G1 needs to be increased — G1 is supplying too much reactive (kVAR) current
G2 has a short circuit in field winding
T01_Alternator.exp: Equal kW (real power) but unequal current means unequal kVAR (reactive power) sharing. Higher current on G1 = G1 more heavily excited = G1 supplying more reactive current. Fix: increase AVR droop on G1 (or decrease droop on G2) until currents equalise. Check: after adjustment, kW should remain equal.

T01_Alternator.q: Explain why adding load to one parallel generator automatically causes the other to share the load.
T01_Alternator.a: Governor droop: as load increases, engine speed droops → governor detects droop and increases fuel → both governors respond to the common frequency change
opts: The ACB automatically reduces current to the loaded machine
Governor droop: as load increases, engine speed droops → governor detects droop and increases fuel → both governors respond to the common frequency change
AVR automatically reduces excitation on loaded machine
Load is balanced by the busbar protection relay
T01_Alternator.exp: Both generators share the same busbar frequency. Droop governors: if frequency drops (more load on busbar), both governors increase fuel → both machines produce more power → load is shared. The droop characteristic ensures stable sharing: if one machine tries to take too much load, its speed droops more, causing governor to back off slightly.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'load transfer' and how is it done when taking a generator off-line?
T01_Alternator.a: Gradually reduce outgoing machine's governor (kW → 0) then reduce AVR (kVAR → 0 or small negative) before opening ACB
opts: Directly open ACB — remaining generator takes load automatically
Gradually reduce outgoing machine's governor (kW → 0) then reduce AVR (kVAR → 0 or small negative) before opening ACB
Increase load on remaining generator first, then trip outgoing
Use preferential trip to shed the outgoing generator's load
T01_Alternator.exp: Sequence: (1) Increase governor on remaining machine to take load. (2) Reduce governor on outgoing machine until kW → near zero. (3) Reduce AVR on outgoing machine until its current → near zero (watch ammeter). (4) Verify outgoing machine shows near-zero current. (5) Open ACB. Never open ACB while outgoing machine is still carrying significant load — causes voltage surge.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'hunting' in a parallel generator system?
T01_Alternator.a: Oscillation of load between generators — caused by incorrect governor droop settings or governor instability
opts: Physical vibration of generator from unbalanced rotor
Oscillation of load between generators — caused by incorrect governor droop settings or governor instability
Hunting is normal during frequency transients
T01_Alternator.exp: Hunting: kW on G1 increases → G1 takes more busbar load → G2 reduces → G2 governor over-responds → G2 overshoots → G1 reduces → cycle repeats. Symptoms: wildly fluctuating ammeters and kW meters. Cause: governor isochronous mode (no droop) or improper droop settings. Fix: enable droop or re-tune governor stability.

T01_Alternator.q: List EIGHT protections fitted to a marine alternator.
T01_Alternator.a: OCR, Over-voltage, Under-voltage, Differential, Reverse power, Earth fault, Bearing temp (PT100), Winding temp (thermistor), Preferential trip
opts: Only OCR and earth fault are mandatory
OCR, Over-voltage, Under-voltage, Differential, Reverse power, Earth fault, Bearing temp (PT100), Winding temp (thermistor), Preferential trip
Only voltage protection is fitted — current is monitored by AVR
OCR, reverse power, and overspeed are the three mandatory ones
T01_Alternator.exp: Full list: (1) OCR — overcurrent. (2) Over-voltage ~110%. (3) Under-voltage ~85%. (4) Differential relay — internal faults. (5) Reverse power relay ~5-10% rated kW reverse. (6) Earth fault — stator earth (95% coverage). (7) Bearing temperature PT100 — alarm 80°C, trip 95°C. (8) Winding thermistor — Class F limit 155°C. (9) Preferential trip — sustained overload load shedding.

T01_Alternator.q: Why is the differential protection relay considered the 'fastest and most sensitive' protection for internal alternator faults?
T01_Alternator.a: It operates instantaneously on any current difference between ends of the winding — does not need to wait for sustained overcurrent
opts: It has a mechanical response spring that is the fastest actuator
It operates instantaneously on any current difference between ends of the winding — does not need to wait for sustained overcurrent
It is connected directly to the main busbar for fastest detection
It monitors all three phases simultaneously while OCR monitors only one
T01_Alternator.exp: Differential relay: CT at each end of stator winding compares ingoing and outgoing current. Under normal operation: exactly equal (Kirchhoff's law). Internal fault: current divides — some goes to earth via fault → unequal CTs → relay operates INSTANTLY with no intentional time delay. Highly sensitive to low-level internal faults that OCR would not detect.

T01_Alternator.q: The preferential trip relay has a dashpot. A large motor starts and overloads the generator for 8 seconds. The dashpot is set to 10 seconds. What happens?
T01_Alternator.a: No load shedding — motor starting overload clears within 10-second dashpot delay and preferential trip does not operate
opts: Preferential trip operates after 8 seconds and sheds loads
No load shedding — motor starting overload clears within 10-second dashpot delay and preferential trip does not operate
AVR reduces voltage to protect the generator
T01_Alternator.exp: This is exactly the purpose of the dashpot: transient overloads (motor starting, thruster acceleration) last only seconds — dashpot prevents unnecessary load shedding. Only if overload persists beyond the set time (10 sec in this example) does the trip operate. This avoids nuisance trips during normal operations.

T01_Alternator.q: Under-voltage relay is set at 85% rated voltage. A 440V system drops to 380V due to a fault. Does the UV relay operate?
T01_Alternator.a: Yes — 380V is 86.4% of 440V which is close to 85% threshold; sustained drop to this level will operate the relay
opts: No — 380V is too close to threshold for relay to operate
Yes — 380V is 86.4% of 440V which is close to 85% threshold; sustained drop to this level will operate the relay
UV relay only operates below 50% rated voltage
UV relay is disabled during fault conditions
T01_Alternator.exp: 85% of 440V = 374V. At 380V (86.4%), the relay is just above threshold — may not operate immediately. But if voltage continues to drop to 374V, UV relay operates. UV relay typically has a short time delay (0.5-2 sec) to avoid nuisance trips on transient dips. Sustained undervoltage causes motor stalling — UV relay disconnects generator/loads.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the PT100 and how does it work in bearing temperature monitoring?
T01_Alternator.a: PT100 = Platinum Resistance Thermometer with 100Ω at 0°C — resistance increases linearly with temperature; connected to monitoring panel
opts: PT100 = Pressure Temperature sensor rated for 100 bar
PT100 = Platinum Resistance Thermometer with 100Ω at 0°C — resistance increases linearly with temperature; connected to monitoring panel
PT100 is a thermocouple that generates voltage proportional to temperature
PT100 is an optical sensor that detects bearing colour change
T01_Alternator.exp: PT100 works on resistance-temperature relationship: R = 100 × (1 + 0.00385 × T°C). At 80°C: R ≈ 130.8Ω → alarm. At 95°C: R ≈ 136.6Ω → trip. Monitoring panel converts resistance to temperature reading. PT100s are embedded in bearing housings. Very stable and accurate — suitable for continuous monitoring.

T01_Alternator.q: Why does earth fault protection typically only protect 95% of the stator winding?
T01_Alternator.a: The 5% of winding nearest the star-point (neutral) has insufficient voltage to earth to drive the earth fault relay
opts: The remaining 5% is protected by the overcurrent relay
The 5% of winding nearest the star-point (neutral) has insufficient voltage to earth to drive the earth fault relay
The neutral end is earthed anyway so earth faults there are harmless
The CTs cannot be installed at the star-point end due to space
T01_Alternator.exp: Earth fault relay operates from the voltage developed between the fault point and earth. At the neutral (star) point: voltage to earth ≈ 0V → a fault there develops no driving voltage for the relay. As the fault point moves toward the line terminal, voltage increases. The relay has a minimum voltage threshold → typically 5% of winding (neutral end) below this threshold is unprotected.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the Polarisation Index (PI) test and why is it more reliable than a single IR reading?
T01_Alternator.a: PI = IR at 10 min / IR at 1 min — ratio shows whether resistance is rising (good dry insulation) or flat/falling (wet/contaminated)
opts: PI measures the peak insulation resistance during 10 minutes
PI = IR at 10 min / IR at 1 min — ratio shows whether resistance is rising (good dry insulation) or flat/falling (wet/contaminated)
PI is the number of megohms per kilovolt of test voltage
PI measures leakage current at rated operating voltage
T01_Alternator.exp: Good dry insulation: resistance keeps rising over time as polarisation occurs → PI > 2. Wet or contaminated insulation: resistance stays constant or drops → PI < 1. A machine might show 5 MΩ at 1 min and 15 MΩ at 10 min → PI = 3 → GOOD. Another shows 5 MΩ at 1 min and 4 MΩ at 10 min → PI = 0.8 → DANGEROUS. Single reading doesn't reveal this trend.

T01_Alternator.q: IR test shows 0.8 MΩ on a 440V alternator stator winding. What action do you take?
T01_Alternator.a: Do NOT energise — 0.8 MΩ is below 1 MΩ minimum; investigate cause (moisture, contamination), dry out winding, retest
opts: 0.8 MΩ is acceptable for wet conditions — run at 50% load
Do NOT energise — 0.8 MΩ is below 1 MΩ minimum; investigate cause (moisture, contamination), dry out winding, retest
Megger again with 1000V to get a more accurate reading
Apply varnish to winding and retest immediately
T01_Alternator.exp: 1 MΩ is the absolute minimum. 0.8 MΩ = DO NOT RUN. Actions: (1) Check for obvious moisture (condensation, bilge water ingress). (2) Use anti-condensation heaters at low temperature to dry gradually — do not apply heat suddenly to wet windings (thermal shock). (3) Blow through with dry compressed air (low pressure). (4) Retest after 4-6 hours heating. Log all readings.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you safely discharge a stator winding after megger testing?
T01_Alternator.a: Connect a high-resistance discharge resistor from each terminal to earth first, then short to earth — never short directly
opts: Remove megger leads — charge dissipates naturally in 10 seconds
Connect a high-resistance discharge resistor from each terminal to earth first, then short to earth — never short directly
Short all terminals together — no earth needed
Leave for 1 hour — capacitive charge self-discharges
T01_Alternator.exp: Megger charges winding capacitance to test voltage (500-1000V). Direct short to earth → arc → shock risk. Procedure: (1) After stopping megger, apply high-resistance (10kΩ-100kΩ) discharge resistor between winding terminal and earth. (2) Allow 4× the test time for discharge. (3) Then apply earth bonding lead. Time constant = R×C — with large winding capacitance, can take minutes.

T01_Alternator.q: What routine checks should you perform on a running alternator during your watch? (Name 6)
T01_Alternator.a: Voltage, current, frequency, power factor, bearing temperature, winding temperature, vibration, abnormal noise, AVR stability
opts: Only check voltage — other parameters are monitored automatically
Voltage, current, frequency, power factor, bearing temperature, winding temperature, vibration, abnormal noise, AVR stability
Remove slip ring cover and inspect during running
T01_Alternator.exp: Running checks (no shutdown): (1) Switchboard meters — V, A, Hz, kW, PF. (2) Trending — compare to previous watch readings. (3) Bearing temperature — PT100 readings or touch-check housing. (4) Listen — abnormal noise (grinding = bearing, whining = rotor rub). (5) Feel vibration — excessive = imbalance or bearing. (6) Check AVR stability — is voltage steady? Log everything.

T01_Alternator.q: An alternator has been sitting in drydock for 3 months in a cold humid climate. Before restarting, what is the FIRST electrical check?
T01_Alternator.a: Megger test (IR test) all three phases to earth and between phases before energising
opts: Megger test (IR test) all three phases to earth and between phases before energising
Check fuel system and prime mover
Connect to shore power and test with full load
T01_Alternator.exp: Cold humid drydock = high condensation risk. Windings absorb moisture → IR drops dramatically. NEVER energise a machine without first confirming IR is acceptable (>1MΩ, PI >2 ideally). If IR is low: dry out with anti-condensation heaters before energising. Also check: oil, fuel, cooling water, governor operation, and perform no-load run before taking any load.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of blowing out a running alternator with dry compressed air?
T01_Alternator.a: Remove carbon brush dust, accumulated dirt, and moisture from air passages and winding surfaces to prevent tracking and overheating
opts: Cool the bearings during heavy load operation
Remove carbon brush dust, accumulated dirt, and moisture from air passages and winding surfaces to prevent tracking and overheating
The compressed air re-magnetises the rotor during service
T01_Alternator.exp: Carbon brush dust (from slip rings) and general dust accumulate in ventilation passages and on winding surfaces. Conductive dust on windings reduces surface insulation resistance → tracking (surface arcing). Blocked ventilation → overheating. Low-pressure dry compressed air (max 2 bar) blown through clears passages. Collect dust — don't just blow it into bearing housings.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the typical specification for air gap variation in a marine alternator?
T01_Alternator.a: Air gap should be uniform within ±10% of the mean value around the circumference
opts: Air gap must be exactly equal all around — 0% variation allowed
Air gap should be uniform within ±10% of the mean value around the circumference
Air gap variation is not critical — only total clearance matters
T01_Alternator.exp: Manufacturers specify air gap tolerance typically as ±10% of mean. Example: if mean air gap = 3mm, acceptable range = 2.7-3.3mm. Variation beyond ±10% indicates bearing wear, rotor eccentricity, or stator bore distortion. The variation creates unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP) proportional to eccentricity — self-aggravating force.

T01_Alternator.q: How many measurement points per pole are typically used when measuring alternator air gap?
T01_Alternator.a: 4 measurement points per pole (top, bottom, left, right) — or at 90° intervals around the full circumference
opts: 4 measurement points per pole (top, bottom, left, right) — or at 90° intervals around the full circumference
16 measurements total regardless of pole count
Only one measurement needed at the largest gap position
T01_Alternator.exp: 4 points per pole gives a complete picture of gap uniformity. For a 4-pole machine: 4 × 4 = 16 measurements. The measurements are taken by inserting feeler gauges through ventilation slots or access openings. Results tabulated: any position deviating by >10% from mean requires investigation.

T01_Alternator.q: During maintenance, air gap is measured and found to be 2mm on one side and 4mm on the opposite side. What does this indicate?
T01_Alternator.a: Rotor is eccentric — likely a worn bearing causing the rotor to sag toward the smaller gap side
opts: Rotor is eccentric — likely a worn bearing causing the rotor to sag toward the smaller gap side
Air gap variation is normal and requires no action
Rotor has been machined incorrectly — scrap and replace
T01_Alternator.exp: 2mm vs 4mm = 100% variation (vs acceptable ±10%). The rotor centre is not coincident with the stator bore centre — it has shifted toward the 2mm side. Most likely cause: worn bearing allowing rotor to sag. Also possible: bent shaft, bearing pedestal misalignment, or improper rotor installation after rewind. Check and replace bearing, realign, recheck gap.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the difference between the governor trip and the mechanical overspeed trip?
T01_Alternator.a: Governor trip = normal speed control; Mechanical overspeed trip = emergency backup that activates at 110-115% speed to prevent destruction
opts: They are the same device with different names
Governor trip = normal speed control; Mechanical overspeed trip = emergency backup that activates at 110-115% speed to prevent destruction
Mechanical trip = faster response; governor = backup
Governor only controls fuel — no trip function
T01_Alternator.exp: Governor maintains normal operating speed. If governor fails → speed rises uncontrolled → mechanical overspeed trip activates at 110-115% rated speed as a last resort. Mechanical trip typically actuates a fuel cutoff lever or solenoid directly — independent of electronic governor. It's a fail-safe backup.

T01_Alternator.q: A diesel alternator rated at 1500 RPM has its overspeed trip set at 113%. At what RPM does it trip?
T01_Alternator.a: 1695 RPM
T01_Alternator.exp: Trip RPM = rated RPM × trip % = 1500 × 1.13 = 1695 RPM. This is within the typical 110-115% range. After the test, verify the trip reset and check that the mechanical linkage is undamaged. Log the actual trip speed and compare to the design specification.

T01_Alternator.q: During overspeed trip test, the ACB must be OPEN before starting. Why?
T01_Alternator.a: To prevent frequency surge from feeding into the main busbar and damaging other equipment and motors
opts: To allow the machine to accelerate freely without generator load
To prevent frequency surge from feeding into the main busbar and damaging other equipment and motors
ACB open allows higher test speed to be reached
Required to reset the mechanical trip mechanism first
T01_Alternator.exp: Two reasons: (1) If generator is connected to busbar at 113% speed, it generates 56.5 Hz (for 50 Hz) — all connected motors over-speed simultaneously → can damage equipment. (2) With ACB open, the machine can freely accelerate to trip speed without electrical load affecting the test. Always open ACB before testing overspeed.

T01_Alternator.q: What loads must the emergency generator supply within 45 seconds of blackout per SOLAS?
T01_Alternator.a: Emergency lighting, navigation lights, steering gear (for 30 min), fire pump, VHF/GMDSS, internal communications, alarms
opts: Only emergency lighting — other loads connect via UPS
Emergency lighting, navigation lights, steering gear (for 30 min), fire pump, VHF/GMDSS, internal communications, alarms
All loads that were connected before blackout
Only bridge equipment and navigation lights
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1 Reg 42: Emergency services include: (1) Emergency lighting — all muster stations, escape routes, accommodation. (2) Navigation lights and signals. (3) Steering gear — must supply for 30 min continuous. (4) Fire detection and alarm. (5) Fire pump. (6) VHF and GMDSS. (7) Internal communications. (8) Emergency bilge pump. (9) Ship's whistle.

T01_Alternator.q: The ETO times the emergency generator during a blackout test and it takes 52 seconds. Is this acceptable?
T01_Alternator.a: NO — SOLAS requires 45 seconds maximum; 52 seconds is non-compliant; deficiency must be investigated and corrected before next survey
opts: Yes — 52 seconds is within the 60-second allowance
NO — SOLAS requires 45 seconds maximum; 52 seconds is non-compliant; deficiency must be investigated and corrected before next survey
Only the Class surveyor can decide acceptability
52 seconds is acceptable for ships over 10 years old
T01_Alternator.exp: 45 seconds is an absolute SOLAS requirement with no tolerance. 52 seconds = non-compliance. Investigate: (1) Battery/pre-heating system — is DG warm enough? (2) Starter motor condition. (3) Fuel system — air lock? (4) Governor response speed. (5) Check starting battery state of charge. Correct fault, retest, and ensure acceptable before any port state control inspection.

T01_Alternator.q: Why must the bridge officer be informed BEFORE a blackout test is conducted?
T01_Alternator.a: Bridge must be in a safe navigational situation — blackout test must not be conducted during confined waters, high traffic, or bad weather
opts: Bridge officer must operate the emergency generator
Bridge must be in a safe navigational situation — blackout test must not be conducted during confined waters, high traffic, or bad weather
The engine telegraph needs to be set to 'stop'
Bridge controls the test timing via alarm panel
T01_Alternator.exp: During the 45 seconds (minimum) between blackout and emergency power: steering is unpowered, radar may lose power, navigation lights are dark. In confined waters, heavy traffic, or poor visibility, this creates serious collision risk. Blackout test should only be conducted in open sea, good visibility, light traffic, with Master's permission.

T01_Alternator.q: SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 40 covers what aspect of electrical systems?
T01_Alternator.a: Main source of electrical power — requirements for generating capacity, voltage regulation, and protection against flooding
opts: Fire detection and fixed suppression systems
Main source of electrical power — requirements for generating capacity, voltage regulation, and protection against flooding
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1 Reg 40: (1) Main electrical power must supply essential services. (2) At least 2 generators must be fitted (for most ships). (3) Loss of any one generator must not leave ship without power for essential services. (4) Voltage regulation within ±2.5% steady-state. (5) Protection against flooding of main machinery space.

T01_Alternator.q: Where EXACTLY must the emergency generator be located per SOLAS?
T01_Alternator.a: Above the bulkhead deck, in a separate compartment, entirely outside the main machinery space
opts: Below the bulkhead deck, adjacent to ECR
Above the bulkhead deck, in a separate compartment, entirely outside the main machinery space
In the forward machinery space only
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1 Reg 42/43: Emergency generator must be: (1) Above the bulkhead (damage control) deck — so flooding of lower spaces doesn't affect it. (2) OUTSIDE the main machinery space — fire or flooding in ER cannot disable it. (3) In its own compartment with fire resistance equivalent to 'A-60' class. This ensures it's available in ANY casualty scenario.

T01_Alternator.q: How long must the emergency generator be able to supply emergency loads continuously?
T01_Alternator.a: 18 hours for passenger ships; 36 hours for cargo ships
opts: 18 hours for passenger ships; 36 hours for cargo ships
Until rescued — no time limit specified
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1 Reg 42/43: Passenger ships: minimum 18 hours. Cargo ships: minimum 36 hours. This reflects different rescue scenarios — cargo ships may operate far from assistance. The fuel tank for the emergency generator must be sized accordingly, with a dedicated fuel day tank that fills automatically.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the SOLAS requirement for the number of main generators on a cargo ship?
T01_Alternator.a: At least 2 generators required; loss of any single generator must not leave essential services without power
opts: Exactly 3 generators — one active, one standby, one emergency
At least 2 generators required; loss of any single generator must not leave essential services without power
Only 1 main generator needed if emergency generator is installed
4 generators minimum for ships over 10,000 GRT
T01_Alternator.exp: SOLAS II-1 Reg 40: 'At least 2 generating sets.' The total installed capacity must be sufficient that essential services can be maintained even if the LARGEST single generator fails. In practice, most ships have 2-3 main generators sized so any one can be lost and the others cover essential services.

T01_Alternator.q: Alternator is running but output voltage is 390V instead of 440V. Governor and speed are correct. What are the possible causes?
T01_Alternator.a: Low excitation: AVR setpoint too low, AVR fault, PMG output low, partial field winding fault, rotating diode failure
opts: Low excitation: AVR setpoint too low, AVR fault, PMG output low, partial field winding fault, rotating diode failure
T01_Alternator.exp: Low voltage with correct speed = insufficient excitation. Systematic check: (1) Adjust voltage trimmer — maybe setpoint is wrong. (2) Check AVR input (PMG) — is PMG giving correct output? (3) Measure AVR output to exciter field. (4) Check rotating diodes with stroboscope. (5) Measure field winding resistance — partial short reduces field. (6) Check for excessive load (low PF load can reduce voltage if AVR is at limit).

T01_Alternator.q: A 440V motor on a ship receives 380V due to voltage dip. What is the effect on motor torque and current?
T01_Alternator.a: Torque ∝ V²: reduces to (380/440)² = 0.745 → 74.5% rated torque; current rises to compensate, risking thermal damage
opts: Torque increases to compensate for lower voltage
Torque ∝ V²: reduces to (380/440)² = 0.745 → 74.5% rated torque; current rises to compensate, risking thermal damage
Speed drops 13.6% with no change in current
T01_Alternator.exp: (380/440)² = 0.745 = 74.5% rated torque. If motor is loaded near full torque: torque deficit → increased slip → more current → more heat. The thermal protection (overload relay) is now more critical. For starting: motor start torque (proportional to V²) also reduced by 25.5% — large motors may fail to start if connected load has high starting torque requirement.

T01_Alternator.q: Alternator output current is unbalanced — R phase 200A, Y phase 200A, B phase 120A. What is the likely cause?
T01_Alternator.a: Unbalanced load between phases, or B phase stator winding partial fault, or B phase CT fault (if readings are from meters)
opts: Governor is hunting — causing current oscillation
Unbalanced load between phases, or B phase stator winding partial fault, or B phase CT fault (if readings are from meters)
Normal variation — alternators always have some current imbalance
Reverse power on B phase due to incorrect synchronisation
T01_Alternator.exp: Unbalanced 3-phase current: (1) Unbalanced load — most common: single-phase loads, unequally distributed. (2) If all loads seem balanced: check if it's a metering fault (B phase CT open circuit shows zero, not 120A). (3) Winding fault on B phase — would also cause voltage unbalance. Check: measure line voltages — if balanced, likely load issue. If voltages also unbalanced → internal winding problem.

T01_Alternator.q: An alternator trips on differential protection while running at 75% load. What fault does this indicate?
T01_Alternator.a: Internal fault in the stator winding — turn-to-turn short, phase-to-earth, or phase-to-phase inside the machine
opts: External short circuit on the busbar
Internal fault in the stator winding — turn-to-turn short, phase-to-earth, or phase-to-phase inside the machine
Reverse power — prime mover has stalled
T01_Alternator.exp: Differential relay ONLY operates for faults within the protected zone (between the CTs at each end of stator winding). External faults (busbar shorts, cable faults) would be seen equally by both CTs → no differential → relay doesn't operate. Differential trip → internal fault. Machine must be shut down, isolated, and inspected/meggered before return to service.

T01_Alternator.q: What does it mean when an alternator 'loses excitation' while running in parallel?
T01_Alternator.a: Field current drops to zero — machine de-excites, loses synchronism, operates as induction generator absorbing reactive power
opts: Field current drops to zero — machine de-excites, loses synchronism, operates as induction generator absorbing reactive power
Stator winding open circuits in all three phases
Reverse power relay trips due to high load
T01_Alternator.exp: Sequence: AVR or exciter fault → field current drops → rotor magnetism collapses → machine cannot maintain synchronism → it slips poles → now runs as induction generator (asynchronously). In this mode: absorbs reactive power from busbar → busbar voltage drops. Detectable: machine's power factor meter goes leading/capacitive, current drops then may fluctuate. Loss-of-excitation relay (or UV relay) should trip.

T01_Alternator.q: What are the signs that an alternator brush is wearing too quickly?
T01_Alternator.a: Frequent brush replacement needed, excessive brush dust, sparking at slip ring, high brush temperature
opts: Brush sparking only in UMS mode
Frequent brush replacement needed, excessive brush dust, sparking at slip ring, high brush temperature
Brush wears faster in tropical climates — normal
Rapid wear indicates wrong field current — reduce excitation
T01_Alternator.exp: Too rapid brush wear indicates: (1) Excessive brush pressure — increases friction wear. (2) Wrong brush grade — too soft wears fast. (3) Slip ring surface rough/eccentric — mechanical wear. (4) High humidity causing electrochemical corrosion. (5) Current density too high — use larger brush or multiple brushes. Investigate before fitting new brush — root cause must be resolved.

T01_Alternator.q: How do you check brush pressure on a slip ring brush?
T01_Alternator.a: Use a spring balance gauge — hook under the brush holder spring, read force while brush is lifted slightly off ring
opts: Press with thumb — should feel firm but not hard
Use a spring balance gauge — hook under the brush holder spring, read force while brush is lifted slightly off ring
Measure brush current with clamp meter — infer pressure
Tap brush holder — if it bounces, pressure is too low
T01_Alternator.exp: Spring balance method: (1) Machine running or stopped. (2) Hook spring balance under brush holder spring. (3) Lift until brush just separates from slip ring. (4) Read force at separation point. (5) Compare to spec (typically 150-200 g/cm²). Too low → adjust spring or replace. Too high → loosen spring. Log reading.

T01_Alternator.q: After dressing slip ring pitting with emery cloth, how do you verify the repair was successful?
T01_Alternator.a: Check contact surface is smooth and bright; observe sparking is reduced/eliminated; monitor brush temperature for 30 min
opts: Megger test the slip ring to earth
Check contact surface is smooth and bright; observe sparking is reduced/eliminated; monitor brush temperature for 30 min
Take the machine off-load and measure field resistance
Install new brushes — old brushes become contaminated from pitting
T01_Alternator.exp: Post-dressing checks: (1) Visual — slip ring surface should be smooth, bright (not glazed or rough). A thin film of brush 'patina' is acceptable. (2) Electrical — sparking at contact should stop. (3) Thermal — brush temperature at normal load should be within limits. (4) If pitting returns quickly → root cause not addressed (pressure, grade, contamination).

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'electrical glazing' on a slip ring and what causes it?
T01_Alternator.a: A hard, shiny, poorly-conducting oxide/graphite film on the slip ring surface — caused by very low current density or wrong brush grade
opts: Normal — glazing is the desired patina for good contact
A hard, shiny, poorly-conducting oxide/graphite film on the slip ring surface — caused by very low current density or wrong brush grade
Glazing is a sign of good lubrication
Glazing occurs from excessive current density
T01_Alternator.exp: Some graphite patina on slip rings is good — it reduces friction and improves contact. But excessive glazing (hard, dark, non-conducting film) blocks current → increased contact resistance → heating → more arcing → more pitting. Causes: insufficient load current density, wrong brush compound, dry conditions. Fix: lightly dress with fine emery cloth to expose clean copper.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the difference between the emergency generator and the emergency battery system?
T01_Alternator.a: Emergency battery provides instant power for <30 min; emergency generator provides sustained power for 18/36 hours after up to 45s delay
opts: They are the same system with different starting modes
Emergency battery provides instant power for <30 min; emergency generator provides sustained power for 18/36 hours after up to 45s delay
Emergency generator only supplies batteries — batteries supply loads
Batteries are for radio only; generator is for propulsion
T01_Alternator.exp: Emergency battery (transitional): supplies certain loads INSTANTLY and CONTINUOUSLY during the 45 seconds before DG starts — typically: UPS for navigation systems, battery-backed emergency lighting (shedding), EPIRB. Emergency generator: starts within 45 seconds and provides sustained supply for 18h (pax) or 36h (cargo). Both are required by SOLAS.

T01_Alternator.q: The emergency generator fails to auto-start during a blackout. What manual procedure do you follow?
T01_Alternator.a: Go to emergency generator room, check fuel/oil, attempt local manual start, transfer loads manually to emergency switchboard
opts: Wait for shore power — manual start is not permitted
Go to emergency generator room, check fuel/oil, attempt local manual start, transfer loads manually to emergency switchboard
Send distress signal — blackout is an emergency requiring rescue
Use battery-only power indefinitely until auto-start problem resolved
T01_Alternator.exp: Procedure: (1) Go to emergency generator space immediately. (2) Check fuel level, oil pressure. (3) Check battery/starting system. (4) Attempt local manual start. (5) If started manually: manually close emergency switchboard breakers in correct priority order. (6) Inform bridge and log. (7) Investigate auto-start failure (starting battery, auto-start relay, fuel solenoid). (8) Repair before next entry to any port.

T01_Alternator.q: What are the minimum acceptable tests for the emergency generator per CLASS requirements?
T01_Alternator.a: Monthly: running test under load for minimum 1 hour; Annual: full blackout test verifying 45-second start
opts: Weekly: visual check only; Annual: full start test
Monthly: running test under load for minimum 1 hour; Annual: full blackout test verifying 45-second start
Quarterly: start test; every 5 years: full blackout test
T01_Alternator.exp: Typical class requirements: (1) Monthly: start and run at load for minimum 1 hour — checks starting system, governor, AVR, and sustained running. (2) Annual (or at surveyor): full blackout test — trip main switchboard, verify auto-start within 45 seconds, verify essential loads fed. (3) Log all tests with date, duration, result. (4) Deficiencies must be repaired and retested.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the full excitation current path in a brushless alternator from start to finish?
T01_Alternator.a: PMG AC → AVR rectifier → DC to exciter stator coil → exciter rotor cuts stator field → 3-phase AC in exciter rotor → rotating diodes → DC field in main rotor → main rotor cuts stator conductors → 3-phase AC output
opts: PMG AC → AVR rectifier → DC to exciter stator coil → exciter rotor cuts stator field → 3-phase AC in exciter rotor → rotating diodes → DC field in main rotor → main rotor cuts stator conductors → 3-phase AC output
AVR → Rotating diodes → PMG → Main stator → Output
T01_Alternator.exp: This is the complete chain — memorise it for oral exams. Key points: PMG is the start (stable, independent). AVR controls the DC fed to the exciter. The exciter works 'inside out' (stator is DC field, rotor is armature). Rotating diodes do the AC→DC conversion on the shaft without brushes. Final output from main stator.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the effect of a failed open-circuit reverse power relay on a generator coming off-line?
T01_Alternator.a: If prime mover fails and relay doesn't trip, generator motors (runs as induction motor), drawing heavy current from busbar, damaging engine/coupling
opts: Generator automatically disconnects via overcurrent relay
If prime mover fails and relay doesn't trip, generator motors (runs as induction motor), drawing heavy current from busbar, damaging engine/coupling
No effect — other protections cover this
Generator overspeeds if relay fails open
T01_Alternator.exp: A failed (open-circuit) reverse power relay means it cannot trip. If prime mover stalls: busbar back-feeds the generator → induction motoring → heavy current → diesel engine driven backward against compression → severe mechanical shock to couplings, gearbox, engine components. The differential relay may eventually trip (if internal fault develops), but the overcurrent relay may also trip — depending on the level of motoring current.

T01_Alternator.q: An AVR has 'under-excitation limiter' (UEL) protection. When does it operate?
T01_Alternator.a: When field current drops too low — prevents operation in capacitive (leading PF) region which can cause loss of synchronism
opts: When terminal voltage drops below 85% — same as UV relay
