When field current drops too low — prevents operation in capacitive (leading PF) region which can cause loss of synchronism
When load exceeds 100% rated — reduces field current
When temperature exceeds Class F limit
T01_Alternator.exp: Under-excitation (low field current) → generator absorbs reactive power → operates at leading PF → stability limit approached → risk of pulling out of synchronism. UEL prevents the AVR from reducing field current below a minimum safe value. Particularly important for large generators near steady-state stability limits. Common in ship's HV alternators.

T01_Alternator.q: Why do marine alternators use salient-pole rotors rather than cylindrical rotors (except on turbine ships)?
T01_Alternator.a: Salient-pole rotors are practical for low/medium speed prime movers (diesels) — many poles without high centrifugal stress; cylindrical needed for high-speed (turbines)
opts: Salient poles are cheaper to manufacture
Salient-pole rotors are practical for low/medium speed prime movers (diesels) — many poles without high centrifugal stress; cylindrical needed for high-speed (turbines)
Cylindrical rotors cannot carry DC field windings
Salient poles produce better waveform quality
T01_Alternator.exp: Diesel-driven alternators run at 750-1500 RPM — need many poles (6-12) for 50/60 Hz. Salient poles (projecting poles with concentrated windings) are easy to manufacture in large numbers and the centrifugal force at 1500 RPM is manageable. Turbo-alternators run at 3000 RPM (50 Hz) or 3600 RPM (60 Hz) — only 2 poles, cylindrical rotor needed to withstand extreme centrifugal forces.

T01_Alternator.q: What is the purpose of applying Class F varnish to stator windings during rewind?
T01_Alternator.a: Impregnates and consolidates the winding — improves insulation, thermal conductivity, moisture resistance, and mechanical strength
opts: Reduces copper resistance for better conductivity
Impregnates and consolidates the winding — improves insulation, thermal conductivity, moisture resistance, and mechanical strength
Class F varnish is mandatory per MARPOL regulations
Prevents rust on the copper conductors
T01_Alternator.exp: Vacuum Pressure Impregnation (VPI) with Class F insulating varnish: (1) Fills all voids between conductors → consolidates winding → eliminates movement and vibration damage. (2) Improves thermal conductivity → heat flows better to stator core. (3) Waterproofs the winding → moisture resistance. (4) Class F rated to 155°C → matches Class F insulation. Properly varnished windings last decades.

T01_Alternator.q: Three-phase voltage is 440V but single-phase measurements show R-N=254V, Y-N=254V, B-N=180V. What fault does this indicate?
T01_Alternator.a: B-phase has a partial winding fault — lower B-phase stator winding
opts: Normal variation — phase-to-neutral voltages can differ
B-phase has a partial winding fault — lower B-phase stator winding
Earth fault on B phase equipment
Governor hunting causing frequency variation on B phase
T01_Alternator.exp: Balanced 3-phase: all phase-to-neutral voltages should be 440/√3 = 254V. R=254, Y=254, B=180 → B-phase voltage low. This indicates reduced B-phase EMF, likely: (1) Partial turn-to-turn short in B-phase stator winding (effective turns reduced → EMF reduced). (2) Check: is B-phase terminal connection loose? (3) If winding fault confirmed → machine off-line for rewinding of B phase.

T01_Alternator.q: After paralleling, the incoming generator immediately takes a heavy surge of current and the OCR nearly trips. What was done wrong?
T01_Alternator.a: ACB was closed with too large a speed/phase difference — incoming machine was too fast or at wrong phase angle
opts: AVR was not set correctly before paralleling
ACB was closed with too large a speed/phase difference — incoming machine was too fast or at wrong phase angle
Load was too high on the busbar for paralleling
Governor was in isochronous mode — should be droop mode
T01_Alternator.exp: Closing ACB with significant phase or speed difference causes a large instantaneous voltage difference between the machines → large equalising current → surge. For 'slightly too fast': heavy load surge on incoming machine. For 'large phase angle': both machines see large differential voltage → can be hundreds of amps. Solution: ensure pointer is barely moving CW at 12 o'clock before closing.

T01_Alternator.q: What is 'isochronous' governor mode and why can't two generators run in parallel in this mode?
T01_Alternator.a: Isochronous = maintains exactly constant speed regardless of load; two isochronous governors fight each other → no stable load sharing
opts: Isochronous means governor controls frequency only — suitable for parallel operation
Isochronous = maintains exactly constant speed regardless of load; two isochronous governors fight each other → no stable load sharing
Isochronous mode is required for parallel operation
Isochronous governors automatically equalise kW sharing
T01_Alternator.exp: Isochronous governor: if any load change occurs, it immediately restores exact rated speed. Two such governors in parallel: if machine A takes slightly more load and slows 0.1 RPM, its governor brings it back to exactly 1500 RPM — but now it's faster than machine B → takes even more load → unstable. Droop governors avoid this: speed droops slightly as load increases → natural stable equilibrium point.

T01_Alternator.q: SOLAS requires generators to be protected against flooding. What is the practical minimum height above tank top for the main generator?
T01_Alternator.a: Above the bulkhead deck level — in practice, typically on the second or third platform above tank top
opts: At tank top level is acceptable if flood detection is fitted
Above the bulkhead deck level — in practice, typically on the second or third platform above tank top
Must be above the waterline mark only
T01_Alternator.exp: The bulkhead deck is the deck to which the ship's watertight bulkheads extend. SOLAS II-1/40 requires main power sources to be protected from flooding that might result from hull breach. In practice, this means generators are placed on elevated platforms — second platform or higher in engine room — well above the maximum expected flood waterline.

T02_HV.q: What does NER stand for in HV systems?
T02_HV.a: Neutral Earthing Resistor
T02_HV.exp: NER limits earth fault current to a safe value (typically 5–10A) in 6.6kV/11kV systems, preventing damage to equipment while allowing fault detection.

T02_HV.q: Typical HV ratings used on large merchant ships:
T02_HV.a: 6.6 kV or 11 kV
T02_HV.exp: Ships with large electrical loads (cruise ships, LNG carriers, drilling rigs) use 6.6kV or 11kV distribution to reduce cable sizes and current levels.

T02_HV.q: What is the minimum safe distance from live HV equipment without barriers?
T02_HV.a: Depends on voltage — typically 1m for 11kV equipment without formal approach
opts: Any distance is safe with PPE
Depends on voltage — typically 1m for 11kV equipment without formal approach
T02_HV.exp: HV safety distances: arc flash zone, restricted approach boundary, limited approach boundary — defined by company/class rules. Formal HV procedures required.

T02_HV.q: What does 'Ex d' protection concept mean?
T02_HV.a: Flameproof enclosure — explosion contained inside, cannot ignite external atmosphere
opts: Flameproof enclosure — explosion contained inside, cannot ignite external atmosphere
T02_HV.exp: Ex d (IEC 60079-1): enclosure withstands internal explosion and prevents flame propagation. Used for motors, junction boxes in Zone 1 & 2.

T02_HV.q: What does 'Ex e' protection concept mean?
T02_HV.a: Increased safety — no arcing parts, enhanced insulation and clearances to prevent ignition
opts: Increased safety — no arcing parts, enhanced insulation and clearances to prevent ignition
T02_HV.exp: Ex e (IEC 60079-7): no sparks or hot surfaces during normal operation. Used for terminal boxes, lighting in Zone 1 & 2.

T02_HV.q: What does 'Ex i' (intrinsic safety) mean?
T02_HV.a: Circuit energy limited so sparks/heat cannot ignite hazardous atmosphere even under fault
opts: Circuit energy limited so sparks/heat cannot ignite hazardous atmosphere even under fault
T02_HV.exp: Ex ia/ib (IEC 60079-11): limits electrical energy (voltage, current, capacitance, inductance). Used for instruments and sensors in Zone 0, 1, 2.

T02_HV.q: What does 'Ex p' (pressurisation) protection mean?
T02_HV.a: Enclosure kept above atmospheric pressure with clean air/inert gas to prevent hazardous atmosphere entry
opts: Enclosure kept above atmospheric pressure with clean air/inert gas to prevent hazardous atmosphere entry
T02_HV.exp: Ex p (IEC 60079-2): purge and pressurize with clean air before energising. Used for large motors and switchboards in Zone 1.

T02_HV.q: What does 'Ex n' protection mean?
T02_HV.a: Non-sparking — equipment that does not produce arcs/sparks in normal operation (Zone 2 only)
opts: Non-sparking — equipment that does not produce arcs/sparks in normal operation (Zone 2 only)
T02_HV.exp: Ex n (IEC 60079-15): simplified protection for Zone 2 (atmosphere present only in abnormal conditions). Lower cost than Ex d or Ex e.

T02_HV.q: Zone 0 in hazardous area classification means:
T02_HV.a: Explosive gas atmosphere present continuously or for long periods
opts: Explosive gas atmosphere present continuously or for long periods
Gas present only in abnormal conditions
Gas present occasionally in normal operation
T02_HV.exp: Zone 0: continuous presence (>1000 hrs/yr). Zone 1: likely in normal operation (10–1000 hrs/yr). Zone 2: unlikely in normal operation (<10 hrs/yr).

T02_HV.q: Zone 1 in hazardous area classification:
T02_HV.a: Explosive atmosphere likely to occur in normal operation
opts: Explosive atmosphere likely to occur in normal operation
T02_HV.exp: Zone 1: ignitable concentrations likely during normal operations. Requires Ex d, Ex e, Ex p, Ex i equipment.

T02_HV.q: Zone 2 in hazardous area classification:
T02_HV.a: Explosive atmosphere unlikely to occur in normal operation, and if it does, only briefly
opts: Explosive atmosphere unlikely to occur in normal operation, and if it does, only briefly
T02_HV.exp: Zone 2: least severe hazardous zone. Ex n, Ex d, Ex e, Ex i all acceptable. Examples: spaces adjacent to Zone 1.

T02_HV.q: What test voltage is used to test HV cable insulation?
T02_HV.a: Typically 2.5× or higher than rated voltage using DC HV tester
opts: Typically 2.5× or higher than rated voltage using DC HV tester
T02_HV.exp: HV cable test: 6.6kV cable tested at approximately 15–20kV DC. Always consult manufacturer recommendations and class society requirements.

T02_HV.q: What is the purpose of the NER in a 6.6kV system?
T02_HV.a: Limits earth fault current, reduces arc energy, protects equipment, allows fault detection with alarm rather than immediate trip
opts: Limits earth fault current, reduces arc energy, protects equipment, allows fault detection with alarm rather than immediate trip
T02_HV.exp: Without NER, solid earth fault = full system voltage / cable impedance = thousands of amps. NER limits to 5–10A, reducing fire risk and equipment damage.

T02_HV.q: What PPE is required when working on HV equipment?
T02_HV.a: HV rated gloves, face shield/arc flash PPE, insulating mat, HV rated tools
opts: HV rated gloves, face shield/arc flash PPE, insulating mat, HV rated tools
T02_HV.exp: HV PPE: gloves rated for voltage level (Class 2 = 17kV, Class 4 = 40kV), arc flash face shield (cal/cm² rated), rubber insulating mat, HV-rated insulated tools.

T02_HV.q: What is the 'ATEX' directive?
T02_HV.a: EU directive governing equipment used in explosive atmospheres (ATmosphères EXplosibles)
opts: EU directive governing equipment used in explosive atmospheres (ATmosphères EXplosibles)
T02_HV.exp: ATEX directive 2014/34/EU: equipment for explosive atmospheres must be certified. Replaced by IECEx in international context. Marine: also class society requirements.

T02_HV.q: In HV maintenance, what is 'prove dead'?
T02_HV.a: Confirming using a HV voltage indicator that all phases are de-energised before working
opts: Confirming using a HV voltage indicator that all phases are de-energised before working
T02_HV.exp: Prove dead: use approved HV voltage detector (not a regular multimeter) on all three phases. This step prevents working on what appears dead but isn't.

T02_HV.q: What are the typical steps in HV isolation procedure?
T02_HV.a: Identify equipment, open CB, open disconnector, fit earth clamp, lock out, prove dead, permit to work
opts: Identify equipment, open CB, open disconnector, fit earth clamp, lock out, prove dead, permit to work
Switch off at local isolator only
T02_HV.exp: HV isolation: 1) Identify correct equipment 2) Open CB 3) Open disconnector/isolator 4) Apply earth clamp to discharge and prevent re-energisation 5) LOTO 6) Prove dead 7) Issue PTW.

T02_HV.q: What is an 'earth clamp' used for in HV work?
T02_HV.a: Applied to proven-dead conductors to earth them, preventing dangerous re-energisation
opts: Applied to proven-dead conductors to earth them, preventing dangerous re-energisation
T02_HV.exp: Earth clamps: three-phase earthing stick applied after proving dead. Protects against accidental re-energisation and induced voltages. Must be removed in reverse order of application.

T02_HV.q: HV switchgear on ships typically uses which medium for arc interruption?
T02_HV.a: Vacuum (VCB) or SF6 gas
T02_HV.exp: Vacuum circuit breakers (VCB): metal contacts in vacuum. SF6 (sulphur hexafluoride): excellent arc quenching. Both replace oil-filled switchgear for marine HV. SF6 is a greenhouse gas — requires special handling.

T02_HV.q: What is the function of the HV earth fault relay?
T02_HV.a: Detects earth faults in HV system via NER current, alarms or trips depending on setting
opts: Detects earth faults in HV system via NER current, alarms or trips depending on setting
T02_HV.exp: Core balance CT or NER CT measures earth fault current through NER. Alarm at low current; trip at higher. With NER, first fault alarms, second fault causes protection to operate.

T02_HV.q: Why must HV motors have special insulation requirements?
T02_HV.a: Higher voltage causes greater stress on insulation; partial discharge can degrade standard insulation rapidly
opts: Higher voltage causes greater stress on insulation; partial discharge can degrade standard insulation rapidly
T02_HV.exp: HV motor insulation: Class F minimum, corona-resistant insulation for slot exits, stress grading tape. Partial discharge testing used for condition monitoring.

T02_HV.q: What is 'partial discharge' in HV insulation?
T02_HV.a: Localised electrical discharge within insulation voids — indicator of insulation deterioration
opts: Localised electrical discharge within insulation voids — indicator of insulation deterioration
T02_HV.exp: Partial discharge (PD) occurs in voids/delaminations in insulation. Gradually erodes insulation. PD measurement: detection via ultrasonic, electromagnetic or chemical (ozone, nitrous oxide) methods.

T02_HV.q: Temperature classification of Ex equipment (T class) refers to:
T02_HV.a: Maximum surface temperature of equipment that must be below ignition temperature of the gas
opts: Maximum surface temperature of equipment that must be below ignition temperature of the gas
T02_HV.exp: T classes: T1=450°C, T2=300°C, T3=200°C, T4=135°C, T5=100°C, T6=85°C. Gas ignition temperatures must exceed the equipment T class.

T02_HV.q: What is IP rating for electrical equipment?
T02_HV.a: Ingress Protection rating — two digits: first=solid particle protection, second=water protection
opts: Ingress Protection rating — two digits: first=solid particle protection, second=water protection
T02_HV.exp: IP65: 6=dust-tight, 5=water jet protection. IP44: 4=solid >1mm, 4=splash from any direction. Marine equipment typically IP44 minimum, weather deck IP56/IP66.

T02_HV.q: Gas Group classification for Ex equipment — Group IIC refers to:
T02_HV.a: Most sensitive gas group — includes hydrogen and acetylene
opts: Most sensitive gas group — includes hydrogen and acetylene
T02_HV.exp: Gas Groups: IIA (propane, least sensitive), IIB (ethylene), IIC (hydrogen, acetylene — most sensitive, lowest ignition energy). Equipment must be certified for the appropriate group.

T02_HV.q: What is a 'permit to work' requirement for HV work?
T02_HV.a: Formal written authorisation confirming isolation, earthing, safety measures, personnel qualifications before work begins
opts: Formal written authorisation confirming isolation, earthing, safety measures, personnel qualifications before work begins
T02_HV.exp: PTW for HV: issued by authorised person, specifies equipment, isolation points, earth clamp locations, work to be done, safety precautions, person responsible. Must be signed by all working.

T02_HV.q: What is the difference between a 'circuit breaker' and a 'disconnector' (isolator)?
T02_HV.a: CB can make/break on load (with arc interruption); disconnector must only be operated when circuit is dead
opts: CB can make/break on load (with arc interruption); disconnector must only be operated when circuit is dead
T02_HV.exp: Critical safety distinction: never open a disconnector/isolator under load. CB first, then disconnector. Some designs have mechanical interlocks to prevent this error.

T02_HV.q: What is the typical megger test voltage for 6.6kV equipment?
T02_HV.exp: Rule: megger test voltage should exceed operating voltage. 6.6kV equipment: typically 2500V or 5000V. 11kV: 5000V+. Always check manufacturer limits before applying test voltage.

T02_HV.q: Why is SF6 gas special in HV switchgear?
T02_HV.a: Excellent arc quenching, high dielectric strength, allows compact switchgear, but is a potent greenhouse gas
opts: Excellent arc quenching, high dielectric strength, allows compact switchgear, but is a potent greenhouse gas
T02_HV.exp: SF6 is ~23,500 times more potent as greenhouse gas than CO2. Requires leak detection, recovery equipment. F-Gas regulations restrict usage. Ships must have SF6 management plan.

T02_HV.q: What is 'electrical bonding' in HV systems?
T02_HV.a: Connecting all metallic parts to common earth potential to prevent potential differences and static build-up
opts: Connecting all metallic parts to common earth potential to prevent potential differences and static build-up
T02_HV.exp: Bonding: all metal structures, cable trays, equipment frames connected to ship's hull earth. Prevents touch voltage, static, and ensures fault current returns to source safely.

T02_HV.q: What are the typical HV voltages used on large merchant ships?
T02_HV.a: 3.3 kV, 6.6 kV, and 11 kV — depending on ship type and power demand
opts: 3.3 kV, 6.6 kV, and 11 kV — depending on ship type and power demand
22 kV is standard on all large ships
T02_HV.exp: 3.3kV: smaller HV ships. 6.6kV: most common on large cruise ships and tankers. 11kV: very large ships with huge power demands (large cruise liners, floating production vessels). Selection depends on total installed power — typically HV justified above ~5MW.

T02_HV.q: At what installed power level is a High Voltage system typically justified on a ship?
T02_HV.a: Above approximately 5–7 MW total installed power
T02_HV.exp: Below 5MW, 440V systems are practical with reasonable cable sizes. Above 5–7MW, the cable sizes for 440V become impractically large and heavy — HV becomes economically and practically justified.

T02_HV.q: State THREE advantages of using a High Voltage system on a large ship.
T02_HV.a: Lower current → thinner cables → less weight; Lower I²R cable losses; Suitable for large loads like thrusters and cargo pumps
opts: Cheaper switchgear; simpler protection; no permits needed
Lower current → thinner cables → less weight; Lower I²R cable losses; Suitable for large loads like thrusters and cargo pumps
HV is safer for personnel; no earth faults possible; no special training
Smaller generators needed; lower fuel consumption; simpler wiring
T02_HV.exp: Key advantages: (1) P = V×I — same power at higher voltage = lower current. Lower current = thinner cables = significant weight/space saving on large ships. (2) I²R losses proportional to I² — lower current = far less cable heating loss. (3) Large loads (thrusters 5–20MW, cargo pumps 2–5MW) are impractical at 440V due to enormous currents involved.

T02_HV.q: State TWO disadvantages of a High Voltage system on a ship.
T02_HV.a: Greater danger to personnel (strict procedures required); more expensive switchgear and specially trained staff needed
opts: Greater danger to personnel (strict procedures required); more expensive switchgear and specially trained staff needed
Cannot be used near water; no protection systems available
Higher frequency operation required; complex AVR systems
T02_HV.exp: Disadvantages: (1) High voltage → lethal at touch — strict permit systems, PPE requirements, authorisation. (2) VCBs, SF6 breakers, HV cables, terminations, joints all cost significantly more than LV equivalents. (3) Personnel must have specific HV authorisation and training. (4) Complex protection and insulation monitoring systems required.

T02_HV.q: What is the minimum safe approach distance from LIVE unbarriered HV equipment (6.6kV)?
T02_HV.a: Approximately 600 mm (0.6 m) — varies by voltage class and ship's safety rules
opts: Approximately 600 mm (0.6 m) — varies by voltage class and ship's safety rules
Contact is safe with rubber gloves only
T02_HV.exp: The flashover distance in air at 6.6kV is approximately 65mm, but safety regulations mandate much larger clearances to account for body movement, tool reach, and arc blast. Typical ships specify 600mm minimum. Without barriers, approach distance is specified in the ship's HV Safety Rules document — ETO must know and enforce this.

T02_HV.q: What is a Vacuum Circuit Breaker (VCB) and why is vacuum used as the interrupting medium?
T02_HV.a: VCB interrupts arc in a vacuum — vacuum has no gas molecules so arc cannot sustain, giving fast and clean interruption
opts: VCB uses SF6 gas under high pressure to extinguish arc
VCB uses oil as interrupting medium — oil vaporises to quench arc
VCB interrupts arc in a vacuum — vacuum has no gas molecules so arc cannot sustain, giving fast and clean interruption
VCB uses compressed air blast to blow out arc
T02_HV.exp: Vacuum (pressure ~10⁻⁴ mbar) contains no molecules to ionise → arc cannot sustain after current zero crossing → arc extinguishes within milliseconds. Advantages: compact, low maintenance, no fire risk, no gas handling. Used for 3.3–36kV switching. The vacuum interrupter bottles contain the contacts and are sealed for life.

T02_HV.q: What is SF6 gas and why is it used in some HV circuit breakers?
T02_HV.a: Sulphur Hexafluoride — excellent arc-quenching and insulating gas; 2.5× better insulation than air; used in GIS and some breakers
opts: SF6 = Standard Filter gas-6 — used as coolant only
Sulphur Hexafluoride — excellent arc-quenching and insulating gas; 2.5× better insulation than air; used in GIS and some breakers
SF6 = Ship Fuel 6 — not related to electrical systems
SF6 is used in marine alternators as a cooling medium
T02_HV.exp: SF6 properties: (1) Dielectric strength 2.5–3× air at atmospheric pressure. (2) Excellent arc quenching — absorbs electrons from arc plasma. (3) Non-toxic, non-flammable, chemically stable (normally). (4) Heavy gas (5× density of air) — contained well in sealed equipment. Downside: extremely potent greenhouse gas (GWP 23,500×CO2) — strict handling and recovery procedures required.

T02_HV.q: What does 'racking out' a VCB mean and why is it done?
T02_HV.a: Withdrawing the VCB from its connected position to an isolated/test/withdrawn position — creates visible physical isolation
opts: Removing the VCB from service permanently
Withdrawing the VCB from its connected position to an isolated/test/withdrawn position — creates visible physical isolation
T02_HV.exp: VCBs are typically drawout (withdrawable) type. Positions: (1) CONNECTED — contacts engaged, circuit live. (2) TEST — withdrawn enough to break circuit but still in chassis (control wiring connected — can test electrically). (3) ISOLATED/DISCONNECTED — fully withdrawn, visible air gap, padlocked. Racking out to isolated position is part of HV isolation procedure before maintenance.

T02_HV.q: What is the procedure for racking OUT a VCB safely?
T02_HV.a: Open the breaker first, verify open, obtain permit, rack to test position, verify dead, rack to isolated, padlock and tag
opts: Rack out while energised — VCB handles this safely
Open the breaker first, verify open, obtain permit, rack to test position, verify dead, rack to isolated, padlock and tag
Rack out then trip — sequence does not matter
Only the HV engineer can rack out — ETO not authorised
T02_HV.exp: Sequence: (1) Trip/open the VCB (de-energise circuit). (2) Verify breaker is OPEN (indicator, position, meter reads zero). (3) Obtain permit to work. (4) Rack to TEST position. (5) Verify circuit is dead (HV voltage indicator, test instrument). (6) Rack to ISOLATED position. (7) Padlock racking mechanism. (8) Apply DANGER tags. (9) Confirm earthing if required. NEVER rack while breaker is closed.

T02_HV.q: What is meant by 'making' and 'breaking' capacity of a circuit breaker?
T02_HV.a: Making = current it can close onto (fault peak); Breaking = current it can interrupt (fault RMS) — both rated in kA
opts: Making = rated current in normal operation; Breaking = overload current
Making = current it can close onto (fault peak); Breaking = current it can interrupt (fault RMS) — both rated in kA
Making = AC rating; Breaking = DC rating
They are the same value — just different names
T02_HV.exp: Making capacity: the peak fault current the breaker can close onto without welding contacts together (asymmetric peak — typically 2.5× breaking capacity). Breaking capacity (interrupting rating): the maximum symmetrical fault current (kA RMS) the breaker can safely interrupt. Both must exceed the prospective fault level at the point of installation.

T02_HV.q: What is a Neutral Earthing Resistor (NER) and where is it fitted?
T02_HV.a: A resistor connected between the HV generator neutral point and earth — limits earth fault current to a safe level
opts: A resistor in series with each phase conductor for protection
A resistor connected between the HV generator neutral point and earth — limits earth fault current to a safe level
A surge arrester at the HV switchboard terminals
A resistor that balances the three-phase voltages
T02_HV.exp: NER is fitted between the star point (neutral) of the HV alternator and ship's hull earth. Without NER, an earth fault on an HV system would draw enormous fault current (limited only by system impedance). NER limits earth fault current to typically 200–400A — enough to be detected by protection but not enough to cause severe damage or arc flash at the fault point.

T02_HV.q: Why is a high earth fault current dangerous in an HV system, and how does NER solve this?
T02_HV.a: High fault current causes severe arc flash, equipment damage, and fire; NER limits fault current to 200–400A — still detectable but safe
opts: High current causes voltage rise — NER prevents overvoltage
High fault current causes severe arc flash, equipment damage, and fire; NER limits fault current to 200–400A — still detectable but safe
NER prevents the fault from occurring
NER trips the circuit before fault current flows
T02_HV.exp: Unresisted earth fault on 6.6kV: fault current could be thousands of amps → severe arc flash → fire, explosion, complete equipment destruction. NER resistance chosen so fault current = 200–400A: (1) Enough to operate earth fault relay (5–10% rated current). (2) Low enough to prevent severe arc damage at fault point. (3) Reduces step/touch potentials around fault.

T02_HV.q: What is the difference between a solidly earthed neutral and an NER-earthed neutral on an HV system?
T02_HV.a: Solid earth: maximum fault current (thousands of amps), severe damage; NER: limited fault current (200–400A), controlled fault, less damage
opts: Solid earth: safer; NER: more dangerous
Solid earth: maximum fault current (thousands of amps), severe damage; NER: limited fault current (200–400A), controlled fault, less damage
They are the same — both limit current equally
NER allows operation with one earth fault; solid earth trips immediately
T02_HV.exp: Solid neutral earth: transformer/generator neutral directly connected to earth → earth fault current = V_phase / Z_system → typically very high. NER: neutral connected to earth through resistor → fault current = V_phase / (Z_system + R_NER) → limited. Ships use NER to balance safety (limit damage) with detection (relay can still see fault current).

T02_HV.q: How do you test a Neutral Earthing Resistor?
T02_HV.a: Measure resistance with a low-resistance ohmmeter; verify value matches specification; check for overheating, cracks, corrosion
opts: Measure resistance with a low-resistance ohmmeter; verify value matches specification; check for overheating, cracks, corrosion
Short circuit the NER and check fault current level
Test is only done by manufacturer during drydock
T02_HV.exp: NER test: (1) Visual — check for cracks, overheating discolouration, corrosion on resistor elements. (2) Resistance measurement — use a low-resistance ohmmeter (Ducter or similar). Measured resistance must match nameplate value within tolerance (typically ±10%). (3) Check connections — tight, no corrosion. (4) Check the NER thermal monitor/trip if fitted. Record in maintenance log.

T02_HV.q: How many busbars are there in a standard marine MSB and what is each for?
T02_HV.a: 3 phase busbars (L1, L2, L3) + 1 neutral busbar = 4 total; or split-busbar has 6 phase busbars with bus-tie breaker
opts: 1 busbar only — all three phases on one bar
3 phase busbars (L1, L2, L3) + 1 neutral busbar = 4 total; or split-busbar has 6 phase busbars with bus-tie breaker
2 busbars — one for power, one for lighting
T02_HV.exp: Standard MSB: L1 (Red/Brown), L2 (Yellow), L3 (Blue/Black) = 3 phase busbars. Plus neutral busbar (not earthed — IT system). Total: 4. Split-busbar design: two sets of 3 phase busbars (3+3=6) connected by a normally-open bus-tie breaker. Split design: loss of one generator section doesn't black out the whole ship.

T02_HV.q: What is the minimum front clearance in front of the main switchboard?
T02_HV.a: Minimum 1000 mm (1 metre) — operator working space
opts: 250 mm — just enough to open doors
Minimum 1000 mm (1 metre) — operator working space
T02_HV.exp: SOLAS and class requirements: 1000mm (1m) minimum front clearance for operator access and working space. Rear access (for cable entries, connections): minimum 600mm. Purpose of front clearance: operator must be able to work in front of live switchboard, open panel doors fully, and retreat quickly in emergency.

T02_HV.q: Why does a marine power system use an IT (Insulated Neutral) system rather than earthed neutral?
T02_HV.a: First earth fault does NOT trip the circuit — IRM alarms only, allowing continued operation while fault is traced
opts: IT system is cheaper to install
First earth fault does NOT trip the circuit — IRM alarms only, allowing continued operation while fault is traced
IT system gives better voltage regulation
Earth fault trips immediately — better safety
T02_HV.exp: Ship uses IT (Isolated Terra = insulated neutral): neutral NOT connected to earth. First earth fault: creates a single-point earth reference but circuit still complete (current flows through fault and ship capacitance) → ship can continue operating. IRM detects the fault and alarms → ETO locates and clears the fault. Vital for ship safety — steering, propulsion must not lose power from a single fault.

T02_HV.q: What thickness rubber insulating mat is required in front of the MSB for a 440V system?
T02_HV.a: Minimum 6 mm thick rubber mat rated for the working voltage
opts: Minimum 6 mm thick rubber mat rated for the working voltage
25 mm — same as for HV systems
Rubber mat only required for HV, not 440V
T02_HV.exp: Requirements: 440V systems: minimum 6mm thick rubber insulating mat placed along the full working area in front (and rear where applicable) of the switchboard. HV switchgear (>1000V): minimum 12mm thick mat. Mats must be rated for the voltage class. Purpose: protection against step voltage and shock if live conductor falls to deck. Must cover entire working area.

T02_HV.q: What is a bus-tie breaker and when is it used?
T02_HV.a: Circuit breaker connecting two sections of a split MSB — closed when one generator section is lost to feed loads from remaining section
opts: A breaker that connects the ship to shore power
Circuit breaker connecting two sections of a split MSB — closed when one generator section is lost to feed loads from remaining section
A backup breaker that bypasses the main ACB
A breaker between MSB and emergency switchboard
T02_HV.exp: Split MSB has two sections (A and B) normally fed by separate generators with bus-tie breaker OPEN. Benefits: fault on section A → only section A trips, section B unaffected. Bus-tie CLOSED: allows one generator to supply both sections (reduced capacity). Critical procedure: before closing bus-tie, ensure loads are within single generator capacity, then use preferential trips if needed.

T02_HV.q: What is a 'Permit to Work' (PTW) for HV work and what does it contain?
T02_HV.a: A formal document authorising HV work — identifies circuit, isolation points, earths applied, work description, authorising officer, time limit
opts: A verbal authorisation from the Chief Engineer
A formal document authorising HV work — identifies circuit, isolation points, earths applied, work description, authorising officer, time limit
A checklist for LV work only
T02_HV.exp: PTW for HV: (1) Circuit identified and described. (2) Isolation points listed and confirmed (padlocked, tagged). (3) Earthing applied — where and by whom. (4) Test for dead — confirmed by named person. (5) Work description — what will be done, by whom. (6) PPE required listed. (7) Authorised by responsible officer. (8) Valid time and date range. (9) Return-to-service procedure. Mandatory — no PTW = no HV work.

T02_HV.q: State the 5-step isolation procedure for HV equipment (in correct order).
T02_HV.a: (1) Identify and isolate, (2) Secure against re-energisation (lock/tag), (3) Test for dead, (4) Apply earths, (5) PTW issued
opts: (1) Apply earths, (2) Lock out, (3) Open breaker, (4) Test, (5) Work
(1) Identify and isolate, (2) Secure against re-energisation (lock/tag), (3) Test for dead, (4) Apply earths, (5) PTW issued
(1) Switch off, (2) Begin work immediately, (3) Tag afterward
(1) PTW, (2) Open breaker, (3) Work, (4) Close breaker, (5) Remove PTW
T02_HV.exp: The 5 steps (ISTET): (1) IDENTIFY and ISOLATE — open breaker, rack out to isolated position on all sources. (2) SECURE — padlock all isolation points, apply DANGER tags. (3) TEST for dead — use approved voltage tester on all three phases to earth. (4) EARTH — apply portable earths to discharge capacitance and protect against inadvertent re-energisation. (5) PTW — issue permit, work begins.

T02_HV.q: Why must you always TEST FOR DEAD before working on an apparently isolated HV circuit?
T02_HV.a: Back-feed from other sources, capacitive charge, induced voltage, or human error could leave circuit live despite open breaker
opts: It is not necessary if the breaker is confirmed open
Back-feed from other sources, capacitive charge, induced voltage, or induced EMF, or human error could leave circuit live despite open breaker
Only test for dead on LV — HV breakers are foolproof
Testing for dead is optional if a padlock is applied
T02_HV.exp: An open breaker is NOT a guarantee of dead circuit: (1) Back-feed from another source (paralleled system, transformers). (2) Capacitive charge stored in cables (especially long HV cables). (3) Induced EMF from adjacent live cables. (4) Human error — wrong breaker opened. The voltage tester proves dead on all three phases. Never assume — always test. 'Assume live until proved dead.'

T02_HV.q: Why are portable earths applied AFTER testing for dead, and what is their purpose?
T02_HV.a: Earths discharge stored capacitive charge and protect the working party if circuit is accidentally re-energised
opts: Earths are applied to improve insulation
Earths discharge stored capacitive charge and protect the working party if circuit is accidentally re-energised
Earths are not necessary if testing confirmed dead
Earths are applied before testing — sequence doesn't matter
T02_HV.exp: Purpose of portable earths: (1) Discharge capacitive charge in HV cables (long cables can store significant energy — dangerous). (2) If circuit is accidentally re-energised (breaker closed by error), earth creates a short → protective relays trip immediately → fast protection. Applied as close as possible to the work location. Applied AFTER testing dead — applying before testing risks arc if circuit is live.

T02_HV.q: Who is the 'Authorised Person' in an HV permit system?
T02_HV.a: A senior officer (CE, EO, or designated HV-authorised officer) who has authority to issue permits and confirm isolation
opts: Any engineer who has read the safety manual
A senior officer (CE, EO, or designated HV-authorised officer) who has authority to issue permits and confirm isolation
The person doing the actual work
A shore contractor appointed by the port authority
T02_HV.exp: HV permit systems define roles: Authorised Person (AP): has training and authority to implement isolations, issue permits, confirm dead, and approve return to service. Competent Person (CP): carries out the work under the permit. These must be separate people. On ships: CE or designated EO is typically the AP. The AP has ultimate responsibility for safety of the working party.

T02_HV.q: What colour are Class 2 HV insulating gloves and what is their maximum use voltage?
T02_HV.a: Yellow — max use voltage 17,000V AC (17 kV)
opts: Yellow — max use voltage 17,000V AC (17 kV)
T02_HV.exp: IEC 60903 glove classes: Class 00=beige (500V), Class 0=red (1kV), Class 1=white (7.5kV), Class 2=yellow (17kV), Class 3=green (26.5kV), Class 4=orange (36kV). For a 6.6kV system: Class 2 (yellow) minimum required. For 11kV: Class 3 (green) minimum. Always use the class rated ABOVE the system voltage, not just equal.

T02_HV.q: What colour are Class 3 HV insulating gloves and what voltage are they rated for?
T02_HV.a: Green — maximum use voltage 26,500V AC
T02_HV.exp: Class 3 (green) gloves: rated for systems up to 26.5kV. Required when working on 11kV systems. Remember: Class 2 (yellow) for 6.6kV, Class 3 (green) for 11kV. The class number corresponds to the proof test voltage, not the maximum use voltage directly.

T02_HV.q: How do you inspect HV insulating gloves before use?
T02_HV.a: Roll the cuff to trap air and inflate — check for holes, cracks, leaks; visually inspect for cuts, contamination; check test date
opts: Connect to megger and measure resistance
Roll the cuff to trap air and inflate — check for holes, cracks, leaks; visually inspect for cuts, contamination; check test date
Dip in water and check for bubbles
No inspection needed if stored in approved container
T02_HV.exp: Pre-use inspection: (1) Roll cuff tightly to trap air — inflate glove by squeezing. Any air leaks indicate holes → reject. (2) Visual — check entire outer surface for cuts, abrasions, contamination (oil, solvents). (3) Check date stamp — must be within periodic test interval (typically every 6 months for electrical retesting). (4) Check colour marking matches required class. Reject any glove that fails.

T02_HV.q: Why are leather protectors worn OVER rubber HV insulating gloves?
T02_HV.a: To protect rubber gloves from mechanical damage (puncture, abrasion) — a small hole in rubber glove = complete loss of protection
opts: To protect rubber gloves from mechanical damage (puncture, abrasion) — a small hole in rubber glove = complete loss of protection
Required only for Class 3 and above
T02_HV.exp: The rubber insulating glove provides the electrical insulation — but rubber is easily punctured by sharp edges, metal burrs, or tool corners. A single small hole → electric path through the glove → shock. Leather protectors worn over the rubber gloves shield them from mechanical damage during work. The rubber glove must be intact — the leather is mechanical protection only, not electrical.

T02_HV.q: How often must HV insulating gloves be electrically re-tested?
T02_HV.a: Every 6 months — visual inspection before every use
opts: Every 6 months — visual inspection before every use
T02_HV.exp: IEC 60903: HV insulating gloves must undergo periodic electrical proof testing every 6 months (some class regulations specify different intervals — follow manufacturer and class society requirements). The test involves applying an AC test voltage higher than the use voltage and measuring leakage current. Visual inspection must be done before every single use — no exceptions.

T02_HV.q: What megger voltage is used to test a 6.6kV HV cable or equipment?
T02_HV.a: 5000V DC megger (5kV megger)
T02_HV.exp: Rule: megger voltage ≈ twice the operating voltage. For 6.6kV: use 5kV megger. For 11kV: use 10kV megger. For 440V: use 500V megger. Higher test voltage stresses the insulation more rigorously — reveals marginal insulation that a lower voltage test would pass. Safety: 5kV is lethal — only authorised persons with appropriate PPE.

T02_HV.q: What is the minimum acceptable IR value for a 6.6kV cable or motor winding?
T02_HV.a: Minimum 6.6 MΩ (1 MΩ per kV of working voltage) — in practice new equipment should read hundreds of MΩ
opts: Minimum 6.6 MΩ (1 MΩ per kV of working voltage) — in practice new equipment should read hundreds of MΩ
100 MΩ is the minimum for all HV
50 kΩ minimum — lower due to longer cables
T02_HV.exp: IEC formula: minimum IR = 1 MΩ per kV of rated voltage. For 6.6kV: minimum = 6.6 MΩ. For 11kV: minimum = 11 MΩ. These are absolute minimums — brand new HV equipment should read many hundreds of MΩ. A reading close to the minimum indicates degraded insulation — investigate before returning to service.

T02_HV.q: What is '200% insulation' as asked by surveyors?
T02_HV.a: The measured IR must be at least twice the minimum acceptable value before equipment is returned to service after repair
opts: Insulation rated for double the working voltage
The measured IR must be at least twice the minimum acceptable value before equipment is returned to service after repair
200% means the test voltage is doubled
Insulation has been applied twice during manufacture
T02_HV.exp: '200% insulation' = a practical rule where after repair, the measured IR must be ≥ 2× the minimum standard. For 440V equipment: minimum is 1MΩ, so 200% means ≥ 2MΩ before returning to service. This provides a safety margin above the absolute minimum — ensures the equipment is in genuinely good condition, not just barely acceptable. Common surveyor/class question.

T02_HV.q: How does an Insulation Resistance Monitor (IRM) work on a ship's IT system?
T02_HV.a: Injects low-level voltage between neutral and earth; measures impedance; low impedance = earth fault → alarms
opts: Measures current flow in neutral conductor
Injects low-level voltage between neutral and earth; measures impedance; low impedance = earth fault → alarms
Monitors all phase currents for imbalance
Applies HV test voltage to detect faults
T02_HV.exp: IRM (also called Earth Fault Indicator): The ship's neutral is isolated from earth (IT system). IRM injects a small voltage (1–5V AC or DC) between the neutral point and ship's hull earth. Measures the circuit impedance. Healthy system: very high impedance (good insulation) → no alarm. Earth fault develops: insulation resistance drops → impedance drops → leakage current rises → IRM alarms at threshold (typically 50–100kΩ).

T02_HV.q: What is the IRM alarm threshold on a typical ship's system?
T02_HV.a: Typically 50–100 kΩ — when insulation resistance drops below this, alarm activates
opts: Typically 50–100 kΩ — when insulation resistance drops below this, alarm activates
0 Ω — only alarms on complete short to earth
T02_HV.exp: IRM alarm threshold: 50–100 kΩ. This is much lower than the megger 'minimum IR' because: (1) The IRM monitors continuously under operating conditions (including connected equipment, long cables, moisture). (2) The threshold is set to give early warning while the system can still operate safely. Below threshold → alarm → locate and clear fault before second earth fault occurs (second fault = circuit breaker trip).

T02_HV.q: After IRM alarms, how do you locate which circuit has the earth fault?
T02_HV.a: Switch off non-essential circuits one by one — when IRM clears, the last circuit switched off contains the earth fault
opts: Read the IRM display — it shows the faulty circuit automatically
Switch off non-essential circuits one by one — when IRM clears, the last circuit switched off contains the earth fault
Test each circuit with a voltmeter to earth
T02_HV.exp: IRM locates that an earth fault exists but NOT which circuit. Isolation procedure: (1) Switch off non-essential circuits one by one, monitoring IRM each time. (2) When IRM clears after switching off a particular circuit → that circuit contains the fault. (3) Restore other circuits. (4) Investigate and repair the faulty circuit before returning it to service. (5) If fault must be cleared quickly — use an earth fault locator device that injects a signal and traces it through the system.

T02_HV.q: Why is a SECOND earth fault on a ship's IT system dangerous?
T02_HV.a: Second fault creates a complete fault loop — large fault current flows, circuit breaker trips → could blackout essential services
opts: Second fault makes the IRM more sensitive
Second fault creates a complete fault loop — large fault current flows, circuit breaker trips → could blackout essential services
Second fault is harmless on an IT system
Second fault automatically clears the first fault
T02_HV.exp: IT system: first earth fault → single earth reference established, circuit still operates, IRM alarms. SECOND earth fault on a DIFFERENT phase: now there's a complete fault circuit (Phase A → earth via fault 1 → earth → Phase B via fault 2) → this is effectively a phase-to-phase fault through earth → large fault current → OCR/earth fault relay trips → circuit lost. Two simultaneous earth faults on an IT system = blackout risk for that section. This is why IRM alarm must be responded to immediately.

T02_HV.q: What is the purpose of electrical bonding in a tanker during cargo operations?
T02_HV.a: Equalise electrical potential between ship and jetty to prevent static sparks that could ignite cargo vapour
opts: Provide electrical supply to the jetty
Equalise electrical potential between ship and jetty to prevent static sparks that could ignite cargo vapour
Connect shore power to ship's switchboard
Reduce electrical noise from cargo pumps
T02_HV.exp: Liquid cargo flow creates static electricity (streaming current — friction of liquid through pipes). If ship and jetty are at different potentials → spark at any metal contact point. In a flammable vapour atmosphere → ignition → explosion. Bonding cable connects ship's hull to jetty earth bar → equalises potential → no spark possible. Must be the FIRST thing connected before any cargo equipment.

T02_HV.q: What is the correct sequence for bonding during tanker cargo operations?
T02_HV.a: (1) Connect ship-to-jetty bonding cable FIRST, (2) then connect cargo hose (bond both ends), (3) then begin cargo transfer
opts: (1) Start pumps, (2) connect hose, (3) connect bonding
(1) Connect ship-to-jetty bonding cable FIRST, (2) then connect cargo hose (bond both ends), (3) then begin cargo transfer
Bonding can be connected at any point — timing doesn't matter
T02_HV.exp: Sequence is critical: (1) Ship-to-jetty bonding cable connected FIRST — before any other connection. This ensures no potential difference before any cargo pipework contact. (2) Cargo hose/arm: bond both the ship flange and jetty flange before coupling. (3) Only then — begin transfer. Disconnect in reverse order: stop transfer → disconnect hose → remove bonding cable last.

T02_HV.q: What is the purpose of bonding all metal enclosures of HV equipment to the ship's earth bar?
T02_HV.a: If insulation fails, fault current flows to earth via bonding → protection relays operate → personnel not electrocuted by touching enclosure
opts: Improve electrical efficiency of the equipment
If insulation fails, fault current flows to earth via bonding → protection relays operate → personnel not electrocuted by touching enclosure
T02_HV.exp: Equipment bonding (protective earthing): if HV winding insulation fails and makes contact with the enclosure (motor frame, switchgear panel, cable tray), the enclosure becomes live at HV. Without bonding: touching enclosure = electrocution. With bonding: fault current flows through bond to earth → relay detects fault current → trips circuit immediately. The bonding provides the return path that triggers protection.

T02_HV.q: Why is a shaft earthing system fitted on ships with diesel-electric propulsion or VFDs?
T02_HV.a: Shaft is insulated from hull by oil-film bearings — stray currents from VFD/alternator find path through bearings → electrolytic corrosion
opts: To provide a safety earth for propulsion motor
Shaft is insulated from hull by oil-film bearings — stray currents from VFD/alternator find path through bearings → electrolytic corrosion
To prevent lightning strike damage to propeller
T02_HV.exp: VFDs (Variable Frequency Drives) generate high-frequency common-mode currents. Oil-film in shaft bearings normally insulates — but VFD common-mode currents can create capacitive coupling across the oil film → micro-arc discharge at bearing surfaces → electrolytic pitting → bearing failure. Shaft earthing device (carbon brush on shaft) provides a low-resistance path to hull, bypassing the bearings.

T02_HV.q: How does a shaft earthing device work?
T02_HV.a: Carbon brush rides on a slip ring or smooth section of propeller shaft — provides direct electrical contact from shaft to hull earth
opts: A grounding cable attached to the propeller blades
Carbon brush rides on a slip ring or smooth section of propeller shaft — provides direct electrical contact from shaft to hull earth
An electromagnetic coupling between shaft and hull
A liquid mercury contact system at the stern gland
T02_HV.exp: Construction: carbon brush held in a brush holder mounted on a fixed structure (bearing pedestal or stern tube housing). The brush rides against the rotating shaft surface (or a dedicated shaft slip ring). This creates a continuous electrical path from rotating shaft to stationary hull → shaft maintained at hull potential → no potential difference → no capacitive discharge through bearings.

T02_HV.q: What is the ETO's responsibility regarding the shaft earthing device?
T02_HV.a: Check brush condition and contact, clean slip ring surface, measure shaft-to-hull resistance (should be near 0 Ω), log readings
opts: No ETO responsibility — this is the Chief Officer's job
Check brush condition and contact, clean slip ring surface, measure shaft-to-hull resistance (should be near 0 Ω), log readings
Measure shaft insulation resistance — should be very high
T02_HV.exp: ETO routine maintenance: (1) Inspect carbon brush — check length (replace when worn to minimum length), check spring pressure. (2) Inspect and clean shaft contact surface — should be smooth and bright. (3) Measure shaft-to-hull resistance using a low-resistance ohmmeter — should be <1Ω (near zero). High resistance = brush not making good contact → bearing corrosion risk. Log all readings in PMS.

T03_Motors.q: What is 'slip' in an induction motor?
T03_Motors.a: Difference between synchronous speed and rotor speed, expressed as percentage of synchronous speed
opts: Difference between synchronous speed and rotor speed, expressed as percentage of synchronous speed
T03_Motors.exp: S = (NS − NR)/NS × 100%. At no-load: ~0.5–1%. At full load: 3–5%. At standstill (starting): S=100%.

T03_Motors.q: Synchronous speed formula for induction motor:
T03_Motors.a: NS = 120f/P
T03_Motors.exp: Same as alternator: NS = 120f/P. For 4-pole, 60Hz: 1800 RPM. Rotor turns slower than NS due to slip.

T03_Motors.q: What is the star-delta (Y-Δ) starting method?
T03_Motors.a: Starts motor in star (reduced voltage: 1/√3 of line voltage), then switches to delta at ~80% speed
opts: Starts motor in star (reduced voltage: 1/√3 of line voltage), then switches to delta at ~80% speed
T03_Motors.exp: Star: phase voltage = VL/√3 = 63.5% of delta voltage. Starting current and torque reduced to 1/3 of DOL values. Used for motors ≥15kW typically. Transient current spike on changeover.

T03_Motors.q: What is Direct Online (DOL) starting?
T03_Motors.a: Connecting motor directly to full supply voltage — highest starting current (6–8× FLC)
opts: Connecting motor directly to full supply voltage — highest starting current (6–8× FLC)
T03_Motors.exp: DOL: simplest starting method. Full voltage applied immediately. Starting current: 6–8× FLC. Starting torque: 1.5–2× FLT. Causes voltage dip on busbar. Used for small motors <11kW typically.

T03_Motors.q: What is a VFD (Variable Frequency Drive)?
T03_Motors.a: Electronic drive that controls AC motor speed by varying output frequency and voltage
opts: Electronic drive that controls AC motor speed by varying output frequency and voltage
T03_Motors.exp: VFD: rectifier (AC→DC) → DC link → inverter (DC→variable frequency/voltage AC). Allows smooth speed control from 0 to above synchronous speed. Also called inverter, frequency converter.

T03_Motors.q: What is the advantage of VFD for centrifugal pumps/fans?
T03_Motors.a: Speed control reduces power consumption significantly — power varies as cube of speed
opts: Speed control reduces power consumption significantly — power varies as cube of speed
T03_Motors.exp: Affinity laws: Power ∝ Speed³. Reducing pump speed to 80% reduces power to ~51%. Major energy savings, soft starting, and reduced mechanical wear.

T03_Motors.q: What is a 'soft starter'?
T03_Motors.a: Electronic device that gradually increases voltage to motor on starting, limiting inrush current
opts: Electronic device that gradually increases voltage to motor on starting, limiting inrush current
T03_Motors.exp: Soft starter: thyristors control voltage ramp-up. Limits starting current to 2–4× FLC (vs 6–8× for DOL). No current transient on changeover (unlike star-delta). After motor runs up, bypassed by contactor.

T03_Motors.q: What is 'rotor resistance starting'?
T03_Motors.a: Inserts external resistance in rotor circuit (slip ring motor only) to reduce starting current and increase starting torque
opts: Inserts external resistance in rotor circuit (slip ring motor only) to reduce starting current and increase starting torque
T03_Motors.exp: Slip ring (wound rotor) motor allows external rotor resistance. As motor accelerates, resistance cut out in steps. High starting torque, low starting current — used for hoists, cranes.

T03_Motors.q: What motor type is used for steering gear?
T03_Motors.a: Usually AC induction motor (two-speed or two-motor systems), some ships use DC
opts: Usually AC induction motor (two-speed or two-motor systems), some ships use DC
T03_Motors.exp: Steering gear: typically two AC induction motors (one duty, one standby) per SOLAS requirement. Some designs use direct drive hydraulic with single motor.

T03_Motors.q: What motor protection is provided by a thermal overload relay?
T03_Motors.a: Trips motor on sustained overcurrent (overload), protecting against overheating
opts: Trips motor on sustained overcurrent (overload), protecting against overheating
T03_Motors.exp: Thermal overload relay: bimetallic strips heat with current, trip contacts after set time. Typically set at 100–115% FLC. Has memory (doesn't reset immediately if motor is hot).

T03_Motors.q: What is an MCCB used for?
T03_Motors.a: Moulded Case Circuit Breaker — provides short circuit and overload protection, can be reset after tripping
opts: Moulded Case Circuit Breaker — provides short circuit and overload protection, can be reset after tripping
T03_Motors.exp: MCCB: combined short circuit (magnetic) and overload (thermal) protection. Available in higher ratings than MCB. Used for feeders and large motor circuits.

T03_Motors.q: What is the purpose of a contactor in a motor starter?
T03_Motors.a: Electromechanical switch that makes/breaks motor circuit under load, controlled by pushbutton or relay
opts: Electromechanical switch that makes/breaks motor circuit under load, controlled by pushbutton or relay
T03_Motors.exp: Contactor: heavy-duty relay with silver alloy contacts. Controlled by low-current coil. Auxiliary contacts provide seal-in (self-holding) and interlocking functions.

T03_Motors.q: What is 'motor insulation resistance' and minimum acceptable value?
T03_Motors.a: Resistance between winding and earth; minimum 1 MΩ before starting, measured with 500V megger
opts: Resistance between winding and earth; minimum 1 MΩ before starting, measured with 500V megger
T03_Motors.exp: IR<1MΩ: do not start. Check for moisture, contamination. Can try drying out (space heaters, external heat). If persistent, inspect winding physically.

T03_Motors.q: What is the synchronous speed of a 6-pole motor on 60Hz supply?
T03_Motors.a: 1200 RPM
T03_Motors.exp: NS = 120×60/6 = 1200 RPM. Rotor speed at full load would be ~1160 RPM (about 3.3% slip).

T03_Motors.q: What is the purpose of star point earthing in a motor?
T03_Motors.a: Not typically earthed — motor frame is earthed; star point (neutral) may be left floating
opts: Not typically earthed — motor frame is earthed; star point (neutral) may be left floating
T03_Motors.exp: Motor frame and stator iron are earthed. Stator winding neutral (star point) is typically not connected — internal fault detection done by differential protection on large motors.

T03_Motors.q: What are the safety interlocks on a main motor starter?
T03_Motors.a: Overload relay, undervoltage trip, zero-speed interlock, thermal protection, remote emergency stop
opts: Overload relay, undervoltage trip, zero-speed interlock, thermal protection, remote emergency stop
T03_Motors.exp: Motor safety: overload relay, short circuit fuse/CB, undervoltage coil (drops out on power failure preventing auto-restart), thermal winding protection, emergency stop pushbutton.

T03_Motors.q: What is 'single phasing' in a 3-phase motor?
T03_Motors.a: One phase supply fails — motor draws high current on remaining two phases, causes overheating
opts: Only one phase connected at installation
One phase supply fails — motor draws high current on remaining two phases, causes overheating
T03_Motors.exp: Single phasing: severe overheating in unprotected motors. Running motor may stall under load. Thermal overload relay should detect high current and trip. Negative sequence relay detects asymmetry.

T03_Motors.q: What is the difference between squirrel cage and wound rotor induction motor?
T03_Motors.a: Squirrel cage: short-circuited bars in rotor (simple, low maintenance); Wound rotor: slip rings allow external resistance connection
opts: Squirrel cage: short-circuited bars in rotor (simple, low maintenance); Wound rotor: slip rings allow external resistance connection
Wound rotor used only in DC systems
T03_Motors.exp: Squirrel cage: rugged, low maintenance, most common on ships. Wound rotor (slip ring): allows external rotor resistance for high starting torque applications (winches, cranes, hoists).

T03_Motors.q: What is 'thermal withstand' rating for a motor?
T03_Motors.a: Maximum temperature the motor can sustain without permanent insulation damage
opts: Maximum temperature the motor can sustain without permanent insulation damage
T03_Motors.exp: Thermal withstand depends on insulation class (A,B,E,F,H). Class F: 155°C total, so ambient 40°C + 115°C rise allowed. Exceeding this permanently degrades insulation.

T03_Motors.q: What causes vibration in an electric motor?
T03_Motors.a: Bearing wear, unbalanced rotor, mechanical misalignment, electromagnetic unbalance (uneven air gap), loose parts
opts: Bearing wear, unbalanced rotor, mechanical misalignment, electromagnetic unbalance (uneven air gap), loose parts
T03_Motors.exp: Motor vibration: regular vibration analysis (velocity mm/s or acceleration g) identifies bearing faults (specific frequencies), unbalance, misalignment. ISO 10816 gives vibration limits.

T03_Motors.q: What is the purpose of the motor space heater?
T03_Motors.a: Prevents condensation in windings when motor is stopped, maintaining insulation quality
opts: Prevents condensation in windings when motor is stopped, maintaining insulation quality
T03_Motors.exp: Space heaters (anti-condensation heaters): 50–200W elements inside motor, energised when motor is stopped. Keeps winding temperature slightly above dew point, preventing moisture absorption.

T03_Motors.q: Ward Leonard system — what is it used for?
T03_Motors.a: Precise speed control of DC motors over wide range, especially cranes, winches, steering gear (older ships)
opts: Precise speed control of DC motors over wide range, especially cranes, winches, steering gear (older ships)
T03_Motors.exp: Ward Leonard: AC motor drives DC generator → variable DC voltage → DC motor. Speed control by varying generator field excitation. Smooth, wide range. Largely replaced by modern VFD drives.

T03_Motors.q: What is the efficiency of a typical marine induction motor?
T03_Motors.a: Typically 85–95% at full load
T03_Motors.exp: Motor efficiency depends on size (larger motors more efficient) and loading. Motors should be sized to run at 70–100% of rated load for best efficiency. Running at <40% load is inefficient.

T03_Motors.q: What are the main types of motor enclosures?
T03_Motors.a: ODP (Open Drip-Proof), TEFC (Totally Enclosed Fan Cooled), TEWAC (Totally Enclosed Water-Air Cooled), Ex-protected
opts: ODP (Open Drip-Proof), TEFC (Totally Enclosed Fan Cooled), TEWAC (Totally Enclosed Water-Air Cooled), Ex-protected
T03_Motors.exp: TEFC: most common marine motor — external fan for cooling, no external air enters winding. TEWAC: large motors with internal cooler. Ex-d/e: for hazardous areas.

T03_Motors.q: What is 'stall current' (locked rotor current)?
T03_Motors.a: Starting current when rotor is stationary — typically 6–8 times full load current
opts: Starting current when rotor is stationary — typically 6–8 times full load current
T03_Motors.exp: LRC (Locked Rotor Current) = 6–8× FLC for squirrel cage motors. This causes voltage dip on busbar during DOL starting. Selection of starting method depends on acceptable voltage dip.

T03_Motors.q: What is an autotransformer starter?
T03_Motors.a: Reduces starting voltage using autotransformer taps (65%, 80%) then switches to full voltage
opts: Reduces starting voltage using autotransformer taps (65%, 80%) then switches to full voltage
T03_Motors.exp: Autotransformer starter: better than star-delta as torque reduction is less severe. Voltage taps: 65% gives 42% torque (65²%), 80% gives 64% torque. Suitable for high inertia loads.

T03_Motors.q: In a 3-phase induction motor, what creates the rotating magnetic field?
T03_Motors.a: Three-phase stator currents displaced 120° in time, in stator windings displaced 120° in space
opts: Three-phase stator currents displaced 120° in time, in stator windings displaced 120° in space
T03_Motors.exp: Key principle: 3-phase currents (120° apart in time) in windings 120° apart in space = constant magnitude rotating magnetic field. This rotating field induces rotor currents → torque → rotation.

T03_Motors.q: What is 'power factor' of an induction motor at full load typically?
T03_Motors.a: 0.8–0.9 lagging
T03_Motors.exp: Induction motors: inherently lagging PF due to magnetising current needed to create rotor flux. At no-load: very low PF (0.1–0.3). At full load: 0.8–0.9. PF correction capacitors used to improve system PF.

T03_Motors.q: What is a 'motor management relay'?
T03_Motors.a: Comprehensive protection relay providing overload, earth fault, thermistor, phase failure, locked rotor protection
opts: Comprehensive protection relay providing overload, earth fault, thermistor, phase failure, locked rotor protection
T03_Motors.exp: Modern motor management relays (e.g. ABB SPAM, Siemens 3RW): integrate multiple protections, data logging, communication (Modbus), motor parameter setting — replacing multiple discrete relays.

T03_Motors.q: What is the torque-speed curve characteristic of a squirrel cage induction motor?
T03_Motors.a: High starting torque at low speed, dip at ~80% speed (pull-out torque region), then near constant torque at rated speed
opts: High starting torque at low speed, dip at ~80% speed (pull-out torque region), then near constant torque at rated speed
T03_Motors.exp: Starting torque: 1.5–2× rated. Pull-out (maximum) torque: 2–3× rated (at ~50–80% synchronous speed). Running torque at rated slip: matches load torque.

T04_Switchboard.q: What does ACB stand for?
T04_Switchboard.a: Air Circuit Breaker
T04_Switchboard.exp: ACB is the main generator circuit breaker on the MSB. Interrupts fault current using arc chutes in air.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the function of a preferential trip?
T04_Switchboard.a: Sheds non-essential loads sequentially when generator is overloaded to maintain essential services
opts: Sheds non-essential loads sequentially when generator is overloaded to maintain essential services
T04_Switchboard.exp: Loads shed in pre-set priority: non-essential first (accommodation, galley), then semi-essential, keeping essential services (steering, fire pump, navigation) alive.

T04_Switchboard.q: What does IDMT mean in relay terminology?
T04_Switchboard.a: Inverse Definite Minimum Time — operates faster at higher fault currents
opts: Inverse Definite Minimum Time — operates faster at higher fault currents
T04_Switchboard.exp: IDMT characteristic: trip time inversely proportional to fault current. High fault current = fast trip. Near-rated current = slow trip. Allows grading between upstream/downstream protection.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is 'discrimination' (grading) in protection systems?
T04_Switchboard.a: Ensuring only the nearest upstream protection operates on a fault, leaving other circuits intact
opts: Ensuring only the nearest upstream protection operates on a fault, leaving other circuits intact
T04_Switchboard.exp: Grading: downstream relay/fuse operates first, upstream waits. Achieved by time grading (delay steps upstream) or current grading (higher settings upstream).

T04_Switchboard.q: What is reverse power relay (RPR) and its typical setting?
T04_Switchboard.a: Detects power flowing into generator (motoring); typically set at 2–8% of rated KW
opts: Detects power flowing into generator (motoring); typically set at 2–8% of rated KW
T04_Switchboard.exp: RPR (32 relay): trips ACB when generator becomes motor (prime mover failure). Set low enough to detect, high enough to avoid spurious trips during load swings.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is bus bar protection?
T04_Switchboard.a: Differential protection that trips all generators if fault occurs on the main busbar
opts: Differential protection that trips all generators if fault occurs on the main busbar
T04_Switchboard.exp: Bus bar fault: most severe electrical fault — short circuit at source. Bus bar protection (87B) compares sum of all currents in/out of bus, trips all CBs instantly on imbalance.

T04_Switchboard.q: What type of earthing is used in ship's 440V distribution system?
T04_Switchboard.a: Isolated (IT) — not solidly earthed; allows first fault without immediate trip
opts: Isolated (IT) — not solidly earthed; allows first fault without immediate trip
T04_Switchboard.exp: IT system: neutral isolated from earth. First fault causes no shock current — earth leakage alarm only. Allows crew to trace and fix fault before outage. Second fault = short circuit.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is a 'section breaker' (bus-tie) on the MSB?
T04_Switchboard.a: Breaker connecting two bus sections — allows split bus operation or bus-to-bus connection
opts: Breaker connecting two bus sections — allows split bus operation or bus-to-bus connection
T04_Switchboard.exp: Bus section breaker: normally open (split bus) for fault limitation, or closed (parallel bus) when all generators in parallel. Allows one generator to supply both sections if other fails.

T04_Switchboard.q: How does an earth fault relay detect earth faults on an IT system?
T04_Switchboard.a: Monitors current through earth leakage detector connected between neutral and earth (or core balance CT)
opts: Monitors current through earth leakage detector connected between neutral and earth (or core balance CT)
T04_Switchboard.exp: On IT system: earth fault relay monitors injected current or uses core balance CT. On detection: alarm first (no automatic trip for first fault). Crew must trace and clear fault.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is load shedding?
T04_Switchboard.a: Automatic disconnection of non-essential loads to prevent generator overload and blackout
opts: Automatic disconnection of non-essential loads to prevent generator overload and blackout
T04_Switchboard.exp: Load shedding (PMS function): if total load approaches generator capacity, non-essential loads auto-shed. Prevents overload trip leading to blackout.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the function of the undervoltage relay?
T04_Switchboard.a: Trips load breakers if bus voltage drops below set value, preventing motors from running in undervoltage
opts: Trips load breakers if bus voltage drops below set value, preventing motors from running in undervoltage
T04_Switchboard.exp: UV relay also prevents motors auto-restarting after power restoration (anti-restrike). Critical for coordinated sequential restart after blackout.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is a 'fuse' and how does it differ from a circuit breaker?
T04_Switchboard.a: Fuse: one-time use, melts to break circuit; CB: can be reset after tripping
opts: Fuse: one-time use, melts to break circuit; CB: can be reset after tripping
Fuse is for high voltage only
T04_Switchboard.exp: Fuses: fast, cheap, reliable short circuit protection. No indication of which phase blew (single phase fuse can cause unbalanced supply). CBs: resettable, trip indication, overload protection.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the typical voltage drop allowed from generator to distribution board?
T04_Switchboard.a: 3% maximum from main switchboard to distribution boards
opts: 3% maximum from main switchboard to distribution boards
T04_Switchboard.exp: SOLAS and class rules: maximum 6% total from generator to utilisation equipment (3% to distribution board + 3% to equipment). Cable sizing must account for this.

T04_Switchboard.q: What are the interlocks on a bus-tie (section) breaker?
T04_Switchboard.a: Cannot close if would parallel unsynchronised generators; interlocked with both bus section voltages
opts: Cannot close if would parallel unsynchronised generators; interlocked with both bus section voltages
T04_Switchboard.exp: Bus tie interlocks: if both sections are live, must synchronise before closing tie. Typically auto-synchroniser used. If one section dead (dead bus), close freely.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is a 'moulded case circuit breaker' (MCCB)?
T04_Switchboard.a: Compact CB with thermal-magnetic trip, rated up to 1600A, for feeder and motor circuits
opts: Compact CB with thermal-magnetic trip, rated up to 1600A, for feeder and motor circuits
T04_Switchboard.exp: MCCB: thermal overload (bimetal) + magnetic short circuit protection in moulded case. Ratings 16A–1600A. Used for distribution feeders, motor feeders, sub-panels.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is an earth leakage circuit breaker (ELCB)?
T04_Switchboard.a: Trips on detection of earth leakage current (typically 30mA), protecting against electric shock
opts: Trips on detection of earth leakage current (typically 30mA), protecting against electric shock
T04_Switchboard.exp: RCD/ELCB (30mA): protects persons from electric shock. 30mA threshold: safe for most humans. Trip time <30ms. Used in accommodation, galley, workshop — areas with personnel exposure.

T04_Switchboard.q: What maintenance is done on main switchboard ACBs?
T04_Switchboard.a: Inspect contacts for wear/burning, clean arc chutes, test trip mechanism, check connection torques, test relays
opts: Inspect contacts for wear/burning, clean arc chutes, test trip mechanism, check connection torques, test relays
No maintenance required for solid state
T04_Switchboard.exp: ACB PM: contact resistance measurement, insulation resistance test, mechanical operation test, relay calibration verification, arc chute inspection/cleaning, thermal imaging under load.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the purpose of current limiting fuses (HRC fuses)?
T04_Switchboard.a: Limit let-through current during fault — clear fault before peak current is reached
opts: Limit let-through current during fault — clear fault before peak current is reached
T04_Switchboard.exp: HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuses: clear fault in <5ms, before fault current reaches peak. Used to protect downstream equipment from high fault levels. Non-resettable.

T04_Switchboard.q: How do you test a reverse power relay?
T04_Switchboard.a: Inject test current/voltage from secondary injection test set, verify trip at set percentage of rated power
opts: Inject test current/voltage from secondary injection test set, verify trip at set percentage of rated power
T04_Switchboard.exp: Relay testing: secondary injection (inject into relay secondary terminals without primary current). Check trip time and current setting. Log results. Annual testing recommended.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the significance of the MSB being of 'dead front' construction?
T04_Switchboard.a: No live parts accessible from front — all live connections behind panels, operator protected from accidental contact
opts: No live parts accessible from front — all live connections behind panels, operator protected from accidental contact
T04_Switchboard.exp: Dead front construction: SOLAS requirement. Operators work at front panel with only instrument faces, meter terminals, control switches exposed. All bus bars, cable connections behind steel panels.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the 'tie breaker' and when is it used?
T04_Switchboard.a: Section breaker connecting two MSB bus sections — closed when running all generators in parallel
opts: Section breaker connecting two MSB bus sections — closed when running all generators in parallel
T04_Switchboard.exp: Split bus operation (tie open): generators feed sections independently — fault on one section doesn't affect other. Parallel bus operation (tie closed): all generators in parallel, more flexible load sharing.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is a current transformer (CT) and its secondary current?
T04_Switchboard.a: Transformer that steps down high current to standard 5A (or 1A) for instrumentation and protection
opts: Transformer that steps down high current to standard 5A (or 1A) for instrumentation and protection
T04_Switchboard.exp: CTs: ratio e.g. 1000:5. Primary: bus/feeder conductor. Secondary: 5A to relays, meters. Never open CT secondary when primary energised — dangerous overvoltage across open terminals.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is a potential transformer (PT/VT)?
T04_Switchboard.a: Steps down high voltage to standard 110V (or 100V) for voltage measurement and protection relays
opts: Steps down high voltage to standard 110V (or 100V) for voltage measurement and protection relays
T04_Switchboard.exp: PT/VT ratio e.g. 440:110. Primary across bus. Secondary: 110V to voltmeters, synchroscope, relays, AVR sensing. Short circuiting PT secondary is dangerous — near short circuit of primary voltage source.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the 'closing coil' and 'trip coil' in an ACB?
T04_Switchboard.a: Closing coil: solenoid that closes breaker contacts; Trip coil: solenoid that opens contacts on relay command
opts: Closing coil: solenoid that closes breaker contacts; Trip coil: solenoid that opens contacts on relay command
T04_Switchboard.exp: Closing coil: pulsed to close breaker (from control switch or auto-sync). Trip coil: pulsed by protection relay to open breaker. Both require control power (110V DC or 24V DC typically).

T04_Switchboard.q: What is 'arc flash' hazard?
T04_Switchboard.a: Release of enormous energy when fault current arcs through air — causes severe burns, blindness, pressure wave
opts: Release of enormous energy when fault current arcs through air — causes severe burns, blindness, pressure wave
T04_Switchboard.exp: Arc flash energy (cal/cm²) depends on fault current and clearing time. PPE: arc-rated face shield and clothing (cal/cm² rated). NFPA 70E/IEC 61482: defines arc flash PPE categories.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the purpose of the 'closing resistor' in some circuit breakers?
T04_Switchboard.a: Reduces switching overvoltage on closing by inserting resistance momentarily
opts: Reduces switching overvoltage on closing by inserting resistance momentarily
T04_Switchboard.exp: Pre-insertion resistor (mostly HV CBs): resistor briefly inserted before main contacts touch, limits overvoltage transient. Removed from circuit after a few ms.

T04_Switchboard.q: What does 'short circuit level' mean for switchgear?
T04_Switchboard.a: Maximum fault current the switchgear can interrupt safely — rated in kA
opts: Maximum fault current the switchgear can interrupt safely — rated in kA
T04_Switchboard.exp: Switchgear kA rating: must exceed prospective short circuit current at installation point. Ships typically: 440V MSB rated 30–60kA. Calculated from generator subtransient reactance.

T04_Switchboard.q: How is the MSB earthed?
T04_Switchboard.a: Frame/structure earthed to ship's hull; distribution system neutral NOT solidly earthed (IT system)
opts: Frame/structure earthed to ship's hull; distribution system neutral NOT solidly earthed (IT system)
T04_Switchboard.exp: MSB metalwork: earthed to hull for safety. Neutral/distribution: isolated. Allows earth fault alarm without immediate trip.

T04_Switchboard.q: What records are kept for switchboard protection systems?
T04_Switchboard.a: Relay settings, test records, fault records, maintenance history — in logbook and PMS
opts: Relay settings, test records, fault records, maintenance history — in logbook and PMS
T04_Switchboard.exp: Good record keeping: enables verification of settings during surveys, trend analysis of faults, demonstrates compliance. Class surveyor may request test records.

T04_Switchboard.q: What is the purpose of synchronising lamps (check sync lamps)?
T04_Switchboard.a: Indicate phase relationship between incoming and bus voltage — used as backup to synchroscope
opts: Indicate phase relationship between incoming and bus voltage — used as backup to synchroscope
T04_Switchboard.exp: Bright/dark method: lamps connected phase-to-phase. All dark at synchronism. Used if synchroscope fails. Must also check voltage and frequency match independently.

T05_Transformers.q: What is the turns ratio of a transformer?
T05_Transformers.a: Ratio of primary to secondary turns; also equals ratio of primary to secondary voltage
opts: Ratio of primary to secondary turns; also equals ratio of primary to secondary voltage
T05_Transformers.exp: N1/N2 = V1/V2 = I2/I1. Step-down: N1>N2, V1>V2. Step-up: N1<N2, V1<V2. Power (VA) is conserved (minus losses).
